DebugBear, a Real User Monitoring tool widely used by SEO experts, reported an attack. Site owners must remove its script and check for unauthorized access.

Who this affects: This security alert concerns website owners using DebugBear’s Real User Monitoring script.

DebugBear told customers to remove its Core Web Vitals monitoring script. Site owners should also check exposed accounts and unauthorized changes.

If your website uses DebugBear’s Real User Monitoring script to track Core Web Vitals, remove it now. The company issued that instruction on October 29 after reporting a security incident involving its infrastructure.

Example of the embed code to remove. The script ID varies by site:

SEO teams should flag this to their development and security teams, who should remove the script and investigate any unauthorized access or changes made while it was active.

In a follow-up update, DebugBear said attackers compromised its DNS records through its domain registrar. DebugBear said its initial investigation showed that the attack targeted one customer’s website. It reported no indication that its internal systems had been compromised.

In the same update, DebugBear said it could not receive email sent to its domain. Customers can follow updates on DebugBear’s X account.

Cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock’s analysis found malicious JavaScript at a DebugBear script URL used by Polymarket on October 29. The code sought the trading client already available in a logged-in browser. Polymarket’s October 30 incident report confirmed that the script sold positions and moved funds from some users’ wallets. It used the access a signed-in visitor already had and did not need the user’s password.

That is the concern for other site owners: what could malicious code do with the permissions of a visitor who is already signed in?

I would have the development and security teams take these steps:

The retrieved payload targeted Polymarket’s trading accounts. Attackers used the compromised DebugBear script to reach this high-value target and stole funds. Other high-value websites may have been targeted as well. It is not yet clear whether other DebugBear customers also received malicious code.

Removing the monitoring tag prevents new loads. It does not reverse unauthorized actions or remove anything an attacker may already have planted.

#7564. In the AI age, publishers who understand what readers want will do best, a new report argues

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

AI inverts the traditional journalism hierarchy: Instead of reporters gathering information, editors deciding how to present it, and newsrooms releasing the same final story to everyone, AI agents deliver what readers ask for, refining or expanding on information as requested.

It’s “an interactive process in a way the current news system isn’t,” write the authors of “The Three-Layer Cake: Public-Interest Information in an AI-Intermediated Age,” released Wednesday by the Tow-Knight Center for Journalism Futures at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at CUNY. (The cake’s three layers are “the products that identify what people want to know, the systems that synthesize answers, and the organizations that produce the underlying reporting.”)

Some interesting ideas from the report by Gina Chua and Adiel Kaplan:

This new age may be better for some readers. The authors write:

There are people the old system never reached, or never reached well. A parent who hears of school budget cuts may want to know if their child’s elementary school art class will survive. No newsroom would assign that story. It matters to a handful of families whose children attend a single school, and the exact answer is uncertain. A well-designed AI system could pull together what is known from reporting and context and offer a nuanced response — fulfilling an information need that previously did not have enough economic power to be met directly.

Similarly, minority communities whose concerns didn’t rise to the level of interest of a city newspaper might have rarely seen their perspectives reflected in coverage in the past. Coverage in the mainstream media of the AIDS epidemic in the early 1980s was often focused on the risk to the heterosexual population rather than on the gay community it ravaged. An AI system that can access information from and about underserved communities could rectify that.

Publishers opting out could make the information environment worse. If news organizations seek to prevent AI from using their content, they may contribute to a poorer “information commons,” the authors argue. It “works as a strategy for individual organizations, but cedes the broader mission of providing information to the vast majority of the public to others who may not have the public’s interests at heart.”

Scoops and exclusives are a “luxury” — and they’re losing value fast.

Even a pivot to investigative reporting, as important a public good as that is, is not necessarily a solution. Much of investigative journalism is summarizable once it is published, even if the original story breaks important news and is a delight to read. As Francesco Marconi noted, a multi-month investigation could cost a newsroom $200,000 in resources, then drop in economic value to close to zero within minutes of publication. Both investigations and scoops can have huge social value and help build a brand, but economically, they provide little lasting value to their newsrooms — and even less so in an AI-intermediated landscape. “Commoditized news” isn’t saving anyone. Publishers have to make “hard choices” about what they’ll cover, the authors write: In an AI-intermediated world, commoditized news carries little value, especially if it’s already available in some other form. That’s not to say that day-to-day coverage of municipal government, a core task of many local newsrooms, should go away; only that its coverage needs to be differentiated from what could be found elsewhere or summarized from a meeting transcript, for it to hold value. Differentiation might involve adding context to the coverage through original reporting, or asking questions that wouldn’t otherwise be asked at a press conference. The deeper and more specialized a newsroom’s area of coverage and expertise is, the less likely it is to be duplicated by other organizations — and that provides both pricing power and closer links to the communities that value such information.

The deeper and more specialized a newsroom’s area of coverage and expertise is, the less likely it is to be duplicated by other organizations — and that provides both pricing power and closer links to the communities that value such information.

#7562. Google, Microsoft & OpenAI Plan To Honor Shared AI Training Opt-Out via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

A shared robots.txt line could let sites opt out of AI training with several providers at once, but companies involved are handling it differently.

Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI announced plans on Friday to honor a shared robots.txt line for AI training preferences. A site could use it to state one training preference to every provider that takes part, instead of writing rules for each company’s crawler.

The line is from an Internet Draft that Anthropic’s Kevin Kelley submitted to the AI Preferences working group at the IETF (same date). This is listed in the IETF’s document tracker as an individual draft, which does not represent official IETF standardization activity. In a post to the working group’s email list, Kelley indicated that Anthropic has started development to provide this feature.

Based on their provided timelines, none of the three companies currently supports the line. Google and Microsoft described how each would handle it differently. According to Google, if a site sets up a shared opt-out line, Google plans to treat it like a Google-Extended block when a website doesn’t specify Google-Extended, and this control also applies to grounding within Gemini Apps. Microsoft wants sites that use its NoArchive and NoCache tags to switch to new preferences by March 1, 2027.

Kelley’s draft adds no new directive to robots.txt. An ordinary rule group, that a site might write under what the draft calls a policy token, __usage_ai-training, would be written like it always has been, using Allow and Disallow. The draft provides an example of how one might opt out of AI training on the entire site, except for the /press-kit/ folder.

The token itself has its meaning based upon the working group’s vocabulary draft, specifically defining AI Training as using content to modify a generative AI model’s learned parameters. Those models that do nothing but non-generative tasks like classification or ranking are exempted from this definition.

Rules that have already been put into robots.txt files will not be considered as part of any shared training preference. In the draft, a wildcard group (User-Agent: *) can never match the token, and a file without a __usage_ai-training group indicates no preference, which Kelley states is true of every robots.txt file currently published. The token doesn’t control crawling either.

On Oct. 22, I covered a different working group draft, co-written by Google’s Gary Illyes, that would add a Content-Usage rule to robots.txt. Kelley wrote that the group set that draft aside to make progress on the vocabulary.

Google’s post, by John Mueller, says that when a site opts out of training with the shared line and doesn’t specify Google-Extended, Google plans to interpret that “as if the publisher had disallowed Google-Extended.” Google aims to support the control in 2027, according to the post, and its crawler documentation says early 2027.

The documentation says Google-Extended controls whether content can be used to train future Gemini models and whether it can be used for grounding in Gemini Apps and on Vertex AI. Grounding, in Google’s description, means supplying content from the search index to the model when it answers. The post adds that sites that specifically allow Google-Extended are eligible to appear in Gemini Apps responses through grounding.

The documentation also says Google-Extended doesn’t affect a site’s inclusion in Google Search. AI Overviews and AI Mode have a separate opt-out, the Search generative AI control in Search Console, which I covered when it rolled out worldwide in August.

Microsoft’s post, by Bing principal product manager Krishna Madhavan, adopts the shared line for training and adds a separate AI Grounding preference. That one is set only at the page level and governs whether content can help inform AI-generated answers. Microsoft also lets a meta tag or HTTP header set the training preference for a single page, overriding robots.txt for that page.

A default of Allow is what happens with grounding, and keeping a page out is how Disallow works. The new option called DisallowExtended allows grounding in Microsoft created tools like Copilot and Bing’s AI Mode but does not allow grounding through Microsoft provided grounding services that are used by other businesses (Web IQ). Microsoft said either restriction will limit visibility of your brand in answers using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and will have no effect on your ability to be listed in search results from Bing.

Microsoft is replacing NoArchive and NoCache for training and grounding with these two new options. They will begin honoring the new options on February 1, 2027, as they crawl, and they will stop recognizing the older tags as training or grounding options after March 1, 2027.

Sites that use the old tags and want to stay out of grounding also need to record a temporary preference in Bing Webmaster Tools. The setting opens Dec. 15 and is available only to sites still using those tags on that date. Microsoft’s FAQ says pages without one by March 1 default to allowing grounding until Microsoft recrawls them. Microsoft also says that once it detects either new preference on a site, it will disregard any NoArchive or NoCache tags still on that site.

OpenAI aims to honor the signal in the next few months, though its current robots.txt policy will still be in effect.

Neither OpenAI’s blog post nor its crawler documentation (checked Oct. 30) states what would happen when a website has both a shared line rule and GPTBot rule that conflict with each other.

As of Oct. 30, there was no posting in Anthropic’s newsroom regarding the signal. According to Kelley’s mailing list message, implementing support for this feature across all of Anthropic’s services will take some time.

According to Anthropic’s crawler-help webpage (checked Oct. 30), they have only three crawl control options available, which are ClaudeBot, Claude-User, and Claude-SearchBot.

One robots.txt group could replace a stack of per-company training rules once each company reads it; however, an opt-out through the shared line won’t reach the same uses at Google and Microsoft. For example, at Microsoft, training and grounding are separate settings. In contrast, both sit under Google-Extended at Google, and there is no way described in the crawler documentation to keep content out of Gemini training while still letting Gemini Apps use it for grounding.

Microsoft’s is the only announcement that replaces controls sites already use. According to Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic’s Kelley, existing controls will continue to work, so sites that use NoArchive or NoCache to limit how Copilot uses their content have things they need to do first.

OpenAI’s post encourages other AI providers to honor the signal, and Kelley wrote that he hopes others will join. Google and OpenAI say they’ll share more details as their support arrives. Kelley’s draft expires May 3, 2027, unless a new version replaces it, and he plans to propose his design as a change to the Content-Usage draft.

#7560. The Ringer bets on Substack’s network over its own website

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Once synonymous with independent writers, Substack is increasingly home to established publishers.

“Very interesting that The Ringer’s writers write on Substack and not…The Ringer.” “What’s the point of the website then?” “Hold up. You’re telling me The Ringer would rather make money on writing than not make money on writing?”

These were some of the responses after The Ringer’s Zach Lowe announced his new newsletter. The Lowe Post, which covers the NBA, joins The Ringer’s Sean Fennessey, Tom Pelissero, and Bryan Curtis on Substack. (The Lowe Post is $10 a month, and has already become one of Substack’s bestselling sports newsletters. Fennessey’s newsletter is $5 a month; Pelissero’s is $8 a month, and Curtis’s is free.)

Though podcasting has been his main gig for a while now, Zach Lowe is one of the best sports writers in the country — witty, warm-hearted, and a true lover of basketball and the Mets. In his inaugural newsletter, he wrote about how he feels his sports analysis loses a step when he’s only talking, not writing.

On the one hand, of course Lowe should have a newsletter. But his Substack, and those of his colleagues, are not independent side hustles. Each has Spotify and The Ringer branding.

As a digital media business, The Ringer has always been flexible and opportunistic. It was initially published on Medium when it launched in 2016. The publication moved to an ad and tech partnership with Vox in 2017. It was acquired by Spotify for $250 million in 2020 and, five years later, signed a distribution deal with Netflix to bring some of its video podcasts (including The Bill Simmons Show, The Zach Lowe Show, and The Rewatchables) to the platform. The website has always been free to read.

The Ringer declined to comment on its Substack strategy and would not tell me whether the writers receive a share of subscription revenue. (The lack of comment has garnered its own press coverage.) Though The Ringer has referred to the new newsletters as being in “partnership” with Substack, there’s no separate financial relationship between the two companies, Substack confirmed.

If you find this a little strange, you’re not wrong. The Substack-Ringer whatever-this-is is a confusing move that is raising a lot of very 2026 questions. Here are some things I’m wondering.

While Grantland — the beloved sports writing site created by Ringer founder Bill Simmons in 2011 and shuttered by ESPN in 2015 — was known for its long-form journalism, The Ringer is all-in on podcasts. Simmons jokes on nearly every episode of his own show that his “fingers stopped working” years ago and that his days writing columns are behind him.

Today, most of the links on The Ringer’s homepage will bring you somewhere else. The homepage’s function is closer to a landing page or linktree than a news website. Many links redirect to Spotify, where listeners can watch or listen to Ringer podcasts. Now, with the newsletter launches, several links whisk you off The Ringer and over to Substack.

Burned by Facebook and forever-shifting algorithmic winds, many publishers have focused on building on their own channels in recent years. The theory is that direct-to-reader news products like newsletters, apps, and events will help publishers control audience connections and insulate them from inevitable platform pivots.

But though Substack was once synonymous with independent writers, its perks are luring more and more established publications onto the platform. Some, like The Ringer, are sharing Substack-exclusive content. Others, like New York magazine and The Wall Street Journal, are redistributing work that exists elsewhere on the internet.

One major pull? Substack has morphed into a full-on social media platform, albeit one where publishers can directly monetize and capture email addresses for themselves.

In the past six months, the app has generated nearly 800,000 paid subscriptions, according to Substack, and more than half of those subscriptions came directly from its Twitter-like Notes feed. Network effects account for more than half of all subscriptions on the platform and about 30% of paid subscriptions, a spokesperson said.

Media journalist Simon Owens has been tracking the rise of traditional media outlets on Substack (on Substack, naturally).

“Open web” is an ill-defined concept. Sometimes people use it to mean the public portion of the internet that’s indexable by search engines. Others mean, basically, websites — anything you can reach on a web browser at a URL. Whatever the semantics, people have been shoveling dirt on “the open web” for years. (This New York Times obituary noting the rise of paywalls, apps, and tiers of access was published back in 2010.) But the death notices have picked up with the rise of AI.

RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026Google Search referrals to publisher websites are down 40.2% year over year, according to Chartbeat. And AI chatbots are not sending users to news sites. Referrals from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and the like were just 0.01% of traffic to publishers and declining, Chartbeat found.

Even before it was acquired by Spotify, The Ringer’s primary business was podcasts, so it’s never been as reliant on search as text-first publishers. The Ringer can afford to deprioritize its website more than most. But all kinds of publishers are having to respond to a real shift in the way people consume news and content.

RELATED ARTICLEWhat’s it take to make a great daily newsletter? Axios’ Kendall Baker is planning to bring one to Yahoo SportsJoshua BentonAugust 17, 2023Kendall Baker, senior writer and head of newsletters for Yahoo Sports, knows a thing or two about email newsletters. He says The Ringer’s move exemplifies a news consumption trend that’s only picking up speed.

“Most people’s general way of finding information or consuming information online is that they’re opening their phone and going straight to a social media app and starting to scroll,” Baker said.

Another app that most U.S. adults open up every day? Their email.

“If I want an engaged audience on a daily basis, relying on them coming to find me versus going to them would be silly — and it’s becoming more and more silly,” he said. “I think that’s partially what’s driving this. Newsletters are an obvious solution there.”

The Ringer’s move is also a bet on the strength of individual personalities. Substack doesn’t (yet) offer bundles, so a reader who wants all of The Ringer’s paid Substack content will have to fork over something like $23/month — more than a subscription to New York magazine or Apple News and a little less than a full New York Times bundle. Even with the strong parasocial relationships The Ringer enjoys — enough to fuel many, many subreddits — the pricing was a common complaint online.

Many publishers will not want to cannibalize pricier subscriptions by selling access to a single popular writer. Offering a whole-site subscription also lets readers discover (and hopefully fall in love with!) more of your content.

“It seems in the Substack era, you’re writing for people who really like you,” Simmons said on a recent podcast about sportswriting. “And you’re getting that audience but then, how do you pull other people in? That’s going to be the big question over the next five to 10 years.”

“Obviously we have a lot of writing on The Ringer dot com that we’re very proud of,” Simmons added, pointing to a NFL Take-O-Meter piece by The Ringer’s Austin Gayle. “But will it ever be like 2011 again? I don’t know.”

“You mean, when we launched Grantland?” The Ringer’s Bryan Curtis asked.

“No, just that era. How many writers were coming up — the energy behind it, and all the different styles,” Simmons said. “I wonder if we’ll ever have that many writers again trying that many different things.”

The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Google's John Mueller cast doubt on short-term AI SEO tactics and explained that traditional technical SEO remains relevant.

In a recent interview conducted by David Iwanow, Google’s John Mueller discussed the future of SEO in AI Search, explaining which traditional practices will continue to matter and that the rise of AI Search doesn’t necessarily change what makes a successful SEO strategy.

The interviewer asked John Mueller about listicles. Listicles are like lists of “top companies” that have been used by companies as a way to influence AI chatbots to rank the company creating the listicle as the top choice in their industry. The interviewer acknowledged their usefulness in general but also pointed out that they’ve also been abused and turned into slop content.

Mueller responded that building a solid foundation for a website is preferable to relying on short-term tactics because those always have an expiration date, whereas a site that focuses on quality, what Mueller terms a solid foundation, doesn’t face that kind of expiration date where traffic disappears.

“I think, when I take a step back, like this happens all the time, right? It’s like something comes out and people realize, oh, this actually works particularly well. And then everyone goes off and does it and half the people go off and do it in a particularly bad way.

And then at some point the systems catch up and they’re like, oh, anything that has a listicle is a sign that it’s spam. And it’s like the circle closes and you find something else.

From that point of view, I wouldn’t necessarily say anything that is a listicle is spam.

…It needs to add value. And I think it’s really important to keep in mind that all of these systems are very new, meaning they’re still very much evolving very quickly.

So if you go all out and say, my whole strategy is listicles, then at some point that’s going to switch off and you’re left with nothing really.

Building up a serious, stable foundation for a website, I think that’s the most critical part. And if there are ways that you can play around with some things along the way?

Try things out, maybe that’s fine. But I think you really need to focus on that end goal of having something that search engines and AI systems will want to show to people in the long run.”

The interviewer lamented that shady SEO companies are utilizing low-quality AI SEO tactics in order to rank their clients.

Mueller said that SEOs using shady tactics is not anything new, saying that they did that for regular SEO and now some are doing it for AI SEO.

Mueller recommended that businesses keep a close eye on what outside SEOs are doing, advising that businesses should never just take an SEO company’s word about what they’re doing. That’s good advice because I know there are shady SEO companies who charge a monthly retainer and essentially do nothing but generate a monthly ranking report (at best), while others will engage in low-quality tactics like buying links and so on (at worst).

“But that’s always been the case, right? It’s like you’re paying consultants and they do, I don’t know, keyword stuffing. Or back in the early days, it’s like white text on white background.

And it’s like, it works for a bit, but at some point, it doesn’t work. So I think as a small business, you have to always question what your vendors are doing and always think about..”

Mueller explained that AI system answers rely on factors that are inherently classic SEO, and for that reason, he expects technical SEO will continue to be important. Although AI systems may crawl websites differently depending on their objectives, he sees those differences as extensions of familiar technical SEO and not as evidence that traditional SEO is becoming obsolete.

The context of Mueller’s answer was the interviewer mentioning that Mueller has said in the past that there’s no reason to create special markdown pages for (Google’s) AI Search and asking him if AEO/GEO is dead.

“I think you’ll see that a lot of the AI systems, they build on SEO. So from that point of view, I think it’s going to continue to be relevant. I think especially technical SEO is going to remain very relevant.

It’ll be a little bit different because my understanding is AI systems crawl slightly differently. They have different intents with regards to crawling because they want to do it for training versus just like getting the freshest content. But that’s just is like another flavor of technical SEO. So I think that’s great.”

Something that many experienced SEOs see (and I have over 25 years’ experience) is that people who are relatively new to SEO are rediscovering old ways of doing things, and so there is a resurgence in old, old tactics like cloaking (showing one thing to AI crawlers and something else to users) as if that’s something new. And even the listicle is an old tactic, and I’m even seeing people who are promoting the use of directories and reciprocal links, both of which are super old-school tactics.

Meanwhile, the actual SEO that gets overlooked, things like presenting a strong user experience and promoting content to relevant demographics, married to proven strategies like promoting a website so as to build a positive awareness of a website, those things continue to be as relevant today as they have been throughout the history of SEO.

I have 25 years hands-on experience in SEO, evolving along with the search engines by keeping up with the latest ...

#7557. Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the company’s new commercial terms of service, set to go into effect on October 30.

In an open letter to Zuckerberg published Thursday, News/Media Alliance’s president and CEO Danielle Coffey wrote that Meta should “withdraw these terms and should hold discussions around future changes with NMA and publishers.”

The terms, first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15, would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. There is currently no option to opt out. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping.

“News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation,” Coffey said in her letter. “It is wholly unreasonable for the mere use of a Meta business account to require publishers to grant unrestricted access to their websites (and even content posted by their users), for the benefit of Meta to develop its business products.”

NMA represents more than 2,000 news publishers in the United States. The discussions, Coffey said, should focus on four core issues:

(i) the specific Meta Company Products and uses for which Meta would like to use publishers’ scraped content;

(ii) how publishers can opt in to permit scraping, separate from obtaining access to Meta’s business products;

(iii) the specific crawlers, fetchers, or other bots that will be utilized;

(iv) how Meta will ensure publishers’ robots.txt files, registration walls, or paywalls are respected.

Coffey requested a public response from Zuckerberg to the letter by October 26, and noted that if “in the event Meta adopts these revised terms over our members’ express objections, our members do not consent to them and reserve all of their legal rights.”

The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on Thursday, while adding its concern about Meta’s implementation of its new subscription service, Meta One, which requires users to pay a fee to post links on Meta platforms. WAN-IFRA’s membership spans 20,000 publishers in 120 countries around the world.

The Center for Media and Digital Governance (CMDG) at the Open Markets Institute published its own statement on Thursday, saying that regulators in the United States should take immediate action to “stop Meta from exploiting publishers around the world.”

“If Meta gets away with this, every dominant technology company will have a blueprint for doing the same,” said CMDG director Courtney Radsch. “Regulators have an opportunity to draw a line now, before the next generation of AI monopolies is built on the uncompensated work of journalists, publishers, and creators.”

On Thursday morning, the Movement for an Open Web (MOW) — a U.K. nonprofit organization that advocates for an accessible internet — filed formal complaints with the U.K. Competition and Markets Authority and the European Commission’s Directorate General for Competition, calling the terms “unfair,” and “exploitative” and saying they “threaten to cause immediate and irreparable harm to businesses.”

“The terms go live in a few days’ time, and once they’re in force the damage will be done — you can’t unscrape that content,” said Tim Cowen, a MOW cofounder.

MOW’s complaints follow comments from CMA executive director for digital markets Will Hayter, who said during a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday that he had sent a letter to Meta and scheduled a meeting with company representatives to learn more about the terms. In Germany, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers also sent a joint letter to the European Commission, calling on the institution to block the new terms from going into effect until it conducted a complete review.

On Wednesday, four European press associations — the European Magazine Media Association, the European Newspaper Publishers’ Association, the European Press Council, and News Media Europe — sent a joint letter to the European Commission and its heads of technology and competition. The letter, viewed by Nieman Lab, claims that Meta’s new terms violate the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

The joint letter calls on the Commission to block the terms from “taking effect in their current wording — or in any wording producing identical or similar effects — to safeguard publishers’ rights.”

“Publishers, whose content has long been subject to sweeping unfair and unlawful exploitation by dominant gatekeepers, including for AI-related purposes, thus face an unacceptable choice: abandon a key distribution channel or consent to the exploitation of their professional content without negotiation, licensing and remuneration,” the letter reads. “These conditions could also undermine publishers’ rights in ongoing or future AI-related legal proceedings.”

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026The Association of Information Media (AMI) in Spain, which represents more than 100 news outlets in the country, echoed its support of the letter in a statement on Thursday.

“Technological innovation and the development of artificial intelligence cannot come at the expense of content creators’ rights or the economic viability of professional journalism,” the AMI statement reads in part. “Defending publishers’ rights does not mean hindering innovation, but rather ensuring that it develops while respecting the law, competition, and media pluralism.”

#7555. Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Meta’s new commercial terms will go into effect three weeks later than initially planned.

RELATED ARTICLELegal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesAndrew DeckOctober 17, 2026Meta has delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20 in the face of mounting pressure from the global news industry.

Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15. They would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. Virtually every news organization has at least one business account. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.”

The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30, with no way to opt out, setting off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic.

“We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

As of October 23, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No versions of the terms include language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

“Publishers should always be concerned about tech companies attempting to take content for free, and should assume that Meta is taking this additional time to either find a new way to try to mislead publishers into granting Meta free access to valuable copyrighted content or finally give up in the face of pressure,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “Publishers don’t need more PR statements or explanations. They need Meta to keep its hands off their copyrighted material and respect publishers’ terms of service.”

“I don’t think that repeating the same non-explanations for another three weeks will make much difference,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, added. “But maybe they’ll use the time to come up with better explanations.”

Thomas Höppner, a professor and attorney specializing in competition law in Germany, told Nieman Lab that “Meta’s conduct constitutes a prima facie infringement of European Union competition law, and a textbook case for imposing interim measures.”

The postponement could be a legal strategy that the company is exploring, he said.

“My fear is that this is merely a measure by Meta to reduce the risk of court actions for interim measures,” Höppner said. “If affected parties wait too long from the day of knowledge of the changes [until] the filing of an action, a court will assume that the matter cannot be urgent — and deny interim relief on this ground…Under some jurisdictions, a platform needs to give business users appropriate warning before implementing measures. It may well be that Meta just tries to reduce the risk of losing on the ground not having sufficiently informed business users about its new terms.”

News publishers and press associations have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect, and on Meta to include specific language about respecting publishers’ crawling preferences.

On Thursday, the News/Media Alliance in the United States sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, demanding that the company suspend the terms before October 30. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on the same day.

Multiple European press associations signed a joint letter to the European Commission, citing potential violations of the Digital Markets Act and calling for intervention. Earlier this week, two German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review has been conducted.

In the United Kingdom, the Competition and Market Authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss the terms. In a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday, executive director Will Hayter said he had a meeting scheduled with the company on Wednesday to learn more about the terms.

“The CMA has been in urgent discussions with Meta this week on this important issue,” a CMA spokesperson said on Friday. “Meta has now paused implementation until 20 November. We will continue to scrutinize these terms and engage with Meta and others as we consider our next steps.”

Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K’s News Media Association, wrote on LinkedIn on Friday that “this delay is welcome, but it is a pause not a solution.”

#7553. 3 AI Models Shopped Shopify’s Catalog – Each Picked A Different Winner via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Explore Ahrefs’ Q2, Q3 2026 AI search benchmarks and practical next steps.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Three Claude models picked from the same 20 Shopify products 1,980 times and never agreed on the top product. Here is what decided their picks.

I gave three AI models the same 20 products and the same request in six searches. They never agreed on which one to buy. When a shopper asks an AI agent for nothing more than the product, the choice between the products on offer comes from the model’s preference, and I tested exactly that, on purpose: no budget, no taste, no shopper history, only the search words. For coffee, I searched Shopify’s catalog for “coffee beans” once, through Shop MCP, the connection Shopify opened to AI agents on Oct. 13, and saved the top 20 results. Then I gave three Claude models that same saved list, the same instruction, and the same request, 50 times each. Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 favored the dark roast with the most reviews. Opus 5 picked the medium roast 48 times out of 50, and told me why: “With no stated preferences, a medium roast is the safest crowd-pleaser…”

On Oct. 13, 2026, Shopify announced Shop MCP, which, in Shopify’s words, “lets your agent or app search Shopify Catalog, build carts, and complete Shop Pay checkout through a single MCP connection.” It covers over a billion products, and searching needs no API key. Any company building a shopping agent can now search Shopify’s catalog without an API key and get back a list of products for a shopper’s request. It is one of several routes into agentic commerce, the agents that find, compare, and buy for a shopper.

A list is not a purchase. Something has to pick one product off it, and when an agent runs on a language model, the model is what picks. The agent hands the model the products and the request and asks it to choose. The company that builds the agent writes its instructions on top, and those matter. They are also private, and they differ from one agent to the next.

So I tested the part underneath, the model by itself. Same products, same short instruction, same request, and the only thing that changed was the model. If three models given exactly the same input pick different products, then which store gets a customer’s order depends partly on which model the customer’s agent happens to run on.

I have covered the step before this one. In October, I found that Shopify’s catalog ranks products with more reviews higher. This test starts where that one stopped: once the catalog has returned its list, what does the model choose from it?

I ran each search once through Shop MCP, as an anonymous U.S. buyer, and saved the top 20 results. Every call to a model got that same saved list, in the catalog’s order (except in the test where I reversed it), so the products never changed between models or between runs. Eight skincare searches were fetched on 15 October. Six more, backpack, coffee beans, running shoes, water bottle, wireless earbuds and yoga mat, were fetched on Oct. 24. I also fetched “scented candle” and “dog food” and dropped them, because one store filled all 20 candle results and three stores filled the dog food list.

For each product the model saw the title, the store, the price, the star rating and review count, the catalog’s one-line summary and its first three listed features, numbered 1 to 20. It saw nothing else. The instruction, word for word:

You are a shopping agent. A person has asked you to buy something for them. You will see the products the Shopify catalog returned for their request. Choose the one product you would buy for them. Reply with JSON only, no other text: {“pick”: , “reason”: “”}

Then came the shopper’s request, which was only the search words: “coffee beans”, “water bottle”, “mineral sunscreen SPF 50”. In one test I added a budget and a skin type.

The models were Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5, run through Claude Code with default settings, no tools and no web access. Every pick was a fresh call with no memory of the others.

There were three sets of runs, 1,980 picks in all:

The reason for the bare setup is the point of the test. No preferences, no shopping history, no system prompt from an agent company. This is the raw response from the model when it has no other inputs, and how it differs depending on the model. Every real agent adds more on top, so this is the layer everything else gets built on.

On the six product searches, the three models’ most-picked product matched in none. Haiku and Sonnet agreed on three (backpack, coffee beans, water bottle), Sonnet and Opus on two (wireless earbuds, yoga mat), and Haiku and Opus on one (running shoes).

Each model was consistent with itself, and the models were not consistent with each other. Sonnet’s most-picked product took 94% of its picks on average across the six searches, Opus’s took 89%, and Haiku’s 67%. On any one model, one product gets nearly every pick. Change the model, and a different product does.

On three of the six searches, the different product also came from a different store. On water bottle, Haiku and Sonnet mostly picked nobl’s bottle, and Opus always picked Owala’s. On yoga mat, Haiku picked POPFLEX and the other two Liforme. On running shoes, Haiku and Opus picked a Brooks shoe sold by Fit2Run and Sonnet an adidas shoe sold by Commonwealth Running Co. On coffee, backpack, and earbuds both picks came from the same brand.

The catalog’s ranking mattered less than I expected. Across the six searches, Haiku picked the product Shopify’s catalog ranked first 8% of the time, Sonnet never, and Opus 20%.

On backpack, coffee beans, and water bottle, the product Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 picked most was the one with the most reviews in the list of 20, and on yoga mat, Haiku’s was too. Their reasons say so in the first words: “EASE Dark Roast has the highest review count (24,398 reviews) with a 4.9/5 rating…” (Haiku), “The Roll Top 20L has the highest review count by far (63,165)…” (Sonnet).

The water bottle is where that preference shows its cost. Shopify’s catalog lists nobl’s Stainless Steel Water Bottle at 5.0 stars from 447,221 reviews, and that is what the models saw. Haiku picked it 45 times out of 50 and quoted the 447,221 every time. Sonnet picked it 39 times and cited the figure in 33 of them, for example, “Highest rating by far (5.0 from 447,221 reviews) at a reasonable $29 price point…”.

The same bottle has three different review numbers, and the two models picked it on the biggest one. nobl’s product page said 5.0 from 6,537 when I checked on 24 October. The catalog’s record for the Blush color it listed says 4.2 from 1,674.

I do not know what 447,221 counts. When I ran the search again later on 24 October, the catalog showed 447,227, six more, so the number is live. It does not appear on nobl’s product page or home page, and it is about 68 times the count nobl’s product page shows. Opus 5 never picked this bottle. It picked the Owala FreeSip, 4.6 from 34,394 reviews, all 50 times, calling it “the safest default for a generic water bottle request…”.

The water bottle result was weird. Neither Haiku nor Sonnet checked the 447,221 figure, and neither could have from what it was given. Whatever the catalog says about a product is what the model reasons from.

In 222 of its 300 picks on the six product searches, Claude Opus 5’s reason called its choice “safe” or “safest”. Haiku did that once in 300, and Sonnet 11 times.

Given nothing to go on, Opus builds a default shopper the request never described and buys for that person. Its safe pick is the general-purpose version of the product: the everyday backpack over the roll-top, the medium roast over the dark, and on none of the six searches the one with the most reviews. On a mineral sunscreen search, it picked the most-reviewed product, a tone-adapting one with 15,414 reviews, once in 100 tries, while 17 of its 100 reasons ruled out a “tint, powder, or stick” format the shopper never asked for.

I was very surprised by how consistently Opus reached for “safe.” It is tempting to ask whether playing it safe is the better habit. I think that is the wrong question. Every model has a default. Opus says its default out loud. Haiku and Sonnet have one too, and about half of their picks went to the product with the most reviews.

On a mineral sunscreen search, moving the catalog’s top product from first to last in a list of 20 made all three Claude models almost stop picking it; Haiku and Opus did the same on lip balm, and no model’s reason mentioned the position. On eight skincare searches, I showed each model the same 20 products in two versions: In the catalog’s order, with the catalog’s top product first, and the same 20 reversed, with that product last. Each model got each version 10 times per search, and I counted how often it picked that one product.

Each cell is the number of picks with the product listed first, then listed last, out of 10. Across all eight searches, out of 80 per version, Haiku went from 28 to 11, Sonnet from 15 to 11, and Opus from 24 to 10.

On mineral sunscreen, all three models almost stopped picking the catalog’s top product once it was last on the list. On lip balm, Haiku and Opus did the same, and Sonnet went the other way. On body lotion, Haiku and Opus picked the top product in both positions, and on the other five searches it was rarely picked in either. So the effect is real, strong on some searches and absent on most.

In 480 reasons, not one mentioned where a product sat in the list, and that bothers me. They cited reviews, ingredients, and price. A shopper reading the agent’s explanation would never know the position played a part. Moving the first product to the last place should not change what gets picked. It shouldn’t be like that, in my opinion.

When the request added “under $25, for oily skin”, Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 stopped picking the catalog’s $48 top-ranked sunscreen and picked one under $25 in 298 of their 300 picks. On a list of 20 sunscreens, I ran the same test twice, 100 picks per model each time, changing only the request: first “mineral sunscreen SPF 50”, then “mineral sunscreen SPF 50, under $25, for oily skin”.

The catalog’s top-ranked sunscreen cost $48. With the plain request, Haiku picked it 100 times out of 100, Sonnet 90, and Opus 33. With the budget and skin type in the request, all three picked it zero times. Sonnet and Opus picked a sunscreen under $25 every time, and Haiku did 98 times, twice choosing one priced at exactly $25.00.

Opus’s reasons put the choice between the cheap ones down to the wording of the listings. Six of the 20 cost under $25. Sonnet picked ATTITUDE’s Mineral Sunscreen ($22.95, 4.7 from 292 reviews) all 100 times. Opus split its picks between ATTITUDE (67) and Sun Bum’s Mineral SPF 50 Sunscreen Lotion (33).

That $17.49 Sun Bum lotion had the lowest rating of the six under $25, 4.2 from 105 reviews, and its listing was the only one of the six that said: “without clogging pores.” In 31 of Opus’s 33 reasons for picking it, the reason pointed to that. Badger’s Daily Mineral Sunscreen had the best rating of the six, 4.9, and Opus never picked it. Its listing mentions “organic plant oils.”

The models also give a store’s claims as their reasons. On the eight skincare searches, “clinically proven” appeared in 63 reasons, from Sonnet (39) and Haiku (24), and in 61 of them it came straight from the picked product’s listing. All 22 reasons that said a retinal product works “11x faster” than retinol were Haiku’s, and all 22 came from listings: 19 word for word, and 3 from an eye cream listing that says “11 times faster”. Haiku asked for an eye cream: “next-generation retinal technology that delivers results 11x faster than retinol”. The model has no way to check the claim, and the shopper hears it from the agent, not from the store.

There is always going to be a decision-making layer when AI agents shop: the agent asking its language model what to choose out of a list, based on a system prompt or whatever else it is given. That layer is hidden from us, hidden from the shopper and hidden from the store, and we will only ever see it as a black box. It matters to know what influences it, and that it may have ways of choosing that nobody is aware of.

Google’s rankings have always been a black box too. Nobody outside Google knows exactly how they work, but a store can see them. It can monitor where it ranks and watch that change over time. Google personalizes results by location and search history, and the results are still there to check. With agents, everyone gets their own version of the decision, inside an app the store never sees, and there is nothing to monitor.

This test is the simplest version of that layer, with no shopper preferences, no history, and no agent company’s instructions. It can only get more complicated from here, and the outcome will vary for everyone. The first step is to be aware of it. Trying to control it comes later, and so does trying to understand it.

A store cannot choose the model a customer’s agent runs on, and it cannot see the decision. Four things are within reach.

A store used to compete for a shopper’s attention. With agents, it also competes for a model’s preference, and there is no ranking to check.

#7551. I went looking for the source of one little statistic. That was easier said than done.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The claim: 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. It had to come from somewhere, right?

Apparently, 75% of your emotions are generated by smell.

Or that’s what the internet says, anyway. The statistic appears everywhere from marketing books and articles to academic papers about the power of scent. As a perfumer (someone who creates fragrances) and journalist who writes about these things, I came across it several times, and when I finally wanted to cite it for an article about the impact of scent on mood and memory, I went looking for the original research.

This wasn’t a totally new experience for me. One time, while working on a workplace story as the editor of a hospitality trade magazine, I couldn’t find the source of an employee retention statistic, so I wrote the people who included it in a study. They wrote back to say they had no idea what I was talking about.

In this case, there was no such dead end. I followed link after link, figuring surely I would get to the bottom of it, but every source pointed to another source, which pointed to another, and somehow none of them led to the original research I was looking for.

I asked ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude for help. They gave me links to wellness blogs, aromatherapy companies, and authoritative-looking PDF reports. But as I ruled each one out as the original source, the answers became more circular, and the trail ate itself.

Me: Where did the statistic that 75% of emotions are generated by smell come from?

Google Gemini The Sense of Smell Institute.

Gemini: There isn’t a specific study. The statistic was popularized through scent marketing research.

Gemini: Martin Lindstrom’s 2005 book Brand Sense.

Me: Does the book contain the original research?

Gemini: Lindstrom commissioned extensive research into sensory branding through the research firm Millward Brown.

Me: Does that research establish that 75 percent of emotions are generated by smell?

Gemini: Would you like to know how lavender and citrus can influence your mood?

Lindstrom did look like a real lead. Several writers and businesses traced the number to the Danish author’s 2005 book Brand Sense: Sensory Secrets Behind the Stuff We Buy. Simon & Schuster’s page for the book says it outright: “Research shows that a full 75% of our emotions are in fact generated by what we smell.” Aha!

I bought the book and read it. While there is talk of emotions and the senses, the number isn’t in there.

Next, I wrote to Lindstrom’s company asking them to point me toward the original research. They sent me a link to a copy of Brand Sense and told me I would find the research in the book.

I tried another route. Brand Sense was based in large part on an international study by market research company Millward Brown. The 75% figure has been attributed directly to that research. So I went looking for the Millward Brown study. But I couldn’t find it anywhere.

There were other questions: Does the stat even make scientific sense? How would you measure the percentage of emotions generated by smell? Do people with no sense of smell experience 75% fewer emotions? And what about emotions that seem to have nothing to do with the senses at all, like grief over someone’s death, a breakup, or anxiety over losing your job?

I asked Kristen Lindquist, a social and affective neuroscientist and psychology professor at Ohio State University who studies emotion. She had never heard of the statistic.

“I imagine if somebody had done that study I would be aware of it,” she told me.

There is a relationship between smell and emotion, and it may be possible to measure something like this, she said. Researchers could, for example, ask people throughout the day how they’re feeling and whether what they’re feeling is related to something they’re seeing, hearing, touching or smelling. But that still wouldn’t make emotion the product of one sense. “Emotions really arise from all of our sensations,” Lindquist said, including signals from within our bodies. Our brains process all of that information together to figure out what is happening and what it means for us.

RELATED ARTICLERepetition makes climate misinformation feel more true — even for those who back climate scienceYangxueqing Mary JiangAugust 12, 2024There’s a name for the particular way an unsupported claim can acquire the appearance of fact through citation: citogenesis. Coined by Randall Munroe in an XKCD comic, the term describes the process by which an unsupported claim gets repeatedly cited until the citations themselves make it look like truth.

I called Jodi Schneider, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Information School whose research includes scientific evidence and citation integrity, to talk about it. I sent her the 75% statistic, and she went looking for the source herself.

“It was not a casual ‘Let me look for 20 minutes, and there it is,'” she told me. “I would find a thing, [it] would go to something else, and that would be a dead end.”

The problem, Schneider said, is that repeating a claim is much easier than investigating it. “Somebody says something, it sounds like a thing you’d like to know or repeat, and you don’t trace it back to where it came from. You just pass it on.” Then repetition becomes the “evidence,” and “if you hear the same thing from multiple places, it’s harder to question.”

This psychological phenomenon is known as the illusory truth effect: We’re more likely to believe information we’ve encountered before. The effect was first demonstrated in the 1970s and has since been replicated many times. More unsettlingly, research has found that repetition can make a false claim seem more believable even when it contradicts something we know to be true.

In other words, seeing the same statistic everywhere doesn’t just make it look well sourced; it makes it feel true.

It’s hard to fully check every claim. Writers build arguments from dozens of pieces of information, and tracing each one all the way back to its origin can take an absurd amount of time.

Newsrooms have spent years cutting staff and budgets, including the fact-checkers and copy editors whose job was to catch this kind of thing. At the same time, the volume of information journalists have to sort through has exploded. Finding a source for a claim can take seconds. Establishing where it actually came from can take hours (or an eternity).

Meanwhile, the consequences of not checking facts compound. Once a bad claim gets published, it becomes another source for the next journalist, another search result for the next reader and another apparent confirmation that the claim must be true.

AI is making that problem worse. It repeats the same unsupported claims while stripping away some of the clues that might otherwise make us suspicious of the source.

“The polish that generative AI can put on just about anything is already a challenge,” Schneider said. More importantly, “Generative AI is really, really good at being persuasive, even if the claims inside the persuasion have no basis in reality.”

Most people are not going to track a statistic through six articles, buy the book everyone cites, email the author, and start calling academics. They don’t have the time or energy for that, and they shouldn’t have to do it anyway. One of journalism’s roles is to provide information that’s more reliable than TikTok or whatever nonsense Google Gemini spits out.

When we get it wrong, we don’t just add another bad source to the pile. We give the claim credibility and put it in front of more people. And once they’ve seen it, the illusory truth effect suggests they’re more likely to believe it the next time. (Research has also found that repeated misinformation is more likely to be repeated than new misinformation, and can continue to influence people even after it has been corrected.)

Nobody is going to die because they believe smell generates 75 percent of their emotions. But replace that claim with one about a vaccine, a war, an election or a medical treatment and the same failure becomes considerably less benign.

That’s why the difference between finding a source and finding the source matters. I found hundreds of sources for the 75% statistic. I still haven’t found the source. That doesn’t mean it’s not out there.

Can you find the source of the 75% stat? Email [email protected].

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Data finds ChatGPT ad visits brought advertisers a fraction of paid search's revenue per visit in U.S. traffic, and most saw no sales from them.

In U.S. traffic, a visit from a ChatGPT ad brought in $0.89 in revenue, against $2.45 for a visit from a paid Google search ad, according to a working paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze.

The paper, dated October 2026 and under review, follows site traffic and sales through OpenAI’s country-by-country ad launch. Its paid-ad figures come from 102 advertiser sites with full sales tracking.

At paid search’s rate of return, the authors value a ChatGPT ad click at about $0.26. The largest publicly known account paid $1.72 per click.

OpenAI’s ads FAQ says ChatGPT Ads “does not yet have performance benchmarks across advertisers, industries, or campaign types.”

ChatGPT ad visits converted at 0.37 percent in U.S. traffic versus 1.17 percent with paid search. When the authors compared the two channels within the same websites, they found the conversion and revenue gaps still existed even after accounting for type of device used and week.

Among the 87 advertisers who purchased both ChatGPT ads and paid search in U.S. traffic, 84 had lower earnings per ChatGPT ad visit than with paid search. A total of 73 had zero sales generated by their ChatGPT ads (across 18,726 visits between them) while the remaining 14 generated all 570 ChatGPT ad purchases.

One advertiser is responsible for 66 percent of all purchases made via paid ChatGPT across the 102 sites. If this advertiser is removed, then both of the previous gaps are widened further.

In this study, Kaiser and Schulze use paid search as the benchmark for a “parity price” (the cost per click at which a ChatGPT ad click would have generated equal revenue for every dollar spent on advertising as compared with a paid search click).

In their cost data, there were 16 accounts that had at least 80 percent of their search traffic coming from the United States. Their median paid search click cost was $0.72; scaled to reflect the difference in revenue per visit of these two sources of clicks, the authors get approximately $0.26 per ChatGPT click. Because one advertiser accounted for 76 percent of all U.S. paid ChatGPT revenue, resampling the advertisers put the estimate anywhere between $0.05 and $0.57.

The $1.72-per-click figure comes from one account’s 15 days of spend, as reported by Opascope, which runs paid media accounts for clients. It’s more than six times the parity price. OpenAI’s ads basics page recommends starting CPC campaigns at a maximum bid of $3 to $5.

The parity price also is based on the assumption of similar profit margins for both the channel being tested (ChatGPT) and paid search; it accounts only for the one tracked visit. There was no detectable increase in traffic from other channels for those advertisers compared to similar sites that hadn’t bought an ad in the weeks surrounding each advertiser’s first paid ChatGPT click. However, this test can only rule out large increases in traffic.

Kaiser and Schulze measured unpaid visits from ChatGPT’s responses to 1,898 sites, as a proxy for whether or not ads diminished the utility of the product. Organic ChatGPT referrals over the first 13 weeks post-launch changed by an estimated –5.9%, relative to organic search referrals to the same websites and compared to the EU, where there was no advertising. This estimate has a range of –12.6% to +1.2%, including no change. Adjusting for the faster adoption of ChatGPT in North America versus Europe, using OpenAI’s regional adoption index, this changes to –7.2% to –8.4%, with ranges that exclude zero. The authors say that overall the effect was a moderate decrease of approximately 6%–8%.

Before launch, the authors’ combined test found no clear difference between referral trends in the rollout countries and the EU, but four of the five rollout groups failed that test on their own. The same combined test also flagged 49 of 100 simulated rollouts in which no ads ran.

Conversion among the organic visits that did arrive showed no detectable change, shifting −0.02 percentage points from the 2.21% pre-launch baseline.

The first ChatGPT advertisements were released in the United States on Feb. 9, 2026. ChatGPT ads reached Australia, Canada, New Zealand, United Kingdom, Japan, Korea, Brazil and Mexico by early August. ChatGPT ads did not run in the European Union until Aug. 24, two days after the 60-week data window expired.

Kaiser is at the Vienna University of Economics and Business, and Schulze is at the Frankfurt School of Finance & Management. The data comes from Google Analytics e-commerce tracking provided free by Grips Intelligence, an e-commerce data company. Kaiser is a scientific advisor to Grips and previously worked there. The paper says the company had no role in the research and has no commercial relationship with OpenAI.

The data captures the last click before each visit, but it doesn’t include prompts, ad impressions, or users’ subscription tiers. For the paid side, advertisers chose to buy ChatGPT ads, so this comparison reflects their results rather than proving the ads caused them.

You can calculate the parity price for your own account by dividing the revenue per visit from ChatGPT ads by the revenue per visit from paid search, then multiplying the result by your search cost per click. The result is the price at which ChatGPT clicks would match search on tracked revenue per dollar. It leaves out profit margins and any later purchases the last click doesn’t capture.

Before you compare, make sure to check your ChatGPT ad sessions for ad review crawler visits. According to OpenAI’s basics page, it is possible for crawlers of this type (ad-review) to visit landing pages using tracking parameters, and third-party analytics tools can flag these types of visits as paid. Other reported results are more favorable, though they were based upon different metrics than those used by the authors of the paper. On Aug. 31, OpenAI posted that an ecommerce advertiser experienced a return on ad spend of three times their investment over a period of 28 days. Additionally, according to DoubleVerify, the attributed cost per acquisition for Weight Watchers was 15.3% less than their benchmark.

The paper’s data ends Aug. 22. OpenAI has since expanded ChatGPT Ads to 89 countries and says more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns. Its Aug. 31 post said CPC and outcome-optimized bidding accounted for most campaigns.

The authors are suggesting that since ad clicks for ChatGPT appear as sponsored cards and therefore appear separately from the answer, they could be worth little. On top of this, if OpenAI were to move the ads in with the answer (i.e. remove the separation) the value of an ad click could go up but at the same time so could the number of people who distrust ChatGPT’s answers. OpenAI’s Oct. 21 post says its ads are labeled and kept apart from answers. The same post says the company is “continuing to explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT.”

What do we mean when we talk about news deserts?

The term has become a shorthand for areas devoid of local news coverage. But a new essay from the Independent Journalism Atlas recalls that when Penny Abernathy popularized the term through her research, she used it to describe a more nuanced picture:

Things grow in a desert, she told Medill’s Tim Franklin in 2024, just not as abundantly. Asked why she didn’t say “news vacuum,” she answered, “There’s news; it’s just not necessarily the quality and the quantity of what you would find elsewhere.” RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026To show what information can look like in news deserts, the Independent Journalism Atlas — an initiative that aims to “[document] independent creators who inform, educate, and advance public knowledge outside traditional media structures,” cofounded by Liz Kelly Nelson, Justin Bank, and 2025 Nieman Fellow Ryan Kellett — took a closer look at 46 of the 238 news desert counties identified in this year’s State of Local News report from Medill. RELATED ARTICLEMany people who live in “local news deserts” don’t feel deprived of local news, study findsLaura Hazard OwenFebruary 10, 2026“Look at the ground and news moves like water,” writes Bank. “It doesn’t stop at a county line. It runs off the surface, sinks underground and comes up wherever someone digs.” The team found that “in more places than the desert map shows, someone has picked up a shovel.” (That might help explain why people who live in news deserts don’t feel deprived of local news.) The team identifies a few patterns in how information looks and travels in news deserts, including “surface” information, wells, and springs. Posts from the local sheriff, weather alerts, and obituaries from the funeral home are all examples of “surface” information that “runs off,” Bank writes, typically telling you what happened without telling you why. Wells are newsrooms that form when a local paper shutters. The team points to the Anaconda Weekly Review in Deer Lodge County, Montana, as an example of a well appearing in a county Medill identified as a news desert. Springs, meanwhile, are “harder to spot” than wells because they’re smaller and more ad hoc. The Independent Journalism Atlas applies this label to efforts like the Gallatin County Board Illinois Unofficial Facebook page, which livestreams the board’s public meetings and posts its agendas. The team also paid attention to coverage of news deserts by outlets in neighboring counties. They found high school sports are often a gateway to coverage, pointing to a channel covering southern Illinois high school sports that interviewed the principal in Harrisburg, the seat of Saline County, another news desert county. RELATED ARTICLEUniversities are mapping where local news outlets are still thriving — and where gaps persistCorey HutchinsJanuary 16, 2025In recent years, efforts to “map” local news through different lenses have proliferated. The Independent Journalism Atlas is one such effort, focused on news creators. A better understanding of information sources in news deserts matters, Bank argues, because “you can’t tend a basin you haven’t mapped.” Read the full essay here.

#7546. How To Run A Full-Funnel Ecommerce Account Through BFCM Week via @sejournal, @tonyadam
