#7523. Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

Most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, announced it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

The grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

For many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” said Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money quickly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1

RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” said María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

“They said to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”

First-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, said Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

“It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” said Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”

The Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” said Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

The funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin said. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2

RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”

“Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” said Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”

The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

“The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” said Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased new software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very quickly,” he said, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

The Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a new website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”

The Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a new media kit, which Olson said has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.)

The open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr said. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to plan ahead.

Many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

The Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” said Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the new hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

The Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

The funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz said.

The Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve company housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, said editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3

The turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

Sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” said Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”

The World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr said. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.)

Other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”

EcoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

The salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz said. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”

“At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she said, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”

Beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she said. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

“I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she said, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”

Planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she said.

Ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she said. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”

NotiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” said CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

California’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

In Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

For instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer said, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

Planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak said. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

“The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak said. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”

Anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he said, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

Press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting company Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

The coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants said the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving quickly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4

This was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” said Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear plan. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he said it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

Sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”

In addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin said 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

Stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar said, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

To small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

So several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she said.

Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

Since 2023, Anglin said, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition says it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

When Press Forward first announced the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee said it felt like “a slap in the face.”

“Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin said. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”

The argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher said. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”

Young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

“I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he said. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”)

Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

Young said he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

Right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak said the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health issues in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”

As for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”

LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he said, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”

A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person said, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”

The Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer said.

“I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”

The Sandpoint Reader, Olson said, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”

Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”

“We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she said. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”

#7522. Sales Development Representative at Chili Piper

Chili Piper is a B2B SaaS company that helps GTM teams turn inbound leads into qualified meetings - instantly. Our Demand Conversion Platform makes it easier for buyers and sellers to connect fast, without the usual friction in the funnel.

A Google Lighthouse update changes how PageSpeed Insights simulates page loads, which can raise lab scores on pages that haven't changed.

PageSpeed Insights is now using Lighthouse 13.6.0, which was released Oct. 27. This version of Lighthouse changes how it simulates how long a page takes to load.

Chrome’s Web Performance Developer Advocate, Barry Pollard, has stated on Bluesky that the updated version of PageSpeed Insights with Lighthouse 13.6.0 is now available. He said this improves the simulated FCP (First Contentful Paint) and the simulated LCP (Largest Contentful Paint), both of which Pollard says will be more accurate than before and generally result in higher scores.

A page may receive a different PageSpeed Insights score without anything on it changing, due to the change in the test. Pollard also said that websites heavily dependent on JavaScript would be more likely to see an impact from the updated test.

Pollard quoted a developer who had posted about how single-page apps (SPAs) had seen a big improvement in their results since the Lighthouse update, citing react.dev. He opened his post stating, “True!”, then added:

“Note this is not SPA-specific (and unrelated to other SPA things we’ve been working on), but more likely to impact JS-heavy sites.”

The experimental soft navigation metrics in Chrome that I wrote about back in October are a separate way of measuring user experience. The data comes from real Chrome users through the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) and Lighthouse uses a simulated test.

By default, Lighthouse will load a page at full speed and then estimate how it would load on a slower connection. The throttling docs say that this simulated throttling matches PageSpeed Insights’ setup.

The release notes for version 13.6.0 of Lighthouse list several changes to Lantern, which is the simulation behind those estimates, aimed at improving its accuracy.

Lighthouse 13.5 used each request’s fetch priority to decide whether or not it blocked rendering. In 13.6, Lantern uses Chrome’s own render-blocking label for each request (and falls back to using priority only when that label is missing).

A second change applies when the LCP element is text that appears in the same frame as the page’s first content. Lantern now estimates that LCP from the same requests and page tasks it uses for FCP instead of from a set that can include every request made before LCP.

Ivan Akulov showed in a GitHub issue how the old simulation handled a test page created with Framer whose only content above the fold was text, so one element counted as both FCP and LCP. Lighthouse reported much later LCP than FCP for that text. Even though preloading the page’s JavaScript modules improved interactive time for the real page, they caused simulated LCP to be worse.

Pollard thanked Akulov in a reply, saying he “kicked off some of these improvements.” The Lighthouse team closed the issue as completed in the Lantern upgrade listed in the 13.6 release notes.

Lighthouse 13.6 has also updated the Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD) audit from Lighthouse 13.5, which I covered in September. When Lighthouse 13.5 was released, it looked for an ARD manifest under the old ai-catalog names even though the spec had changed to ard.json. So if your website only used the new name but you didn’t include a line in your robots.txt file called Agentmap, it would show as Not Applicable.

With this update, Lighthouse 13.6 will look for an Agentmap line, a rel="ard" link tag or Link header and /.well-known/ard.json prior to looking for the ai-catalog names. And if Lighthouse 13.6 finds the manifest only at an ai-catalog location, it will note that ARD consumers are not required to check there.

The performance score listed for your page in PageSpeed Insights is based on data generated by Lighthouse. According to Google’s PageSpeed Insights documentation, lab data are results of a simulated load using a single device running on a fixed set of network conditions. They note that “having good lab data does not necessarily mean real-user experiences will also be good.”

Field data (also shown in the same report) represents real visits to your website within the last 28 days, as reported by CrUX. Each PageSpeed Insights report includes the version of Lighthouse used to generate results, next to the emulated device.

PageSpeed Insights scores from before and after the Lighthouse 13.6 update weren’t measured with the same simulation. Part of a higher lab score on a page you just optimized may come from the new version, and charts that track lab scores over time may show a jump at the switch to 13.6.

Before reporting an improvement, check that both reports name the same Lighthouse version, and compare the field data.

Lighthouse’s release notes say its team expects 13.6 to ship in the DevTools of Chrome 159, which is now in Chrome’s desktop Dev channel and in Canary. As of Nov. 2, Chrome’s release schedule lists Chrome 159 for stable release on Dec. 8.

An open issue on Lighthouse’s GitHub is also looking into cases where Lantern’s simulated LCP runs far above measured LCP, using large JavaScript and SPA sites as examples.

#7520. Your buyers are sending agents. Will they recommend your brand?

For most of my career, marketing and sales have run on a single assumption: a person is paying attention. We wrote for human eyes, optimized for human clicks, and designed every interaction for human discernment. That assumption is starting to break.

Buyers are sending AI agents out ahead of them that have been tasked to read what you publish, compare you against the field, and hand the user a shortlist, often before that user lands on your site or talks to sales. At the same time, marketing and sales teams are building their own AI systems to keep pace. Both shifts are landing at once, and together they change how demand gets created and how trust gets earned.

This is the biggest shift in marketing since search itself. The brands that come out ahead will be the ones that get their foundation right first, because there is no AI strategy without a data strategy.

We have optimized for machines before; that was the whole idea behind search. What is happening now is a different order of magnitude. Agents are constantly reading, comparing, and recommending next steps based on users’ prompts.

That changes my job and yours. An agent now reads our story, determines whether our brand looks clear and trustworthy, and uses that read to decide whether we make the shortlist it hands to a decision-maker. Clear, consistent, well-structured content is what tips that decision and most brands will never know when they have been left off the list.

Enterprise marketing has always been episodic. We run a campaign, pass a lead, let sales run a play, and start over. Agent-driven buyers no longer move on that calendar, so our engines must evolve.

The shift now is toward an always-on system that reads each customer continuously, puts the best opportunities first, and evolves in the moment. This new process is rewiring how marketing and sales work together, from a handoff between two teams into one operation looking at the same customer at the same time.

But none of it works without a trustworthy foundation. If revenue or pipeline means six different things in six systems, layering AI on top will only scale the confusion. Governed, well-understood data is what lets an always-on engine move fast without getting reckless. When everyone has access to the same models, data becomes your differentiator because customer history and context are yours alone.

There is of course a grim version of this future as well. Infinite personalization collapses into infinite noise and every inbox fills with confident, hollow outreach. I think that outcome is a choice, not an inevitability.

Used well, AI takes the mechanical work off our teams: the assembling, formatting, and first draft nobody enjoys. When it gives back time, that time is only worth something if people spend it where machines cannot: understanding a customer, building a real relationship, making the call on what comes next.

That does not happen by accident. It takes leaders willing to rewrite roles, retrain teams, and give people room to experiment. But the judgment, creativity, and taste required to plan and execute differentiated marketing at scale will always remain human.

Your next customer may arrive as an agent or send one ahead. When that agent builds its shortlist, I want Snowflake on it, and I want your company on it too. That is the work in front of every marketing and sales leader now.

Google's John Mueller clarified whether site owners can use robots.txt to block Googlebot from downloading specific resources that users see.

Google’s John Mueller answered a question about whether it’s okay to block Googlebot from indexing an age-verification popup that website visitors are required to see. His answer offers some clarity about whether it’s okay to purposely hide some kinds of content from Googlebot and explains how site owners can do it.

Google requires publishers to allow Googlebot to crawl everything that a user might see but that wasn’t always the case. There was a time in the early days of SEO where SEOs blocked Google from downloading JavaScript and CSS files in order to optimize the crawl budget and encourage better website indexing.

But there came a time when Google began rendering web pages and subsequently required site owners to allow Googlebot to download all resources that a user would see. Some sites that continued to block Google from downloading critical resources temporarily lost their rankings.

So the question about whether it’s okay to block Google from indexing a popup is reasonable.

The SEO asked on Reddit whether it’s okay to use robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from indexing an age-verification popup that a website is legally required to display to visitors.

The person described a hypothetical website that loads an age-verification popup from a separate domain through an API. The question was whether blocking Googlebot from crawling that external domain would prevent the popup from being rendered.

“Say I have a website websiteA.com – for legal reasons it has an age verification pop up that sits on a separate domain and is inserted on the page via an API. Lets call it verificationpopup.com

Lets say I wanted to block Google from seeing this – if I added a disallow on verificationpopup.com/robots.txt would that prevent Google from rendering the pop up?

(this is purley a hypothetical and apologies for the stupid Q, I am not very tech minded)”

Mueller confirmed that using robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from rendering the age-verification popup would generally work. He also suggested an alternative approach that involves blocking a JavaScript file responsible for loading the popup.

“That would generally work. If you’re using a specific JS script file to do this, you could also disallow that specific javascript file via robots.txt. (If you only have one JS file that does a bunch of things, I wouldnt’ do that”

Mueller’s response indicates that Google’s algorithms may be looser than it used to be, at least toward something like this age verification popup. His answer confirmed that site owners can use robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from rendering an age-verification popup, even when the popup is displayed to website visitors.

He returned hours later to elaborate in more detail about two ways to accomplish this, addressing two ways the popup is loaded and which resources the site owner can control.

Mueller explained that the first approach involves blocking Googlebot from crawling the external domain that provides the age-verification popup.

In the situation of an external domain that’s the source of the resource that needs blocking, the external domain’s robots.txt can disallow crawling and Googlebot will not fetch those resources and therefore cannot use them to render the popup. Mueller said that this is common with resources related to advertising where a JavaScript file responsible for showing ads is blocked by robots.txt.

the embedded site’s content is blocked by robots.txt. If you embed content from verificationpopup-com on your site (say via iframe or by calling a script on verificationpopup-com, etc), and verificationpopup-com disallows all crawling, then crawlers that follow robots.txt (like Googlebot) would not fetch that content, and would not use it in rendering.

This is how many ads services work. Googlebot wouldn’t crawl these URLs like a separate page, but it would try to fetch them during the course of rendering, and if robots.txt blocks it, then it doesn’t fetch the content, and can’t use it. You need to make sure that your pages still load when those URLs are not fetched, but for something like this, that’s usually not a problem.

Your site uses a specific JS file to load this, and you block that yourself. For example, perhaps you use a “load-verification-popup.js” file to do this. If you block that page with robots.txt on your site, then the script won’t be loaded during rendering (blocked by robots.txt).

In my experience, this is less common, but it’s an option. If the robots.txt on verificationpopup-com is not something you can influence, you’d need to do this, if you wanted to prevent it from being visible/used during rendering.”

So to recap, the second approach involves blocking a JavaScript file that’s used to load the popup that’s on another domain where using a robots.txt is not an option.

The interesting part of Mueller’s answer is that he confirmed a way to deliberately prevent Googlebot from rendering an age-verification popup that human visitors are required to see.

He also explained that the website must continue to load properly when Googlebot cannot fetch the blocked resources. For an age-verification popup like the one described in the question, he indicated that this is usually not a problem.

The overall takeaway is that it’s okay to use robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from downloading and rendering an age-verification popup, even though human visitors are required to see it. Mueller’s answer shows that website owners exercise some control over which resources Googlebot uses during rendering, including resources that are a part of the experience presented to visitors.

#7516. Senior Strategic Finance Manager at DuckDuckGo

Hi, we're DuckDuckGo, the online protection company and remote-first team of 400+ on a mission to raise the standard of trust online. Founded in 2008 and profitable since 2014, annual revenue now exceeds $100m USD and millions use our browser on Mac, Windows, iOS, and Android, our search engine, and the DuckDuckGo subscription. We also offer private, useful, and optional AI, including Duck.ai, which lets you chat privately with ChatGPT, Claude, and other AIs, all in one place.

Our culture of trust, inclusivity, and empowered project management underpins everything we do, where each team member takes full ownership of their projects, from scoping and execution to postmortem. If you're seeking end-to-end ownership of your work, you've come to the right place!

We're looking for a Senior Manager Strategic Finance to help lead DuckDuckGo's FP&A processes and strategic finance initiatives. You'll partner with cross-functional leadership on key decisions and evaluate the scale and profitability of new products, M&A and other strategic investments.

You'll build financial models for scenarios such as product expansion, search monetization, marketing ROI, and potential acquisitions. You'll review and summarize financial results and play a key role in quarterly forecasts (P&L, Balance Sheet, Cash Flow) and annual and long-term planning. You'll also own recurring deliverables, including forecast variance, user metrics, P&L and headcount analyses. You'll help scale the team's processes, using AI tools like Claude and BI tools like Tableau and Grafana to make workflows more efficient.

We're a collaborative, transparent, self-motivated team. If our core values (build trust, question assumptions, and validate direction) resonate with you, you'll fit right in!

8+ years in strategic finance (FP&A, corporate development, investment banking, or consulting).

Advanced Excel and financial modeling, including three-statement forecasts.

Track record of owning complex, ambiguous analysis end to end and tying it to clear metrics.

Experience building working relationships with business partners and collaborating toward company objectives.

An instinct for automating recurring analysis, including with AI tools.

Clear, concise writing for senior leadership in a remote, async environment.

Dashboard experience: Tableau, Grafana, and Sage Intacct are a plus.

Sales finance, GTM, corporate finance, or M&A a plus.

U.S. GAAP accounting and reporting knowledge.

Ad-based/subscription, technology, or public company experience a plus.

$190,500 to $214,767 USD / $253,500 to $284,417 CAD annually and stock options. Compensation is transparent across the organization, and all team members within the same professional level and global region receive the same compensation.

Eligibility for company-sponsored health benefits is limited to team members based in the United States. This program does not extend to team members located in other countries, such as Canada or the UK.

Our Team Member Support Guide explains how we prioritize your wellbeing including paid parental leave, office setup, and co-working allowances.

Hiring works best when it's a two-way street. Learn how we help you get to know DuckDuckGo, envision your future role here, and find out more about how we hire.

DuckDuckGo provides equal work opportunities to all team members and applicants, and it prohibits discrimination and harassment of any type on the basis of race, color, ethnicity, caste, religion, age, sex (including pregnancy), national origin, disability status, genetics, protected veteran status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or any other characteristic protected by our policies or federal, state, or local laws.

We want to ensure that our hiring process is accessible. If you need reasonable accommodation for any part of the application process because of a medical condition or disability, please send an email to careers@duckduckgo.com to let us know the nature of your request.

You’ll be required to attend meetings on camera via video conferencing

Expect to travel at least two times a year: once for our all-hands meetup and again for a team retreat (each around 4-5 days). While extenuating circumstances may impact attendance, everyone is strongly encouraged to attend.

While we offer a flexible work arrangement with no core hours, expect an average full-time commitment of 40 hours per week.

A successful candidate must pass a background check as a condition of joining the team.

By applying for this role, you confirm that all information submitted is accurate and complete. You further acknowledge that providing false or fraudulent information during the application process is cause for denial of an offer, revocation of any existing offer, or other adverse action, up to and including termination after the start of your commencement of work.

Disclosure Statement: Use of AI in Hiring Process

As part of our commitment to enhancing our recruitment process, we utilize artificial intelligence (AI) technology to assist in reviewing and summarizing job applications and test projects, including those tools integrated into our recruitment vendor platforms. We use AI to flag potentially fraudulent applications, analyze and summarize applicants’ experience, interviews, and project performance, and help streamline our selection process.

Human Oversight and Accountability: The AI technology is designed to support our hiring team by providing insights and summaries of applications and evaluations of test projects against scoring rubrics. All final evaluations and hiring decisions, however, will be made by our hiring team, who will consider the AI's input alongside other factors.

#7515. Express unwraps holiday campaign to build on brand metric gains

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

CMO Joe Berean explains how “Holiday, Hamlin Style” was inspired by the organic social engagement of the retailer’s spring campaign.

Express has enlisted a family of pop cultural figures for its holiday campaign, according to details shared with Marketing Dive. The “Holiday, Hamlin Style” effort reimagines holiday traditions and unites actor-model-reality TV star Lisa Rinna; her husband, actor Harry Hamlin; her daughter, model Delilah Belle Hamlin; and Delilah’s boyfriend, “Love Island” veteran Mick Maio.

Rinna, who began her career as a model and on soap operas before becoming a breakout star on “The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills,” has a long-standing place in pop culture and connects with different consumer groups in different ways. She also has displayed a gift for virality, whether on reality TV or competition shows including “Dancing with the Stars” and “The Traitors.”

“That connection that she has to people just really comes through so authentically and translates so well into today's social media era. That's exactly what we captured on the campaign, too,” Express CMO Joe Berean said. “We designed it as one that can have that polish of a traditional holiday campaign, but really be social-first.”

The social-first push is in line with Express’ other marketing efforts, like the Expressionists, its community of creators, associates and brand ambassadors that is helping to bring to life “Dress to Express,” a brand platform centered around instilling confidence and inspiring self-expression.

Express in August launched a fall campaign, “Too Easy to Look This Good,” that featured NFL player Tee Higgins and pop star Tinashe, weeks before her album “Popstar” took the charts and the pop culture world by storm. The campaign generated the brand’s highest earned media and highest paid media traffic to its website for the year so far. From Q2 into Q3, Express saw brand awareness increase 3% and consideration increase 2%, Berean said.

“We're looking to move the needle in terms of bringing our brand back, reigniting the heat of the brand at its heyday and even exceeding that,” Berean said. “We've seen this sequential improvement of awareness and consideration, which is exactly the intent, especially as we're going into this crowded holiday season.”

Express has been looking to reheat its brand since filing for Chapter 11 in April 2024. The retailer and its Bonobos subsidiary are owned by Phoenix Retail, a joint venture from Simon Property Group, Brookfield Properties, Centennial and brand management firm WHP Global.

The campaign is Express’ latest effort that seeks to build buzz for the brand with celebrity-led activations, and arrives as the retailer works to engage both its existing customer base and a new generation of shoppers.

“The intent of the holiday campaign is to break through during a very crowded holiday season, make a splash and have it be scroll-stopping with Lisa's one-liners and dance moves and this really loving, authentic and stylish family dynamic that only they can bring,” Berean said.

“Holiday, Hamlin Style” follows a successful spring campaign that also featured Belle Hamlin and Maio. “It Couple, It Looks” launched in April and delivered the brand’s highest organic social engagement of the year so far, the retailer reported. In addition, Express said it has seen success with the multigenerational marketing approach in a Mother’s Day campaign starring model Karolína Kurková and her daughter.

“We've been trying different tactics to reach new customers… and those customers span generations,” Berean said of the holiday campaign. “To have a total family dynamic with mother, daughter, father and boyfriend was strategic, in that sense, to appeal to a wide audience.”

Shot in Los Angeles, the holiday campaign includes a series of seasonal vignettes and is set to remixes of Tchaikovsky’s “The Nutcracker.” It will run across video, social, digital and in-store channels throughout the season, highlighting styles priced from $38 to $298. The campaign arrives as big box retailers Target and Walmart and retail brands including Anthropologie and Sephora launch holiday campaigns.

“The competition is starting earlier. It's getting more aggressive. So having talent and campaigns that can really connect with people and break through is the name of the game,” Berean said.

#7514. Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Grokipedia shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

When I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia said “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”

I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

That article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D.

Still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia.

The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Scale a global AI content factory with approved local facts and human expertise to help AI search reflect each market's products, rules, and customers.

For more than 25 years, I have heard the same complaints from local marketing teams. “This doesn’t sound like us.” “Our customers don’t ask that question.” “That product isn’t even sold here.” “Why are we publishing a U.S. case study on the Japanese site?”

At headquarters, these complaints were usually treated as resistance. Local teams simply wanted control, and they didn’t understand the cost of supporting 30 or 40 markets. They were slowing down a process that had been carefully engineered for speed and consistency.

I understood that view. I also spent a lot of time explaining the local side of the argument to global teams who weren’t necessarily happy to hear it.

Now AI is giving enterprises the ability to produce content for every market faster and more cheaply than ever. And AI search is showing us, very clearly, what happens when that content is the same everywhere.

The local teams may have been right all along.

This article examines why the traditional global content model is breaking down in AI search, and how to build an AI-powered content factory that scales without erasing what makes each market unique.

Most multinational content operations were designed to solve one problem: how to publish the same message in many languages without the cost growing at the same rate as the number of markets.

The industry developed very good tools for that problem:

The key performance indicators followed the same logic: cost per word, TM leverage, reducing turnaround time, and accelerating time-to-market for a global launch. A high TM match rate was the key to maximizing KPIs and building confidence in uniform messaging.

When local teams pushed back, the rationale for pushback was hard to quantify. It was typically framed in terms of tone, nuance, or lack of cultural fit. When matched against a dashboard of cost savings, “it doesn’t feel local” rarely won the argument.

In traditional search, the cost of that decision was manageable. Hreflang told search engines which language and country version to show, so a translated page could still rank in its market. If the page was thin, it usually ranked a little lower. It didn’t disappear.

See also: Lost In Translation: How Language Changes Which Brand AI Recommends

AI search changes the unit of competition. Traditional search selected a page. AI search builds an answer from facts, passages, and evidence collected from many sources. That shift exposes a significant problem the traditional efficiency model created.

When search engines find a cluster of pages that are essentially the same, they don’t fully process and store every version. One version is selected as the canonical and processed in full. The others are treated more like alternate names that point back to it, carrying only enough information (URL, language, country) to be served in the right context.

AI systems refer to this as canonical tokenization, the process by which text across different languages is split, compressed, and processed. It is efficient for the search engine, and it works reasonably well when the job is to swap one URL for another on a results page.

It works much less well when an AI system is retrieving passages to build an answer. The passage it retrieves often comes from the canonical version, and once that passage is pulled out of the page, it no longer carries the URL that told everyone which market it belonged to.

I described the result in How AI’s Geo-Identification Failures Are Rewriting International SEO: When markets look the same, the strongest instance of your content wins. In most global companies, that is the U.S. or main English site.

So a buyer in Germany may get U.S. product availability. A patient in Japan may read about a product or use that is not approved there. A Spanish-language query from Spain may be answered with content written for Mexico.

This is the uncomfortable part for those of us who built global content programs. Translation memory was designed to maximize content reuse at scale. AI retrieval systems are designed to discard reuse.

Every sentence we reused across 30 markets now makes those markets look more alike to a machine. The higher our TM leverage, the stronger the case that our local pages were alternate versions of one global page, not unique sources worth retrieving in their own right.

When local teams said “this doesn’t feel like our market,” they were describing exactly what an AI system now concludes.

The twin engines of the marketing agility framework describe two forces every multinational has to run at the same time:

Research on the framework found that organizations perform best when both engines are running. Most global content programs, however, were built almost entirely around the global engine. The local engine was treated as a cost to be minimized, because local responsiveness was expensive. Every market-specific page needed a writer, a reviewer, and a budget line.

The usual way enterprises use AI today is to make the global engine faster: translate more content into more languages with fewer people. That produces more of the same near-identical pages, only quicker. It is a faster photocopier.

The bigger opportunity is to use AI to make the local engine more affordable. If AI handles the tedious and time-consuming activities of drafting, translation, structuring, and formatting, people in each market can spend their time on what only they can provide: local evidence, local questions, and local judgment.

A content factory built for AI search starts from a different premise. The product isn’t pages. The product is governed, market-scoped knowledge, and pages are one of the ways that knowledge is published.

Before anything is written or translated, the organization needs a single source of truth where its important claims live. Each fact should record:

This sounds like a governance exercise, and it is. It is also the only reliable way to prevent a fact that is true in one market from being published or retrieved as if it were true in all of them.

This is the most important change to the translation workflow. Not every sentence should be treated the same way.

Translation memory is still valuable for the first category. Product names, for example, should be identical across languages so that AI systems recognize them as the same entity. It is, however, a mistake to let TM leverage fill the second category. When a market-variable slot is empty, the factory should flag it, not copy the U.S. version into it.

With the fact registry and the segment rules in place, AI can now handle most of the production work by drafting from approved facts, translating and structuring pages around real questions, and verifying that the right source has been integrated for every market-variable slot.

This is where the cost savings come from now. The savings don’t come from reusing more sentences. They come from automating everything related to local evidence, so local teams can supply that evidence without bearing the full cost of producing the page.

The global engine contributes what should be identical everywhere; the local engine contributes what must differ. Both meet in the fact registry, and AI assembles each market’s pages from it.

“Keeping the human touch” is often understood as keeping a human post-editor at the end of the machine translation process. That role is becoming harder to defend on quality alone. A recent localization benchmark published here on Search Engine Journal found AI workflows outscored human translators in four of six content types.

I don’t read that as the end of human involvement. I read it as a signal that the human value has moved upstream.

In an AI content factory, people in each market are needed at four points:

Notice that these are the same things local teams were complaining about for years. They were never really asking for better translation. They were asking for their market’s reality to be represented.

This also changes how global SEO and content teams should be organized. The roles and service-level agreements I described in Effective SEO Organizational Structure For A Global Company need to include ownership of local evidence, not only local publishing.

Because AI systems retrieve passages that lose their URL context, each important passage has to carry its own market information. A few simple rules make a large difference:

These rules are easy to build into an AI-assisted workflow. They are much harder to apply consistently when 40 vendors are translating by hand.

Most global teams can tell you how many pages they published per market. Very few can tell you what an AI assistant says about them in each market.

That measurement should be part of the factory, not a one-time audit. Build a fixed set of priority prompts for each market, in the local language, and run them across the major AI assistants on a regular schedule. Then track four things:

Market leakage is the metric I’d watch most closely. It is the most direct measure of whether your local content is being recognized as local. It also gives local teams something they never had in the old model: evidence that their concerns are affecting the business.

Test in local languages, not just English. An English-only visibility check will not show you what a buyer in Seoul or Madrid is seeing.

Consider a composite example drawn from patterns common to global medical device manufacturers.

The company has a well-run global site with a dozen market versions. The technical setup, by traditional international SEO standards, is mostly correct, including hreflang and localized URLs. By traditional international SEO standards, it passes.

When viewed for geographical signals market by market, the picture is completely different:

None of these are translation problems. Each one is a missing piece of local knowledge, and each one was probably raised by someone in that market at some point.

The fix follows the factory model: Register the facts by market, mark which content is market-variable, have local teams supply the evidence and the questions, let AI assemble and structure the pages, and measure what AI assistants say in each language afterward.

The global content model wasn’t wrong to pursue efficiency. For a long time, local responsiveness at scale was simply too expensive, and search engines, using hreflang, were forgiving enough that translated pages could still compete.

AI search removes that forgiveness. When content is the same or very similar everywhere, AI systems collapse them into a single entity, and the strongest version speaks for every market.

AI also removes the excuse. The work that made local content expensive (drafting, translating, formatting, structuring) is exactly the work AI does well. What remains for people is the work local teams were asking to do all along.

So before you scale your content factory with AI, ask a simple question: Are you using AI to publish more of the same, faster? Or are you using it to give each market what it was asking for, finally?

Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”

Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI says it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

#7509. Google Favors High Ad Strength RSAs, But Lower-Rated Ads Convert Better via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
