Explore Ahrefs’ Q2, Q3 2026 AI search benchmarks and practical next steps.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Brad Geddes analyzed 5,900+ Google Ads accounts. Higher ad strength RSAs win more impressions, but pinned, lower-rated ads often convert better. What to change.

If you run responsive search ads, Google is now steering more impressions toward whichever ad in an ad group carries the higher ad strength rating. That ad has the better conversion rate only 45% of the time.

A new study by Brad Geddes, co-founder of Adalysis, analyzed more than 5,900 Google Ads accounts to answer a question PPC managers have argued about since RSAs became the default ad format. Does higher ad strength lead to better performance?

His answer is yes for some ads and no for others. The difference comes down to one setting, which is pinning.

I’ve known Brad since May 2011, when he became the PPC Faculty Chair at Market Motive while I was the faculty chair of Video and Content Marketing. And as one of the co-authors of Digital Marketing Fundamentals, which Wiley published in 2023, I asked Brad to contribute the chapter on Digital Advertising. So, I can vouch for his Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness (E-E-A-T) in PPC and paid media.

When Brad previewed the findings in a LinkedIn post last week, calling ad strength “one of Google Ads’ most misunderstood metrics,” I went back to read his full study, which follows up on the company’s 2022 ad strength study. That gives us a four-year view of how Google’s ad serving has drifted.

Here is what the data shows, where it collides with what Google says, and what I’d change in your accounts before holiday traffic peaks.

Start with the official position, because Brad’s numbers only become interesting against it.

Google’s Help Center describes ad strength as a guide for the ad creation stage. It says the rating “doesn’t directly influence your ad’s serving eligibility” and isn’t used to calculate Ad Rank, Quality Score, or auction wins.

Ginny Marvin, Google’s Ads Product Liaison, has been just as direct. In a March 2024 post on X, she wrote that ad strength “isn’t used directly in the auction & shouldn’t limit your testing.”

I take Google at its word on the mechanics. But “not an auction input” and “doesn’t affect which of your ads gets shown” are two different claims, and Brad’s data speaks to the second one.

The most useful part of Brad’s study isolates ad groups with two active RSAs that carry different ad strength ratings. Both ads share the same keywords, bids, and budget, which strips out a lot of noise.

In those ad groups, the higher-rated ad received more impressions 63% of the time. An Excellent ad beat a Poor ad on impressions in 78% of ad groups. Ads two ratings apart, such as Excellent versus Average or Good versus Poor, won 66% of the time. Even the closest matchup, Good versus Average, went to the higher-rated ad 59% of the time.

The higher-rated ad had the higher CTR in 52.5% of ad groups, barely better than a coin flip. It had the higher conversion rate in only 45%, which means the lower-rated ad converted better in 55% of ad groups. On conversions per 1,000 impressions, a metric Adalysis calls CPI, the lower-rated ad won 54.3% of the time.

Then there’s cost. The lower-rated ad had the lower CPA in 51.5% of ad groups, and across all ad groups the higher-rated ads ran an 11.8% higher CPA. In Brad’s example, a lower-rated ad with a $100 CPA would face a higher-rated rival at $111.80.

Brad’s warning for anyone running ad tests is Google “will serve the higher-rated ad more often, even if it has a worse conversion rate or CPI.”

See also: Why a Sky-High CTR Does Not Mean Your Ads Are Actually Working

Because Adalysis ran a similar study in 2022, Brad can show which way Google’s serving has moved.

Google is leaning harder on the higher-rated ad when it picks which ad to show, and that pick lines up with clicks a little better than it did four years ago. It does not line up with conversions any better. Brad concludes that Google “has increased its reliance on ad strength to determine what ad to show in an auction over the years.”

That’s his reading of observational data, and Google would likely dispute the word “reliance.”

Before anyone decides ad strength is useless, look at who the lower-rated ads are.

Brad attributes most of their conversion edge to pinning. In most of the mixed-strength ad groups, one ad was pinned and the other wasn’t. Pinned ads tend to earn lower ratings, and they also tend to post higher conversion rates.

That makes sense to anyone who has pinned a headline on purpose. You pin a price, a required disclaimer, or a qualifier because you want to filter the click rather than chase it. Ad strength rewards variety and keyword coverage, and a pinned ad written to pre-qualify buyers works against both.

The unpinned results look very different. Among unpinned ads, CTR rose with every step up in ad strength, and so did CPI. Conversion rates rose slightly at each step except Poor to Average. For those ads, Brad’s conclusion is that chasing a higher rating generally pays off.

So, the honest summary isn’t that ad strength doesn’t matter. It’s that ad strength predicts performance well when you leave Google’s system alone and poorly when you’ve deliberately overridden it.

See also: Google Ads Bid Strategy Testing: What Changed In 2026

Only a third of unpinned ads in the dataset reached Excellent, and Brad’s asset counts show why stuffing in headlines won’t get you there.

Without pinning, an ad can reach Good with as few as seven assets. For Excellent, Brad recommends at least 11 different headlines. Volume alone doesn’t do it, though. Only 44% of ads with 15 or more headlines reached Excellent, and in the most extreme case, an ad with 38 assets was still rated Poor.

Once you pin, the minimum asset count to reach Good jumps to 10. Pinning two positions now caps an ad at Good and often leaves it at Poor or Average, which is stricter than what Adalysis saw in 2022. If you pin all three headline positions, Brad suggests aiming for about 13 assets.

There is a workaround. Pinning three or more different assets to the same position still leaves room for Excellent, while pinning only one or two caps the ad at Good. Position matters too, since headline one carries more weight than headline two, which carries more than headline three.

I’ve been in paid search since 2003, and Google has asked advertisers to trust a diagnostic label for most of that time. Quality Score came first. Google’s Ads Product Liaison has said it is also a diagnostic rather than an auction input, yet the expected CTR, ad relevance, and landing page signals behind it clearly shape what we pay. Ad strength looks like the same kind of label.

My read is that Google and Brad can both be right. The rating itself may never enter the auction. But the things that raise it, more distinct headlines, better keyword coverage, and fewer pins, give Google’s system more combinations to work with when it predicts which of your ads will earn the click. In your account, the outcome is the same either way. The higher-rated ad gets the traffic.

That’s where I think practitioners should push back. Google’s ad selection appears tuned to clicks, and your business generally gets paid on conversions. An 11.8% CPA gap across ad groups is not a rounding error at holiday budgets. Treat ad strength as a traffic allocator you have to manage, and stop treating it as a score you have to win.

See also: How To Measure PPC Performance When AI Controls The Auction

Sort your RSAs by pinning status before you read a single rating. Tag each ad as unpinned, partly pinned, or fully pinned in Google Ads Editor or a report export. The rating means something different in each group, so judge each group on its own.

Push unpinned ads to Excellent with variety, not volume. Brad recommends at least 11 headlines that mix keywords, benefits, features, calls to action, and authority statements. If an unpinned ad sits at Average with 15 headlines, the likely culprit is repetition. Rewrite the near-duplicates before you add more.

Rebuild pinned ads instead of abandoning them. Brad’s process is to remove the pins, build the ad to Excellent, then re-pin and keep adding assets until the rating reaches at least Average, or Good if you pin a single headline. Where you must pin, pin three or more variations to that position. If you pin all three headlines, plan on about 13 assets.

Judge tests on CPI and CPA, and give mismatched tests more time. Brad says it’s fine to run ads with different ratings in the same ad group. Expect the lower-rated ad to collect far fewer impressions, though, since an Excellent ad took the impression lead in nearly four of five matchups against a poor one. That stretches the time it takes to reach statistical significance. If the lower-rated, pinned ad wins on CPA, keep it running. Don’t pause a winner to fix a label.

Brad closes his study with a line every PPC manager should keep handy. He writes that “often, the human ability to create compelling ads will outperform the machine’s ability to serve the ads properly.”

I agree with one caveat. The machine still decides how often your best human-written ad gets seen. So, ad strength is something to check against your own conversion data, ad group by ad group, rather than a grade to celebrate.

Google tells us what the rating isn’t. Brad’s 5,900 accounts tell us what it does.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Two rank trackers' data shows unrelated Google results that follow one word of the query, mostly below the top spots. Here's how to check a ranking drop.

In mid-September, most unrelated results discovered by SE Ranking using Google rank checking were only about one word of the original search term. Almost all of them started at position 9 or worse.

SE Ranking released an analysis today based on 10,000 Google US desktop keywords it tracks for research purposes. Rank tracking firm Nozzle documented a related pattern in an Oct. 22 report on what it describes as Google ignoring part of a query. According to Nozzle’s findings, page 2 started dropping words on Sept. 16 while page 1 dropped words four days later (Sept. 20). Both firms sell rank tracking software and track ranks through their respective products.

On Oct. 23 I covered how rank tracking providers say they handle the altered Google results; prior to that, on Oct. 14 Roger Montti reported Nozzle’s initial analysis. Both data sets show that most changes occurred in positions below the top positions. Nozzle’s data shows that most of the changes it saw occur on page 2. As such, when reviewing your late September/October ranking reports, check drops below the top positions and on page 2 first.

The primary example of a single-word result set offered by SE Ranking is for the search term “business bank line of credit.” The top 9 results on this search were all financial institutions (banks/lenders) such as Chase Bank, PNC Bank and LendingTree. Results found on page 2 were unrelated to banking or lending as they included videos of music, the LINE messaging application and The Line Hotel; therefore these results only used the word “line” in relation to the original query, rather than answering the query.

In 84% of the cases SE Ranking flagged, the unrelated listings were about one word of the query. The rest followed two or more words. Single-word keywords in its data never came back with unrelated results, which the company says could be because there was no other word for the results to follow.

In one of Nozzle’s examples, “easy strawberry jam” on Sept. 30, the AI Overview still gave a jam recipe while the organic results were about the word “easy,” including the TV series Easy. Nozzle found the page title still showed the full query on 99.8% of the pages that dropped words, with no “Showing results for” notice.

SE Ranking saved up to 50 organic results per keyword, and none of the groups of unrelated results it found started in the top five. They started at positions 6 to 8 in 3.5% of affected result sets and at position 9 or lower in the other 96.5%. SE Ranking notes that a quick look at the top results could make such a page seem fine.

Since Sept. 16, page 2 ignored part of the query on 12.6% of the desktop searches Nozzle could judge on both pages, compared with 2.2% for page 1. On 93.6% of the page 2s that dropped words, page 1 still answered the query.

The way SE Ranking and Nozzle assess a search issue differs, therefore their rates cannot be compared directly to one another.

On Sept. 16, the estimated percentage of keywords in SE Ranking’s sample whose saved result list included any unrelated listing was 0.09%. On Sept. 17 the estimate was 57.3%, and by Sept. 24, which was the end of the test period, the percentage had grown to 67.2%.

Nozzle will flag a search results page if a term that has historically appeared in search results for the keyword appears in 20% or less of those results. Using this method, Nozzle measured that page 1 or page 2 lost terms on approximately 13.9% of the desktop searches it judged on both pages from Sept. 16 through Oct. 21. The highest rate of losing terms was approximately 39.9% on Sept. 28. Nozzle also observed short-term spikes in the occurrence of the pattern since March.

Nozzle viewed this as a different failure type from the “poisoned” search results it reported in October where the query is still answered; however the keyword’s typical websites do not appear. According to Nozzle’s data, when a page lost terms, the keyword’s subsequent search page(s) within 3 days provided an answer to the query about 85.8% of the time.

The numbers shown in SE Ranking’s daily report spanned from Sept. 17 through Sept. 24. SE Ranking’s baseline tests run in October utilized differing collection settings. A sampling of cases was assessed by two independent AI reviewers, and 40 disputed cases were manually reviewed. SE Ranking adds that its data only covers organic listings and can’t tell Google’s intent or what searchers saw, and that Google hasn’t publicly explained the results.

SE Ranking notes that if an unrelated result has taken over the lower part of a search engine results page (SERP), a website which normally appears there may appear to be missing from a tracker report without its rank necessarily changing for people using the Google search engine.

Before reporting a late September/October drop at position 9 or lower or on a second page, go through the collected results from your last update to see if the pages that took your place were related to just one word in the query. Then go back to your next update and look at Search Console data for impressions and clicks on the same query, as SE Ranking suggests.

AccuRanker, whose page 1 history check I described on Oct. 23, has updated its post to say pages 2 and beyond have a related problem, with results for only one word of the query. It says it will cover that in a separate article. Check with your tracker to see whether it reviews page 2 or stops at page 1.

#7506. What Reddit’s Q3 earnings mean for marketers amid major traffic shift

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform’s ad revenue climbed 54% YoY, but signs of a slowdown persist.

Despite ad revenue growing 54% year-over-year, Reddit’s stock took a nosedive after the closing bell following the release of its Q3 earnings Thursday, largely due to slowed user growth and plunging referral traffic. Revenue overall grew 53% to $895 million YoY.

The social media platform, which went public in 2024, has been riding a wave of explosive growth driven by increased advertising capabilities and its high citation rate by artificial intelligence. However, as growth shows signs of tapering off and daily active users remain flat quarter-over-quarter, Reddit’s future is less clear.

Below, Marketing Dive pulled together three numbers from Reddit’s most recent earnings materials that marketers should be aware of as the platform becomes a bigger player in the online advertising space.

Reddit’s ad revenue growth outpaced overall revenue growth by a point. While strong, ad revenue made bigger gains earlier in the year and grew 64% YoY in Q2 and 74% YoY in Q1.

Click volume grew more than 50% in the most recent quarter and conversion volume more than tripled YoY, said Jen Wong, Reddit’s chief operating officer, during an earnings call. The platform forged deeper relationships with existing advertisers, with average spending and new advertiser acquisition both on the upswing, Wong reported. There was also a more than 50% YoY growth in mid-market advertisers in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as North America.

As shoppers are increasingly bombarded by synthetic content, Reddit remains a go-to for those looking for a human opinion and half of U.S. shoppers verify AI recommendations on the platform, according to Wong. This makes Reddit a prime environment for advertisers looking to go after high-intent audiences.

“We see significant opportunity ahead for our business, and we're making progress reflected in strong customer retention, growing share of wallet and more always-on advertiser relationships. These trends give us confidence in Reddit's ability to deliver durable, differentiated growth,” said Wong, during the call.

The average number of referrals dropped per week in October

The number of U.S. daily users fell from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in Q3 while international users rose from 77.1 million to 79.6 million, according to a shareholder letter.

This falloff can be, in-part, attributed to a sharp decrease in referral traffic. In October, referrals are falling by over one million per week on average. If the trend continues, Reddit’s daily active unique user count could fall by low double-digits next quarter, according to the letter. Changes to how consumers use AI overviews on Google, which continue to routinely cite Reddit, are in no small part behind the drop, according to Steven Huffman, co-founder and CEO of Reddit, during an earnings call.

“The reality is the AI Mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not to anybody as far as I know. So it's just a fundamental shift in how Google works,” said Huffman during the call. “It used to be a traffic driver. Now it's not.”

The platform has existing relationships with AI developers. Just before it went public in 2024, the platform signed a $60 million-a-year AI content deal with Google. A few months later, it entered into a similar deal with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. Both deals are set to expire in 2027. Google is still “crawling” the platform “as hard as ever,” per Huffman. He also maintains that Reddit is one of the most Googled terms, meaning demand for the platform remains high.

To help combat user loss, the platform is shifting to a “logged-in only” experience, Huffman announced during the call. Logged-in users make up the bulk of Reddit’s engagement and are more valuable to advertisers, according to the co-founder. It will also help to protect the platform’s data.

The QoQ revenue growth of Reddit’s Ads API ecosystem

Reddit continues to build out its advertising tools. During the quarter, Reddit Max, an automated campaign offering, entered public beta, according to Wong. Automation is one area of focus for the company, along with expanding Reddit for Business and delivering increased value to advertisers.

Reddit is also seeing strength in video, with video ad revenue growth more than doubling YoY in Q3, according to the shareholder letter. During the quarter, the platform launched a 15-second engaged video view, building on the momentum of a six-second option. Retailer JCPenney saw a 4-point lift in ad awareness and a 90% higher completion rate with the longer videos compared to the shorter ones, per the letter.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Discover effective strategies to generate demand and measure results for your B2B marketing campaigns successfully.

Adding another B2B marketing channel only helps if your team can capture the interest it creates and evaluate whether that investment is working. A promising traffic report is not the same as evidence that a campaign generated additional demand.

In How To Create Demand You Can Actually Convert (And Prove), Shaun Bruno, Senior Growth Marketing Manager at CallRail, and Colin Saunders of Matter Made explained how they approached channel selection, secured funding for tests, and measured results before scaling spend.

Bruno described how CallRail simplified its marketing mix around paid search and the landing pages needed to convert existing demand. The team then strengthened measurement, clarified its ideal customer profile, and built out consideration and retargeting programs before investing further in awareness.

That sequence mattered more than copying CallRail’s full channel mix. As Shaun Bruno put it:

“But the important takeaway is that you don’t need to run all these channels.”

His broader point was that the bottom of the funnel needed to support the demand created at the top. More reach would not repair a landing page, offer, or follow-up process that failed to convert interested buyers.

Saunders distinguished between the buying patterns his agency encountered among smaller businesses and enterprise accounts. For SMB and mid-market programs with existing search demand, paid search offered a way to reach people actively researching a solution and establish acquisition benchmarks.

Enterprise programs often needed more education and time to engage a buying group, so his team leaned more heavily on paid social. He presented these as starting approaches, not a universal channel split for every business.

The channel decision also depended on what the buyer would encounter after the click. Saunders connected positioning, the offer, and creative: a demo request, an educational resource, and a product video served different needs. He described testing creative and landing-page content against the audience’s stage rather than expecting one asset to do every job.

The presenters emphasized defining a test’s business purpose before pitching a new platform. Saunders outlined three requirements: identify the problem, agree on the measurement and reporting cadence, and set a timeframe with a decision date.

For a lean budget, he recommended narrowing the audience or geography instead of spreading spend across a national market. A smaller test could investigate a specific segment, provided leadership understood what it could reveal and how long it needed to run.

He also stressed connecting advertising data with CRM outcomes. Form submissions could provide an early signal, but the team needed visibility into whether those leads became opportunities and customers. That distinction helped turn a request for more traffic into a business case for further investment.

Bruno’s connected TV example showed why the session’s testing walkthrough went beyond a campaign dashboard. CallRail initially saw encouraging website visits and trial activity from its CTV pilot through LinkedIn. Bruno cautioned that an ad exposure followed by a conversion did not establish that the ad caused it.

To investigate further, the team ran a 60-day holdout test with an audience eligible for CTV exposure and a control group that was not. Both groups entered the same downstream campaigns. Bruno described using the comparison to support a broader rollout, then monitoring acquisition efficiency as spend increased.

The useful lesson was the progression: early signals justified a more rigorous experiment, and that experiment informed the next investment decision. The pilot was a case study, not a guarantee that another advertiser would see the same result.

Bruno separated three ways of examining marketing’s contribution:

These views answered different questions. A rise in branded search could strengthen the case for further investigation; it was not interchangeable with a directly attributed conversion or proof of incremental revenue.

In their discussion of emerging LLM advertising, Saunders described limited reporting and the difficulty of evaluating indirect effects. The presenters also discussed self-reported attribution as another source of context, rather than treating any one measurement as the whole story.

During Q&A, an attendee asked whether Saunders’ recommendation to start enterprise programs with paid social meant LinkedIn. He said LinkedIn was typically the starting point, while paid search still had a role.

Bruno added a distinction between finding new prospects and re-engaging people who had already visited the site. The likely location of the buyer guided prospecting; retargeting could reach that same person elsewhere. Saunders described YouTube retargeting as one way to begin testing the channel before expanding into prospecting.

#7504. Anthropic: Autonomous Systems Security Engineer

Anthropic’s mission is to create reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems. We want AI to be safe and beneficial for our users and for society as a whole. Our team is a quickly growing group of committed researchers, engineers, policy experts, and business leaders working together to build beneficial AI systems.

Claude is trained and served on hardware in data centers Anthropic operates and in sites partners build and run for us. DCSE secures that footprint: the sites, the hardware moving through them, and the people and vendors who touch it. You'll be the engineer who owns autonomous systems across that footprint as one security domain, from both sides: drones, ground robots and automated vehicles for patrol, inspection and moving hardware, including the security of that automation inside secure areas, and the detection systems that tell us what is flying over or operating near a site uninvited.

You set the approach, select and integrate the platforms and sensors, write the requirements vendors build to, and run what you ship, from the operating model where operators assign missions and machines carry them out to the playbook that turns a detection into an identified track and a well-evidenced handoff to whoever holds authority over the airspace. Interdiction is not part of this role. The goal is security that runs itself: coverage, fleet health and evidence verified continuously, with tools and AI agents doing the routine triage. We favor simple, standard controls and tools that can be verified over elaborate ones. We use Claude throughout our engineering workflow and expect you to as well.

You'll work with the rest of DCSE, including its physical security systems engineers and the engineers on its security monitoring platform, with Anthropic's data center operations and legal teams, and directly with site operators, equipment vendors and aviation and public safety authorities. The role is based in San Francisco, with remote applicants in the US considered, and involves regular travel to data center sites, which are critical infrastructure.

Autonomous security and inspection systems: own the drones, ground robots and other autonomous platforms for perimeter patrol, incident response and infrastructure inspection: platform selection, operating model, operator qualification, maintenance, and the data path from machine to analyst

Tools, automation and AI agents: build the integrations that carry detections, tracks, telemetry and fleet health into the team's security monitoring platform, and the tools and agents that triage detections, check fleet health and assemble evidence. When a review keeps costing people time, you build the tool or agent that retires it

Detection of uncrewed systems: engineer the sensing that tells us what is flying over or operating near a site, what it is and who needs to know: sensor selection and evaluation against live targets, per-site coverage, classification and false-alarm handling, and the playbook from first detection to handoff, with evidence retained

Security of site automation: engineer the controls on automated vehicles, robots and similar machines that move hardware or work inside secure areas: identity and access, network isolation, what they may record and where it goes, fail-secure behavior, their place in chain of custody, and acceptance before they enter a site

Health monitoring: define and test heartbeats, loss-of-coverage and lost-link alarms and fail-secure behavior, so a silent sensor or machine shows as a fault, not a quiet day

Vendor requirements and acceptance: write the requirements, evaluate against live flights and runs, and hold vendors to what they ship

Have engineered autonomous or sensing systems in the field (drones, ground robots, automated vehicles, or RF, radar or optical detection sensors): selected, integrated or secured them for an operation other people relied on, and verified what they actually do against real targets or runs rather than a datasheet

Have integrated systems you did not build (vendor APIs, SDKs, appliances, machine and sensor telemetry) into a platform that outlives any one of them

Read and review code, design the data systems behind security tooling, and build automation (often with AI coding agents) using Git and code review

Have done this work hands-on for data centers, critical infrastructure or a large hardware fleet

Own a domain end to end: set the approach, carry it through with vendors, site operators, partners and authorities, and run it as something people depend on every day

Remote pilot certification (for example FAA Part 107) and experience flying beyond visual line of sight under a waiver or exemption

Experience with counter-drone (counter-UAS) detection, airspace surveillance or air traffic data systems

Experience running a robot, drone or automated-vehicle fleet in an industrial, logistics or data center setting: fleet management, mission planning, safety cases

Experience securing embedded, operational technology or robotic systems: device identity, network segmentation, update control, logging

Experience with physical security operations at large sites, with law enforcement or aviation authorities, or at sites you did not fully control: cloud, colocation or GPU cloud operators

Have built AI agents or automation that replaced recurring manual work

#7503. FinOps Data Engineer at Supabase

About the RoleWe're looking for a FinOps Data Engineer to help drive cost optimization and cloud financial governance across our AWS infrastructure and GCP footprint. You'll work cross-functionally with Engineering, Finance, and Product to find and ship savings, build the tooling necessary to maximize efficiency of every dollar spent in the cloud, and cultivate a culture of cost awareness across engineering teams. This role owns the data side of that mission: the models, pipelines, and analysis that make cost, usage, and margin numbers trustworthy across the company.This is a hands-on engineering role, not an analyst seat. You'll do the schlep work other teams don't have time for, digging into a bucket's access pattern, writing the dbt model or Python pipeline that ships the fix, building the cost-vs-revenue mart that answers a margin question once instead of every time, and chasing a number until it reconciles. Strong communication matters as much as technical depth, you'll regularly explain a savings case or a data model's implications to an engineering team, a finance stakeholder, and a leadership audience in the same week.What You'll Be Responsible ForIn this role, you'll:

Find and ship savings across AWS and GCP: Analyze billing, usage, and cost trends to identify opportunities, rightsizing, storage lifecycle policies, data transfer, and spot/auto-scaling. Take ideas from identification through to a realized dollar figure, not just a recommendation.

Build and maintain the FinOps data pipeline: Design and run the BigQuery/dbt models that turn raw billing and usage data (CUR, Storage Lens) into reconciled, trustworthy mart tables, the foundation everything else in FinOps is built on.

Build cost-vs-revenue and customer segmentation models: Model unit economics and margin by product line and customer segment, and extend coverage as new products and segments come online.

Apply data science to cost and usage data: Build forecasting models, detect anomalies statistically rather than by threshold alone, and quantify savings opportunities (e.g. storage lifecycle, request-cost patterns) with rigor a spreadsheet can't match.

Build and maintain cost attribution: Tagging policies, cost allocation, and chargeback/showback so engineering teams can see and own their own spend. This is foundational work other savings work depends on.

Automate cost governance: Build automated cost reporting, anomaly detection, and alerting. Write the scripts and infrastructure-as-code (Python, Terraform, Lambda) that enforce cost policy rather than relying on manual review.

Partner with engineering on architecture decisions: Bring cost into the room early, cost-efficiencies are cheaper to get right at design than to retrofit.

Work with Finance on forecasting and reporting: Support budget tracking and financial KPIs; build dashboards and self-serve analytics engineering and finance can both read.

Have strong AWS expertise and working GCP knowledge, including pricing models, billing structures, and cost optimization mechanics.

Have data engineering depth: dbt, BigQuery (or an equivalent modern warehouse), SQL at scale, and data modeling for analytics (dimensional modeling, incremental models, testing).

Have data science fundamentals: statistical forecasting, anomaly detection, and experimentation, and know when a rigorous model beats a rule of thumb.

Have automation and scripting skills: Python, Terraform/ pulumi, Lambda, or Bash.

Are comfortable with cost/billing tooling: AWS Cost Explorer, Cost & Usage Reports, GCP Billing Reports, and BI/dashboarding (we use Hex).

Have experience with, or are comfortable picking up, Linear and Notion as the system of record for tracking and documenting FinOps work.

Experience with a dedicated cloud cost management platform (e.g. CloudZero, Vantage, or similar) is a plus, not required.

Can analyze cost data and present it clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences.

Have prior experience spanning data analytics, data engineering, or data science in a FinOps, cloud cost management, or cloud governance context.

Are energized by doing the unglamorous, high-leverage work (the schlep) that unblocks other teams, and by working cross-functionally without positional authority.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

#7502. After AI backlash, Svedka challenges consumers to create Super Bowl ad

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The Sazerac-owned vodka brand is pivoting after using artificial intelligence to produce its 2026 big game debut.

Svedka is handing over the reins for its next Super Bowl ad to consumers, per a press release. The Sazerac-owned brand is challenging consumers to make a 15-second commercial featuring its ready-to-drink Vodka Water cocktail offering, which launched this summer and is sold in a clear can — what the brand claims is a category-first innovation.

Consumers can submit ads to a microsite until Dec. 1, with the winner receiving a $500,000 prize. The contest comes after the vodka brand faced controversy earlier this year for using artificial intelligence to bring its fembot mascot to life as part of its first Super Bowl ad. Despite the backlash, Sveda has been the top volume growth driver in U.S. spirits in the last year, per Nielsen data cited by the brand.

“We're proud of what we accomplished in 2026, but we heard plenty of people say they could do a better job. And we welcomed the debate,” Sara Saunders, group president and CMO at Sazerac, said in a statement. “We can't wait to see how fans bring the brand's newest innovation to life.”

Svedka is making a digital tool kit available to consumers as they create ads that can be “AI-led, hilariously low-budget, unexpectedly cinematic or creatively ambitious,” per press details.

To launch the contest, Svedka teamed with Andy Cohen for an interview with the Svedbot appearing on YouTube in which the reality TV host notes that the previous ad was called “bold, bizarre and a dystopian nightmare.” Cohen will also help to evaluate the submissions.

Svedka’s 30-second national ad that ran during Super Bowl LX was managed by the brand’s in-house team with production by AI innovation lab Silverside. The spot represented the first national Super Bowl commercial dedicated solely to vodka in over three decades, and featured a brand mascot that had recently returned to advertising after a 12-year hiatus.

#7499. Google says AI chatbots are hurting its bottom line

The company may be losing its stronghold on discovery as more users turn to tools such as ChatGPT and Claude for answers.

Google said that the rising use of artificial intelligence chatbots, including its own AI answers, has impacted its core ad business, and could become an even bigger revenue impediment moving forward.

As part of parent company Alphabet’s Q3 earnings update last week, Google reported that search volume grew by 12% in Q3. That’s a much slower growth rate than Q2’s 17% growth or Q1’s 19% growth. The report also showed that the company’s search revenue was flat in Q3.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai initially said that the company’s evolving AI Mode search saw strong momentum and its AI overviews drive improved discovery and searcher engagement.

But later in the company’s earnings call, Google SVP Anat Ashkenazi said that while AI Mode usage is rising, the growth of these discovery options is having an impact on its ad business.

As per Ashkenazi: “It's worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode. To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here. Our ad experiments have shown promising results and we're now scaling ads within both AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and more queries; including, as I mentioned, international markets and multiturn ads in the U.S.”

Google’s search results are declining over time. As more people use AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Meta’s Muse Google’s discovery usage could be impacted, even though the company has long held an unassailable lead in search.

As Ashkenazi said, Google is planning to resolve this by increasing ad displays in its AI products, which will help to offset some of those losses. But as more people rely on conversational answers for their queries, that shrinks the opportunity for Google to display query-relevant ads, which is the core driver of its ad business.

Essentially, Google is harming its own revenue potential by implementing AI answers. Yet, at the same time, it’s possible that the broader industry shift towards AI chatbots would have forced Google’s hand on this front either way.

It’s unclear whether Google should continue to pump out AI chatbot responses to queries, especially if that’s only going to end up costing the company more money.

It seems like a losing equation, as AI development costs rise and search ad revenue declines. This also highlights a broader mismatch around AI usage in general because the cost-to-benefit ratio may not match up.

In addition, up to 10% of Google’s AI overviews provide incorrect information, according to a report from The New York Times in July. Also,many others provide flawed or incorrect links, so it begs the question as to whether these AI responses provide real value.

This could be a key note in the rising skepticism around AI tools more broadly.

#7498. WPP Media posts first growth in 2 years as turnaround stays on track

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Sequential quarterly improvements at WPP were cited by executives as evidence that Elevate28 is working, though creative further deteriorated in Q3.

WPP inched further toward a recovery in Q3, with like-for-like revenue less pass-through costs declining 2.1% to roughly $4.39 billion, or 3.27 billion pounds, according to an earnings statement. Organic revenue growth, a metric the ad-holding group shares for easier comparisons to its competitive set, was up 0.5% for the period.

Sequential quarterly improvements — LFL revenue was down 6.7% in Q1 and 2.8% in Q2 of this year — were cited by executives as signs that WPP’s Elevate28 turnaround plan remains on track, including the goal of returning to positive growth in 2027. The company upheld its full-year guidance for 2026.

The network’s media segment posted growth for the first time in two years and after seeing declines of 8.3% and 2.8% in Q1 2026 and Q2 2026, respectively. The U.S. was the biggest contributor to a 0.3% increase in revenue for media, WPP CEO Cindy Rose said on a call discussing the results with investors.

WPP Media secured large pieces of business that could provide future tailwinds. It retained global media duties for The Coca-Cola Company following a review that saw the North American division — which WPP previously held — switch from Publicis Groupe to Omnicom. WPP did not participate in the pitch for Coke’s North America account.

“We made a tough call between spending yet another six weeks pitching for North America versus delivering against what we had already won,” Rose said in response to an analyst question about the decision. “It was a fine judgment call, which I made, and it's as simple as that really.”

DoorDash deepened its relationship with WPP during the quarter, naming the agency network its first global media partner in September. DoorDash recently announced plans to acquire the grocery delivery platform Instacart for $17 billion, which could benefit WPP on the advertising front. WPP has worked with DoorDash for eight years but the remit now spans more than 40 markets.

Rose was asked about other agencies winning clients without engaging in a traditional pitch process. That is how Publicis nabbed PepsiCo from Omnicom, and Publicis has said it is generally picking up more business without needing to pitch.

“You're not going to find anybody that says, ‘I love pitching.’ The cost and burden of the process seems to be increasing. But I think what's really important to me is that my clients fully understand the implications of the decisions they're making,” Rose said on the call.

“These are really high-stakes decisions with material business consequences and they deserve careful consideration,” Rose added. “I don't think we do ourselves any favor as an industry of professionals by encouraging clients to bypass proper due diligence.”

WPP’s results were a mixed bag elsewhere. Its production arm grew 2.5% in Q3, building on positive gains from the prior quarter, but creative further deteriorated, down 5.1% year over year compared to a 3.5% decline in Q2. Some of the creative slide was attributed to polarization across different client verticals, with some industries pulling back on spending, as well as a slower ramp-up in new business.

WPP Creative is undergoing some leadership transitions as well. Jon Cook is departing VML after over three decades while Tyler Turnbull, formerly of Omnicom’s McCann, recently joined as global CEO of WPP Creative.

#7497. Instagram offers to pay creators for long-form content

Creators were offered as much as $500,000 to post videos to Meta’s new Features product, according to Business Insider.

Instagram is reportedly offering some creators up to $500,000 to post long-form content as it looks for new ways to drive interest in its latest content experiment.

Last week, Instagram announced initial testing of its new Features option, which will let creators post videos of up to 90 minutes.

Yet despite providing the capacity to share longer videos, creators don’t have much incentive to do so because YouTube’s Partner Program offers significantly more potential to earn money from that content.

Instagram Chief Adam Mosseri has acknowledged this, and said in a Threads post on Thursday that “the economics matter a ton,” and that he and his team are exploring multiple options to help long-form creators get paid.

According to Business Insider, the first effort on that front is a series of one-off payments to big-name stars.

As per BI: “The Meta-owned platform has offered select creators $50,000 to post long-form video to its new ‘Features’ product, while others have been offered six-figure deals, some of which have reached $500,000.”

Meta didn’t confirm or deny the details. Instead, a Meta spokesperson told Business Insider that Meta is “funding Features content directly with some creators,” and that it’s “excited to see the content going live."

Which suggests that this will be a significant part of its new long-form push. Though Meta should know better than anyone that this type of upfront payment process won’t drive ongoing interest or adoption.

That’s because Meta has done this before. The company offered creators big money deals in the past to post to its long-form content option IGTV.

As reported by SMT sister publication Marketing Dive in 2021, Meta said it would pay out $1 billion to creators in 2022, including special payments to creators who allowed ads in their IGTV content, in order to boost interest in posting long-form videos in the app.

That didn’t raise user interest in the option, and by early 2022, Meta was already moving to shut down the separate IGTV app.

Other platforms have tried similar one-off payment approaches to entice creators to post longer clips. Earlier this year X offered a $175k prize for users who used Grok to generate their own version of “The Odyssey” movie.

Generally, these types of promotions lead to a spike in posts related to the promotion. But in most cases, they don’t spark a sustainable increase in video content posting or consumption.

Maybe Instagram has a better plan in place this time, but without a sustainable revenue share system in place, it’s hard to see the platform’s new long-form option appealing to a lot of creators.

#7495. Where agency strategists see opportunity as AI challenges their worth

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

While strategists fear the tech will replace their roles, the majority agree that there are also reasons to be optimistic, according to a WARC report.

The advertising industry has faced significant challenges this year, marked by agency consolidations at major holding companies and sweeping headcount reductions. Between August 2025 and August 2026, the industry recorded a loss of 6,900 jobs, per Emarketer.

While there are many factors behind the cuts, one of the most prominent has been the rise of artificial intelligence across all aspects of the industry. From data analysis to campaign generation, AI’s adoption has been swift across nearly all marketing disciplines, leaving many executives apprehensive about the future.

Still, 66% of agency-side strategists agree there are clear reasons to be optimistic, according to WARC’s Future of Strategy 2026 report.

“We’re not saying the problems are solved, but we are saying the tides may be turning,” said Lena Roland, content director at WARC Strategy. “After a period of layoffs and consolidation, there’s a sense that things might be stabilizing and strategists can [begin] to look forward again.”

The reasons for the guarded positivity are simple: Clients are seeing a need for thinking that is rooted in human insights, Roland explained. Strategy influence with clients jumped to 50%, up from 41% in 2025, per WARC.

“This indicates that clients are increasingly recognizing the value of strategy, particularly at a time when growth is harder to achieve,” Roland said. “AI can help us understand the world as it is; strategists can help us understand what it can become.”

Ironically, AI is helping fuel strategists’ confidence. Nearly two-thirds, 65%, of the 489 agency-side strategists surveyed said AI gives them time for more nuanced, strategic work. Simultaneously, 55% believe the tech will refocus strategy on human perspectives. WARC’s report was fielded in August.

“Strategists are positioned as the best people to be guardians of reality by grounding ideas in real human insights,” Roland said. “In an age of AI, humanity is a competitive advantage. AI can’t replace human judgment or intuition, and it can’t ask the questions that are really worth asking.”

Not yet, anyway. Despite their optimism for the near-term, strategists are more wary about the long-term. More than half of the strategists polled in WARC’s study — 56%, up from 41% last year — are concerned that AI will eventually advance enough to replace them.

“They’re more optimistic about the future, but they’re also realistic about the scale of change,” Roland said. “The strategists that will thrive are those who learn to use AI well, while still bringing the human perspective, critical thinking and commercial understanding that makes their work valuable.”

However, the technology could become a double-edged sword: The same tools that strategists are using to move upstream with clients could also be leveraged by account executives, explained Michael Farmer, chairman and CEO at marketing consultancy Farmer & Company.

“When agencies talk about AI [right now], they’re not talking about how they can do a more strategic job for their clients,” Farmer said. “If they have the will, the senior account executives can [use AI] to offer more strategy.”

Doing so would elevate account executives to more of a business partner role, rather than one more akin to a traffic manager whose job is to get stuff out the door, Farmer said. He explained that over the past 30-some years, the account executive role has been diminished through the rise of programmatic negotiating, the unbundling of media and creative and the introduction of strategists in the late ‘90s and early 2000s.

“They took away a responsibility that the account people already had,” Farmer said. “They used to tell me when I first got started that the strategist was ‘the conscience of the consumer’ … They were there to kind of provide discipline between caring about the brand and caring about the brief that they got from the client.”

Often, that meant rewriting the briefs accordingly, Farmer said. Now, AI can often write those briefs as well — if not better — than a strategist can, which is reflected in the sentiment from strategists that they have more time to think beyond the brief. Agencies and their strategists will need to find how to prove their value beyond their traditional remit.

“Strategy as a discipline has too often been treated as a supporting function, or even thrown in for free, rather than recognized as a valuable service in its own right,” Roland said. “There’s an opportunity now for strategists to become genuine growth partners, helping shape not just how a brand communicates, but where the business goes next.”

Fortunately for strategists, many are already aware of the need to prove business results. In WARC’s survey, 80% of strategists said they must develop stronger evidence to prove their business impact, and 57% said they need a new value proposition and compensation model.

“AI is a great opportunity, but you have to be a strategist to realize that it could help you tap that unrealized potential,” Farmer said.

Which is ultimately why strategists see hope in the face of AI’s headwinds. Businesses will always be under pressure to demonstrate growth and will always need people who can find new ways to achieve it, whether that is on their own or with the help of AI, Roland explained.

“Businesses will always need people who can diagnose and solve problems,” Roland said. “The best strategists will use AI to get beyond the obvious and connect creativity to commercial outcomes, helping businesses see possibilities they couldn’t see before.”

Editor’s note: Informa, which owns a controlling stake in Marketing Dive’s publisher Informa TechTarget, is also invested in WARC. Informa has no influence over Marketing Dive’s coverage.

#7494. Meta hires bipartisan political team

The company brought in multiple executives with ties to major players on both sides of the U.S. political fence, according to Axios.

Amid questions around the impact and value of its artificial intelligence projects, Meta has recruited a new bipartisan political team to try and sway U.S. politicians to its side.

According to a report from Axios, Meta hired or promoted a range of senior executives in order to win favor with both sides of the political aisle.

Meta appears to be vying for support on both sides of the political aisle as it continues to face intense scrutiny over the impact of its platforms, its broader influence on American and global society, and its massive data center projects.

Employing former political officials is nothing new for major corporations, though the rate of Meta’s steadily increasing political spend is notable.

As reported by Open Secrets, Meta spent $26.29 million on federal lobbying in 2025, with both 2024 and 2025 seeing big spending jumps on this element.

Clearly, the company is concerned about potential restrictions and impacts, which is why it’s working to win favor in any way that it can.

Axios also reported that Meta President Dina Powell McCormick met with the Democratic House Commission on Artificial Intelligence in August to discuss the company’s evolving AI strategy, including its major infrastructure spending.

At least some of Meta’s data center projects have prompted calls for restrictions on such works, due to impacts to local infrastructure and residents.

Those concerns relate to water contamination and usage, as per reporting from the BBC, while NPR has reported on damage to local roads. The Guardian has also reported on noise pollution problems, while, Consumer Reports reported on impacts to electricity supply.

Meta said it works proactively to address these concerns as part of each data center build-out. But questions remain as to the viability of these projects and the value that they may or may not bring to these regions.

The best person for this role is someone who’s energized by customer interaction, comfortable navigating technical systems, and skilled at turning ambiguity into clarity. By improving the quality of initial problem discovery, you’ll help the entire support organization resolve issues faster, more accurately, and with less wasted effort.Alloy operates in a hybrid-work environment. We look to foster collaboration and community by having our local employees onsite three days a week, and remote employees onsite once a quarter.

As a Technical Support Engineer 2, you will be responsible for triaging incoming support cases, leading customer discovery conversations, building high-quality handoffs for senior engineers, and directly resolving straightforward tickets—all using our ticketing system, Zendesk. You’ll be leveraging your technical skills, problem-solving instincts, written communication, and verbal skills to clarify customer issues and build trust with professionalism and empathy.

Alloy is looking for a Technical Support Engineer 2 who combines strong customer instincts with a solid technical floor. The role is ideal for someone who thrives in a fast-paced, reactive environment, values continuous learning, and can get scrappy. You’re energized by frequent customer interaction, comfortable leading short calls to clarify issues, and disciplined enough to turn ambiguous intake into structured, actionable support work. You demonstrate independence while recognizing when to seek guidance for novel or ambiguous situations.

We are looking for someone to work during MST time zone hours.

We value building connections and fostering relationships with both our customers and each other. #7491. X launches new bonus program for video creators

The reward-based effort offers cash incentives to participants for posting videos on the platform.

X has launched a new program to entice video creators to post in the app, with its Video Kickstart program offering cash incentives for users who post a lot of video clips each month.

As explained by X: “The Video Kickstart Bonus is an invite-only pilot program that pays creators a bonus for posting their own short-form, vertical videos on X. Post 15 qualifying videos on 15 different days during a program period, and you earn the bonus for that period.”

Each video needs to be shot in vertical format and be under three minutes long to qualify. X added that videos must be original, though creators will be allowed to post videos they’ve previously shared to other platforms, “as long as they are yours.”

X said selected creators will be invited into the program and need to enroll in the program to get a share of bonus payments.

“The program runs in periods of about one month,” X said. “Each period has an enrollment deadline and a last day to post, and you can find both in your invitation and in Creator Studio.”

X also said that creators who sign up for the program will also be fast-tracked into its Original Content Rewards Program, through which they’ll be able to earn a percentage of any ads shown in relation to their posts.

X has been trying to make video a bigger focus in the app, in order to better align with content consumption trends and get people spending more time in the X feed.

In July, the platform launched an updated livestream studio process and offered $1 million in funding for livestream creators to help raise awareness of the option. In August, X added new video overlay options, and last month it rolled out an updated video composer, which includes a range of improved creative options.

In 2023, X reported that video consumption was rapidly rising in the app. The company said it would be working to improve its video presentation tools to align with this shift.

X is lagging behind a little in getting video posting options out there, but as more people spend time consuming video content, X is clearly looking to draw an increasing amount of video content from its users.

#7490. TikTok inks new content deal with Women’s Tennis Association

The partnership expands an existing relationship and will include livestreamed coverage and behind-the-scenes content.

TikTok announced a new partnership with the Women’s Tennis Association, which will see the app host exclusive women’s tennis content and establish new tournament coverage hubs in order to help drive more engagement in the app.

TikTok said it’s been working with the WTA over the past year to help expand the association’s presence in the app. As a result, the WTA’s TikTok account has surpassed a million followers. WTA content also saw a combined 250 million views and engagements over the past year, which is an increase of 41% year over year.

This deal formalizes TikTok’s partnership with the WTA.

As per TikTok: “On November 3, ahead of the 2026 FAGE WTA Finals in Indian Wells, TikTok will exclusively livestream the official Draw Ceremony, giving fans around the world a center court seat as the matchups are revealed. The livestream will set the stage for the season-ending championship taking place November 8–15, where fans will see the world’s top eight singles players and doubles teams will compete for one of the most prestigious titles in women’s tennis.”

The WTA will also work with TikTok to create a new “WTA Creator Club,” which is designed to engage digital creators in WTA coverage. The program will feature opportunities for creators to access tournaments around the world.

“Participating creators will capture and share the sport through unique viewpoints, offering fans an authentic look at life on Tour, from behind-the-scenes moments to the stories beyond the court,” TikTok said.

There will also be new WTA content access powered by TikTok’s GamePlan offering, which will bring together related content for tournaments and events.

“Player-led storytelling will remain a central focus, with the WTA and TikTok working together to help more athletes build their presence on the platform,” TikTok said. “WTA stars are already using TikTok to share their personalities, interests and experiences beyond competition, connecting directly with fans and helping audiences across sport, fashion, lifestyle and entertainment discover women's tennis.”

Sports content has become a bigger focus for TikTok, with a rising number of fans now turning to the app for insights and highlights.

In 2024, TikTok published a report that found that 59% of its users thought watching sports content in the app was more entertaining than watching the actual games.

TikTok also announced a content partnership with the ATP last year.

#7488. Site Reliability Engineer at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

Supabase manages millions of Postgres instances and is growing. We have strong teams across observability, release engineering, and incident management — and we're concentrating our reliability efforts into a dedicated SRE practice that ties the discipline together across the platform.

You'll be embedded within Service Operations, and your primary job is to make every engineering team more reliable — not by owning their infrastructure, but by establishing the practices, frameworks, and feedback loops that let them own reliability themselves. You'll work across the org: sometimes setting the standard, sometimes pair-programming a fix, sometimes helping a team define their error budget, sometimes telling them it's exhausted.

This role is ideal for someone who has a strong vision for how SRE should work and thrives in async, fast-paced environments where influence matters more than authority.

Partner with service teams to define meaningful SLIs and SLOs grounded in customer experience, and build the error budget policies that turn them into engineering decisions

Own and evolve the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process — conducting reviews for new services and major changes across observability, alerting, runbooks, capacity, and graceful degradation

Strengthen the incident-to-improvement pipeline: connecting postmortem findings to operational readiness gaps, identifying repeat failure patterns, and driving systemic fixes

Act as the reliability expert teams pull in for architecture reviews, failure mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design

Identify and quantify operational toil across the org, and build or advocate for automation that eliminates it

Help teams design sustainable on-call practices: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction

Track and report on org-wide operational maturity, surfacing systemic gaps and driving remediation

Have 7+ years of experience in SRE, production engineering, or reliability-focused roles, including experience shaping SRE practices and driving adoption across engineering teams

Have a software engineering mindset — you write code and build tools, not just configure them

Have hands-on experience defining and operationalizing SLOs/SLIs at scale, including error budget policies that actually influenced engineering decisions

Have deep experience with incident response, postmortem facilitation, and turning incident learnings into systemic improvements

Have worked with large-scale multi-tenant systems (bonus: managed database platforms or Postgres)

Are proficient with cloud infrastructure (AWS preferred) and infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi preferred, Terraform/CDK also acceptable)

Communicate clearly and persuasively — this role requires influencing without authority across a distributed org

Have experience in async or globally distributed teams

Are energized by making other teams more effective rather than being the one who fixes everything

Experience with Kubernetes-based platform operations

Familiarity with OpenTelemetry, VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, or similar observability tooling

Experience building developer-facing reliability tooling (SLO dashboards, ORR frameworks, toil tracking, DORA metrics)

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

#7484. How the sausage is made: Inside Johnsonville’s political parody campaign

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A campaign that culminates with today’s midterm elections sought to engage Americans around a distaste for politics while avoiding partisanship.

On Nov. 2, Johnsonville gave out 1,000 $20 promotional codes that will cover the ingredients for a sausage dinner. The brand also set up shop in Rosa Parks Circle in Grand Rapids, Michigan, the epicenter of a hotly contested Senate race, to dole out free food and product vouchers.

The reason for the sausage fest was simple: Johnsonville’s research shows that consumers are sometimes so consumed by politics — like on the eve of a contentious election day — that they forget to make plans for dinner.

In an environment where Americans rank politics and government as the most important problems facing the country, according to Gallup research, most brand marketers have steered clear of politics, to say nothing of brands that have been dragged into the political muck against their will.

That’s not the case for Johnsonville, the Wisconsin-based sausage brand that launched a campaign in September parodying the tropes of political advertising, suggesting that Americans choose “Sausage for Dinner” in 2026. The effort includes a TV spot, events, an Amazon Ads collaboration and the kind of yard signs and merchandise used by political candidates, with local billboard ads calling for “Affordable Protein for the People” and “A Sausage in Every Air Fryer.”

“This idea is really about parodying the genre and making something fun that stands out amongst all of the dark negative stuff that's just bombarding all of us,” said Jamie Schmelzer, vice president of marketing at Johnsonville.

No matter how politically polarized the country has become, a distaste for politics unites Americans. More than eight in 10 agree that society has become too political, about three-quarters say they hate political advertising and 84% think their community could make better use of the billions spent on political ads this year, per Harris Poll data commissioned by Johnsonville.

“This campaign is talking about politics, but it's not saying anything partisan,” said Schmelzer. “We're all going through this together, regardless of whether you're left, right or independent.”

Or, as Rob Riggle says in a PSA-style campaign video in which the comedian portrays a sausage envoy: “Sausage will unite the mild Italians with the Cajuns, the Mexicans and the Polishes in a glorious crockpot of freedom that will make your tongue burn red, white and blue."

Along with feelings on politics, Johnsonville’s Harris Poll data revealed an insight around how people are constantly struggling to think of what to eat for dinner. The stress caused by politics and current events is only exacerbating that struggle, with more than one-third of Americans saying they were so consumed by current events at least once in the last year that they forgot to figure out what to have for dinner.

“It [was] going to get even noisier, right on top of back to school time, when everybody's getting back in the routine of figuring out what to put on the table for dinner every night, amidst activities and all the other things that come with that time of year,” Schmelzer said about the campaign’s launch timing. “It felt like the right way for our brand to help out by just providing ideas for dinner.”

To help make dinner planning easier, Johnsonville teamed up with Amazon Ads Brand Innovation Lab as part of the campaign. The brand and platform rolled out a custom experience that let consumers browse 30-minute recipes and add ingredients directly to their Amazon Grocery carts. The Nov. 2 promotional code push was also part of the Amazon tie-up.

“For us, [Amazon’s] ability to get everything you need to make dinner on your doorstep quickly was great, and for them, making sure that Americans know that if they need an idea in a pinch, Amazon has the capability,” Schmelzer said.

The “Sausage for Dinner” campaign also includes a purpose-driven partnership with Hunger Free America, with Johnsonville pledging $100,000 to fight food insecurity and the first 100 customers to join the cause receiving a campaign swag bag. The Amazon collaboration saw the e-commerce giant donate $1 to the organization for every hour of eligible viewing of a curated collection of comedies — including “Black Sheep,” “Head of State” and “A League of Their Own” — available through Fire TV.

“We thought a charitable component was really important to this. Groceries are expensive, and that is not a partisan perspective, either. It's affecting everybody,” Schmelzer said. “Sometimes it's about not having the idea [for dinner], but for some people, it's also a financial challenge, and so we wanted to do what we could to help.”

#7482. Companies may need to restrict AI use to manage costs

Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI and Meta have all spent enormous amounts of money to build out their artificial intelligence projects, but have yet to see returns.

The pressure is rising for artificial intelligence projects to show some level of return, with industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic both posting massive losses in their earnings results, and xAI reducing access capacity due to non-viable cost-to-revenue calculations.

First, on OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the biggest AI players, which are both looking to launch their respective IPOs sometime soon.

As reported by Reuters, OpenAI is facing another year of heavy financial losses, with the company recently informing its investors that its projected 2026 revenue could be significantly lower than it had previously forecast.

As per Reuters: “OpenAI has told investors its annualized revenue for September was almost $50 billion, a drop ​from what it signaled earlier, a person familiar with the ‌matter told Reuters on Thursday. The company previously indicated to investors at a separate event that its revenue run rate for last month was approaching $70 billion.”

According to AI Funding Tracker, OpenAI has already weathered more than $20 billion in operating losses in the first half of 2026, with revenue of around $12 billion for the same period. The company had hoped to win more investor confidence ahead of a planned IPO with a better Q3 performance.

But a lower-than-expected revenue result could mean that OpenAI is on track to post a major financial loss in 2026.

Anthropic, meanwhile, recently shared that while its revenue is increasing, its costs are also set to skyrocket as the company spends big to keep up with the evolving AI development race.

As reported by CNBC, Anthropic reported a significant Q3 2026 revenue increase, rising almost 1,127% year over year to $17 billion. At the same time, the company also announced plans to spend more than $895 billion on compute and infrastructure over the next few years.

CNBC added that while Anthropic’s revenue is up 47% quarter over quarter, its compute and infrastructure costs increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared to the same period last year.

Meanwhile, xAI owner Elon Musk told Grok Bot users on Nov. 1 that the company had implemented new restrictions on access because “the cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.”

Taken alongside these other notes, this is pretty much a summary of the entire AI industry, as companies pour more and more money into AI projects without a clear revenue pathway to justify that investment.

Meta is facing the same challenges. The company has seen strong early adoption of its Muse agents, which are its big hope for driving consumer AI adoption. However, Meta has also committed hundreds of billions of dollars to AI development and support infrastructure, which sets the bar very high for a cash flow-positive result.

Indeed, based on the company’s existing financial commitments to AI projects, it’s got a long, long way to go.

In 2025, Meta generated $200.97 billion, with $4.8 billion of that coming from non-advertising intake, which includes AI subscriptions.

In order to break even on its current AI spending commitments, Meta would need to generate around $100 billion per year from AI subscriptions and partnerships over the next decade.

In other words, Meta needs to build a whole new business offering that generates half as much income as one of the most profitable businesses in the world if it hopes to even come close to turning its AI investment into a profit anytime before 2036.

The operational cost-to-benefit ratio is almost too high to fathom. Moreover, with AI projects continuing to face opposition and negative perception increasing among consumers, many companies may be forced to reconsider their approaches and re-examine the openness of their AI models.

Restricting usage would reduce costs, as Musk said, but it could also slow adoption.

Then again, maybe taking generative AI tools out of the hands of the public, and reducing the amount of AI slop being published to social apps, would lead to a better outcome overall.

Doing that could also make it cost-prohibitive for scammers to generate AI replicas of other people’s content, which is an issue that Instagram Chief Adam Mosseri recently highlighted as a major concern.

Essentially, the cost crunch could soon see AI tools reducing their usage limits, which could lead to less AI use overall.

The question then is whether Meta will end up winning by eating the losses that other companies can’t in order to maximize the take-up of its Muse agents.

#7481. Meta delays commercial terms update indefinitely

The company’s upcoming commercial terms of service update has prompted regulators to seek more insight into the specific details.

Meta’s planned commercial terms of service update has become a significant topic of concern for the company, and it may now be forced to abandon the update altogether in order to avoid additional scrutiny.

Earlier this month, Meta began informing business users of an upcoming update to its commercial terms of service, which included a change in wording that could have allowed Meta to scrape the website of any business that maintained a Facebook or Instagram presence.

Legal experts raised the alarm, which prompted regulatory groups to pose questions about the change.

Meta has maintained that the purpose of the update is not related to data scraping, and is instead to help with data gathering for the sole purpose of ad targeting. Even so, in response to these queries, Meta delayed the launch of the updated terms, shifting the implementation date from Oct. 20 to Nov. 20.

Then last week, as reported by Reuters, Meta said that it could end up delaying the rollout indefinitely in order to address concerns raised by regulatory groups.

Among those is the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority, which, according to The Next Web, has opened an investigation into Meta’s commercial terms for businesses. The European Publishers Council is also assessing next steps amid rising concerns about the gathering of business data to power AI models.

It’s impossible to know the intention of Meta’s planned update, but it does seem plausible that the initial update was not intended to empower broad-scale data-scraping, and that Meta’s inclusion of the term “scraping,” which has a different context in the AI era, has caused this new issue.

But either way, Meta is now working to address concerns ahead of the planned update.

Meta has made a copy of its updated commercial terms available for review, with a note at the top of the screen still indicating that they will go into effect on Nov. 20.
