#7476. As Publicis closes LiveRamp deal, some brands say they’re jumping ship

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Liquid Death confirmed it plans to move away from the platform, which follows ad-holding companies shifting off the service due to the acquisition.

Publicis Groupe closed its $2.2 billion acquisition of data-collaboration platform LiveRamp on Monday, according to a press release. The finalization of the deal follows the companies agreeing to a consent order with the Federal Trade Commission last month which seeks to preserve LiveRamp’s neutrality. Even with those regulatory guardrails in place, some brand marketers appear to be jumping ship.

“You should be worried Publicis Groupe and LiveRamp. Yes we will leave. I am first in line,” Benoit Vatere, chief media and digital commerce officer at Liquid Death, posted on LinkedIn following the news. “Who in their right mind will let an holdco own your data and graph [sic]. Do you really think we are that stupid? All Liveramp competitors, tag yourself in the comment, business is coming your way.”

Vatere’s comment section was flooded with people promoting LiveRamp alternatives. A representative for Liquid Death verified that the beverage brand plans to move away from LiveRamp. Direct Publicis competitors in the agency space, including WPP and Omnicom, have signaled their intentions to wind down use of LiveRamp for months. Publicis did not immediately respond to a request for comment on potential brand marketer defections.

Publicis has positioned the deal, which was first announced in May, as a key piece of its strategy around artificial intelligence, including the ability to develop more sophisticated agentic frameworks on behalf of clients. The release shared more details of how the integration, which pairs LiveRamp tech with Epsilon data, will work to provide a plug-and-play option for bringing together and activating different data sets.

Publicis CEO Arthur Sadoun and Chief Strategy Officer Carla Serrano also appear in a video explaining the benefits of the LiveRamp acquisition, stating it provides a third option for clients who are contending with either walled gardens that provide scale but take away control or the need to hire consultants to develop custom solutions that are time-intensive and costly.

“Our answer is the industry’s first AI growth engine, combining the speed, simplicity and instant results of plug and play, with full ownership and control, so clients can drive business impact without giving up autonomy over their data, their technology, or their future,” said Sadoun in a statement.

Clients can enhance their own first-party data sets with capabilities from LiveRamp’s RampID and Epsilon’s Identity offering. This will allow them to add more customer attributes and promises to make billions of more prospects addressable, the companies claim. The souped-up data sets can also be activated across LiveRamp’s ecosystem, which encompasses a wide range of publishers, tech platforms, walled gardens, retail media networks and large-language models — including OpenAI’s ChatGPT — as well as Publicis’ own media network.

Clients at the same time will not need to navigate the same level of legal processes, custom integration work or security considerations needed to broker partnerships with third-party platforms since Publicis and LiveRamp already have those relationships “pre-wired,” the release said. Publicis and LiveRamp reaffirmed that clients will maintain full ownership and control of their data and intellectual property and will not be locked into using specific technology partners.

#7472. Levi’s claymation holiday campaign celebrates handmade craft amid AI bloat

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

“Let’s Get Fuzzy” is centered on a 60-second spot that required four hours of filming for each second of animation.

Levi’s is taking inspiration from a 30-year-old campaign for its holiday effort. “Let’s Get Fuzzy” serves as a call back to the 1995 ad “Clayman,” the brand’s first global commercial and the first full-length spot completely shot in claymation, according to the brand. The brand’s decision to leverage claymation — which is considered to be incredibly labor intensive — could be welcomed by consumers, the majority of whom are growing tired of AI-generated content, particularly in advertising.

The 60-second video opens on a remote cabin in a snow-covered wilderness where friends are enjoying a holiday gathering. The night takes a turn as a ferocious yeti named Gus tries to break into the cabin before successfully running through the wall. Right when all hope seems to be lost, one of the characters throws a red sweater at the yeti in an apparent act of self defense. However, the sweater fits Gus perfectly, stopping his rampage and leading him to join the party as a welcomed guest.

The campaign, which launched two days after Halloween, meshes holiday aesthetics with vibes of the spooky season with its framing and soundtrack choice, akin to cult classics like “Dead Snow.” The video required four hours of filming for each second of animation, and the set and characters were made by hand, according to press details. No AI was used in the filming process, per the brand.

The collection is available via the brand’s website and app, as well as at select retail locations.

“Our Levi’s Let’s Get Fuzzy campaign was an opportunity to experiment with immersive and tactile world-building,” said Kenny Mitchell, global CMO at Levi’s, in press materials. “Anchored by a film created entirely with stop-motion claymation, it’s also the celebration of the craft and human creativity synonymous with the Levi’s brand.”

Generative AI has become an increasingly common tool for marketers as the industry looks to cut costs and meet the demands of an ever-evolving cultural landscape. However, cost savings and quick turnaround times come at a price. Consumers routinely find AI creative as “annoying,” “boring” and often “confusing,” according to a 2024 study by NielsenIQ. Half of consumers prefer brands that don’t use generative AI in advertising and other forward-facing messaging, per a 2026 Gartner study.

Levi’s isn’t the only company looking to use handcrafted creatives this holiday season. E.l.f. and Prada also launched handmade, stop-motion style holiday campaigns. Retail giants Walmart and Target both launched their campaigns before Halloween. The holiday shopping window has continued to get earlier as consumers hunt for the best value amid budgetary pressure.

Parent Levi Strauss & Co. reported a third-quarter revenue of $1.6 billion, a 4% year-over-year increase, according to an earnings release. Michelle Gass, CEO, president and director of Levi Strauss, noted on an earnings call that there has been less brand-building moments this year and that the brand’s back-to-school campaign did not generate the anticipated demand and traffic. The company plans to deepen its marketing investments and place more of a focus on mid-funnel marketing, according to Gass.

DuckDuckGo provides equal work opportunities to all team members and applicants, and it prohibits discrimination and harassment of any type on the basis of race, color, ethnicity, caste, religion, age, sex (including pregnancy), national origin, disability status, genetics, protected veteran status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or any other characteristic protected by our policies or federal, state, or local laws.

We connect with candor and care, seeking out diverse perspectives from our customers, communities and each other.Life at Axon is fast-paced, challenging and meaningful. Here, you’ll take ownership and drive real change. Constantly grow as you work hard for a mission that matters at a company where you matter.

The Technical Support Representative provides first class technical support to Axon Fusus customers through multiple communication channels which include phone, email and chat. This is a customer-focused, technical, hardware, and software-related support position with responsibilities for meeting or exceeding performance and quality goals.

#7469. The 2026 ADWEEK Innovator 50: Building Relevance for Tomorrow

“If you can dream it, you can do it” has never been more true.

From advancing emerging technologies to delivering breakthrough ideas that drive real business impact, the 2026 ADWEEK Innovator 50 recognizes the executives shaping the future of marketing and advertising by pushing the boundaries of what’s possible.

These innovative leaders across disciplines at agencies, brands, tech firms, and media companies are moving at the speed of technological and cultural change, ensuring their businesses remain relevant tomorrow.

SVP of Digital Shopping Experiences, Albertsons Companies

With over 2,200 stores in 35 states, Albertsons Companies knows how to connect with consumers in the aisles. Jill Pavlovich has brought the same rigor to its digital storefront, advancing the ecommerce side of the business by integrating AI into the shopping journey through conversational search and personalized recommendations using first-party data. Among her biggest advances have been enhancing product discovery through AI and expanding shoppable recipe capabilities to reduce the daily stress of meal planning. Customers using Albertsons’ new AI-powered tools generated up to 26% higher average order values, demonstrating AI’s commercial potential in retail by helping to move customers more easily from inspiration to purchase.

Global Chief Marketing & Innovation Officer, APR

Having watched the AI revolution begin at Accenture, Edmond Handwerker recognized genAI’s potential to fundamentally reshape the marketing operating model. Since joining APR in 2024, he’s repositioned the company from a production consultancy to an AI-enabled production intelligence firm that gives clients more control by combining proprietary technology and one of the industry’s richest intelligence datasets, collected from 400 global brands. Instead of reviewing individual hero campaigns, APR now analyzes production investment across a client’s entire marketing ecosystem through its Acero platform, then operationalizes its insights at scale through its Capri system. With these assets, APR has won nine of 10 competitive pitches in the past year, while client engagements have generated $75 million in annual savings and cut production costs by 84%.

This is the year beehiiv grew beyond newsletter advertising, becoming a broader creator media platform that spans monetization, distribution, audience control, and paid access, pushing the industry to take creator-led media seriously. Under Tyler Denk’s leadership, beehiiv’s ad network doubled revenue to $15 million in ARR, publisher payouts topped $1 million monthly, and the platform grew to more than 50,000 active users. He rebuilt the network from a largely manual operation into a self-serve, increasingly programmatic system serving everyone from independent writers to major publishers. With advertisers including Roku and HubSpot investing in the channel, he’s established a model competitors are racing to match, strengthening the economics of creator-led publishing.

Head of Fox Creator Studios, Fox Entertainment

Above anything else, Billy Parks is a relationship builder, cultivating the trust of creators to bring them under the studio umbrella. He’s leading Fox Creator Studios in understanding what audiences want and turning that into original IP, scalable franchises, and new revenue opportunities. In the past year, Parks has secured seven creator partnerships representing more than 65 million followers, spanning both scripted and unscripted series, as well as mobile-native food and automotive storytelling. His model connects creators’ cultural credibility with Fox’s production, financing, advertising, and global distribution capabilities. One of his early successes, the YouTube sketch comedy series Read the Room with Josh Richards, generated more than 60 million views in its first four weeks and was greenlit for additional seasons.

VP & GM of DG Media Network, Dollar General

Austin Leonard is pushing retail media beyond the digital shelf, building Dollar General Media Network into a connected commerce platform that encompasses advertising, digital sales, and 21,000-plus stores. He brokered partnerships with The Trade Desk and Kevel to unify onsite and offsite activation, and with Google to bring Dollar General’s purchase data into YouTube and DV360. He also expanded the DG In-Store Radio Network to nearly 12,000 locations, making physical stores a scalable media channel. Under his leadership, DGMN generated $170 million in fiscal 2025 ad revenue, while championing industry-wide standards for measurement and commerce media innovation.

Scott Futterman has grown Drmtlgy into an estimated $200 million skincare business without outside equity, proving that clinical credibility and community-driven marketing can rival traditional beauty playbooks. Over the past year, he led the brand’s launch in more than 1,400 Ulta Beauty stores, beating sell-in forecasts by 200% and generating more than $5 million in retail sales. Futterman’s commitment to evidence over hype drove an independently conducted clinical trial of Drmtlgy’s Needle-less Growth Factor Serum against a $295 competitor; results published in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology showed 30% greater visible improvement overall. By fostering trust, committing to transparency, and engaging in long-term relationship building with its community, Futterman has created a marketing model that can resonate well beyond the beauty category.

Co-founder & CEO, Innovid PRESIDENT & Chief Innovation Officer, Mediaocean

Since co-founding Innovid in 2007, Zvika Netter has been a driving force behind some of the biggest changes in advertising, from interactive video to connected TV and now agentic AI. His latest bet is Nivo, an AI foundation that connects data, decision-making, and execution across the advertising lifecycle. Rather than generating recommendations alone, its specialized agents turn intelligence into action, cutting campaign workflows from weeks to minutes. Clients including Canvas Worldwide, FanDuel, Optimum, Paddy Power, and Tailwind EMEA are seeing up to 90% workflow efficiency gains, 40% less media waste, and 45% more impactful creative. Named Mediaocean’s chief innovation officer in February, Netter is extending this vision through Prisma and Protected.

In the Wild west of AI-driven media buying, Zach Epstein is grounded in causal evidence, not attribution or platform-reported performance. The CEO of Haus introduced Architect, an agentic optimization system that combines incrementality testing, predictive modeling, and business context to recommend how marketers allocate budgets across channels and campaigns. Built on real-world experiments, its explainable recommendations help marketers move from measuring results to making better investment decisions. As AI increasingly automates media buying, Epstein is making the case that independent evidence must guide the algorithms controlling advertising spend, bringing greater accountability to marketing’s most consequential decisions.

AI in advertising can do so much more than content generation, and Tejas Manohar is turning the technology on campaign execution. The Hightouch co-CEO has spearheaded an agentic marketing platform that uses customer data, brand guidelines, and performance signals to help marketers analyze opportunities, develop creative, and take campaigns live. Hightouch Ad Studio cut Otrium’s campaign production timelines by 70%, while boosting clickthrough rates 13% and conversions 15%. The platform has powered nearly 10 billion AI decisions across more than 800 customers. In April, Hightouch raised $150 million at a $2.75 billion valuation, accelerating Manohar’s vision for AI-powered marketing.

With livestreams gaining popularity beyond gaming and sports, Alexander Guerrero has evolved NexTide Media from a livestream creator network into a full-stack AI-powered advertising platform that helps brands plan, safeguard, optimize, and measure campaigns in real time. LiveGuard monitors livestream content and automatically pauses ads when brand safety guidelines are breached; Kraken turns creator conversations into actionable audience intelligence. The platform’s campaigns have delivered more than four times the engagement of traditional digital advertising, while also thinking outside of the box for clients: For corporate travel management platform Engine, Guerrero developed a custom activation based on the insight that nearly half of its B2B target audience games and watches livestreams weekly.

General Manager of Advertising, Instacart

Having a product background shapes Ali Miller’s approach to innovation at Instacart, listening closely to consumers and partners to build technology that solves real problems and creates better shopping experiences. She’s connected Instacart’s first-party purchase data to campaigns across social, streaming, and programmatic channels, leading to Instacart Ads surpassing $1 billion in revenue in 2025 with more than 9,000 active brand partners. She expanded AI-powered campaign optimization, introduced shoppable short-form video, and launched Ads Studio, a full-service creative marketing offering that has delivered over 420 campaigns with nearly 200 CPG brands. Through partnerships spanning Meta, Roku and TikTok, Miller is linking brand discovery to measurable sales, helping advertisers connect fragmented consumer journeys to actual purchases.

The complexity of commercial real estate makes it ripe for AI innovation. As global CMO of commercial property services and investment firm JLL, Siddharth Taparia has built a dedicated AI marketing team, prioritized digital content for GEO to grab share of voice in LLMs, and deployed over 30 use cases to accelerate content production by 65%. Recognizing that brand awareness doesn’t guarantee conversion, he moved JLL beyond the traditional B2B tactics of commercial real estate. The firm has emerged as a leader in brand-to-demand integration, which has raised marketing-originated revenue by 149% since 2023 and marketing-influenced revenue by 407%, with JLL’s brand value up 24% year-over-year to $1.6 billion.

The fragmented road of the customer journey is being smoothed by the AI innovations of Jamie Domenici. The Klaviyo CMO is advancing autonomous marketing, steering the company’s evolution into an autonomous B2C CRM where intelligent agents act on customer data to drive results. Customer Agent and Composer automate service and campaign creation, while integrations with Anthropic, Canva, and Shopify bring AI into marketers’ existing workflows. On platforms, Klaviyo Social Marketing folds creator content, social engagement, and DMs into unified customer profiles. The bottom line has grown alongside Klaviyo’s ambitions, with revenue up 32% to $1.2 billion in 2025, while customers generated $3 billion in attributed Black Friday/Cyber Monday revenue. Domenici also champions adoption through global industry events, sharing these practical use cases for AI in marketing.

Making conversational AI into a viable business required Koah CEO Nic Baird to rebuild its advertising infrastructure from the ground up. Recognizing that legacy adtech couldn’t account for how people research and make decisions in AI chats, he rebuilt Koah around user intent and real-time behavioral analytics. The results are striking: Koah delivers clickthrough rates roughly four times higher than legacy adtech across AI environments and has served more than 65 million native ad impressions, all backed by a human team that has grown 175% over the past 12 months. Publishers including Liner and Luzia have reported significant performance gains, while Koah’s $20.5 million Series A signals growing investor confidence in a new advertising channel.

Director of Data Intelligence, AI & Innovation, LLYC

Brands looking for blunt feedback on their products can ask Mercedes de la Guardia, who’s turned generative AI into a practical research tool. As communications and consulting firm LLYC’s director of data and AI, she helped develop Synthetic Audiences, a human-guided methodology that tests creative, messaging, products, and packaging before launch. For one technology client, de la Guardia designed a synthetic jury of 27 different audience profiles to evaluate 51 creative assets, producing 459 assessments in 72 hours and uncovering gaps in the evidence needed to drive purchase. The approach has demonstrated an average 90% compatibility with traditional focus-group findings while compressing research timelines.

The only solution to the closed-model economics of AI video, as LTX CEO Zeev Farbman sees it, is open-weight technology that gives creators and enterprises greater control over costs, intellectual property, and deployment. LTX-2, released in January, enables production-ready audio-video generation on local hardware or private cloud infrastructure, at roughly one-eighth the cost and one-seventh the render time of closed models. The model family has surpassed 11 million downloads on Hugging Face, signaling demand for accessible alternatives as cost increasingly becomes a factor in AI adoption. With LTX-3 on the horizon, Farbman is steering LTX beyond video toward world models, expanding what open creative technology can make possible.

One of commerce’s biggest assumptions is that it begins with search. The 10 million monthly users of agentic commerce platform Glance know there’s a better way. Mansi Jain launched the AI-powered product discovery app in May 2025 during New York Fashion Week, and in roughly a year has logged installs across 80 million devices. The platform uses visual, personalized recommendations to move consumers from inspiration to purchase, with 40% of MAUs adding items to cart and 15% transacting. Jain has expanded Glance across mobile and connected TV, including a first-to-market Samsung smart TV shopping experience, opening new territory for brands to connect discovery, media, and commerce in a measurable, cross-platform way. Jain is also bringing more women into AI by hosting events at industry gatherings such as Shoptalk and Cannes Lions.

In transforming full-service agency Mod Op’s operations for the AI era, Tessa Burg is guided by two pillars: productivity and possibility. Beyond efficiencies, she built a proprietary technology stack that delivers marketing services in a new way. To create it, she started with people, founding and leading Mod Op’s Ad Council that spans every department, which yielded 13 enterprise initiatives within six months. Burg conceived and launched Orion, an in-house intelligence platform that has powered more than 700 AI agents, generated $3 million in measurable value, and contributed to $5 million in incremental client revenue. Its workflow platform is used by more than 95% of employees, while Burg has trained 400-plus staff in AI development so far.

Local media is getting access to the technology necessary to compete with national advertising giants with Madhive. CEO Jim Wilson has built the company into an omnichannel platform serving more than 8,000 local sellers, with its AI-powered Maverick suite automating campaign planning, targeting, and optimization. In live campaigns, Maverick has delivered 17.5x return on ad spend, 4x higher conversion rates and 112% more foot traffic. Its 2026 AI agent launch lets advertisers manage campaigns through natural-language commands, bringing advanced intelligence directly into everyday workflows. Through partnerships spanning local broadcasters and streaming platforms, Wilson is advancing a more competitive, accountable future for local advertising.

Since launching autonomous marketing platform Notch less than a year ago, Vinay Jain has shown that AI isn’t just capable of assisting marketers—it can operate as one. Drawing on nearly eight years building Meta’s ad infrastructure, including Lead Ads—which grew from zero to $1 billion in annual revenue—he launched Notch’s Max, an autonomous agent that plans strategy, creates ads, launches campaigns, and optimizes budgets across Meta and TikTok. Max has generated over 85,000 ads for more than 16,000 advertisers thanks to its Brand Brain memory layer trained on proprietary data, continuous feedback loops, and ecommerce integration, helping triple Notch’s revenue in six months. By bringing campaign management into ChatGPT and Claude, Jain is also challenging the dashboard-centric model of digital advertising.

The past year has brought a strategic shift to Pacvue, with president Melissa Burdick guiding the retail media platform into something entirely new: an agentic commerce grid that connects planning, activation, and measurement across retail, social, streaming, and AI. Pacvue’s new platform, Prism, connects every touchpoint along a customer journey to business outcomes, with early results showing a 5% lift in total ROAS and 12% higher sales. Pacvue now manages more than $12 billion in ad spend across more than 100 retail networks. Burdick is also expanding access to AI training and mentoring women in commerce, building the talent pipeline alongside the technology.

VP & Chief Marketing and Communications Officer, Texas A&M University

Meeting audiences where they are is the bread and butter of most advertising, but higher education hadn’t seen the like until Texas A&M University’s Ethan Braden. He elevated the school to No. 6 in global visibility, up from No. 21 two years ago, with an unconventional marketing strategy around motorsports, research, service, and popular culture. Texas A&M’s NASCAR activation linked sponsorship with engineering, safety, manufacturing, and other institutional priorities; the university was also a primary team sponsor in the IndyCar series, where it debuted a service-centric brand film featuring Lyle Lovett. Braden also launched a university-owned media platform that has generated 76.8 million search impressions, while YouTube content generated 75 million views and earned-media mentions rose 83%.

Bas Korsten is pushing creative agencies into territory once reserved for scientists. As a follow-up to The Next Rembrandt and the Mammoth Meatball, he was the dreamer behind T-Rex Leather, which used AI modeling and biotechnology to grow leather from a genetic blueprint reconstructed from 66 million-year-old dinosaur collagen. The April debut generated 4.63 billion media impressions, lifted Lab-Grown Leather’s share price 279%, and increased luxury brand inquiries tenfold. Korsten is also advancing AI across VML’s creative operations while championing award-winning innovations spanning healthcare and sports commerce. Under his leadership, VML won 53 Cannes Lions in 2026 and saw 35% organic growth.

President of Worldwide Marketing & Distribution Paramount Pictures

Theatrical campaigns feel fresh again under the leadership of Josh Goldstine. At Paramount, he’s infusing legacy franchises with fresh relevance to engage a new generation of moviegoers. A campaign for Scream 7 took the villain Ghostface from the screen to the real world, including UFC matches and Supercross races, and even a crossover with rapper Ghostface Killah. The film’s comedy counterpart, Scary Movie, brought a haunted living room to Times Square along with integrations with Bravo’s hit series Summer House. By stoking social buzz and expanding the genre appeal of horror, Scream 7 became the franchise’s highest-grossing film, earning more than $200 million worldwide, while Scary Movie delivered a franchise-record opening and $224 million in box office revenue, becoming the first R-rated comedy since 2017 to surpass $100 million domestically.

By approaching every campaign through his expertise as a filmmaker, Andrew Panay is making Hollywood-worthy ads at an impressive scale. Through Panay Brand Studios, he delivered more than 175 pieces of content for T-Mobile and Microsoft in a year, including Super Bowl campaigns. His character-driven Microsoft Copilot spots helped propel the product from 15 million to 30 million paid seats by mid-2026. Panay also launched Cyprus, a generative AI production studio, and 3×360, a sprint program delivering refined creative concepts in three days through human-AI collaboration. His model unites filmmaking, technology, and speed, pushing brands to compete more effectively for cultural attention.

Marketing’s next battleground is AI-powered search, and Profound CEO James Cadwallader is leading the charge for brands. As consumers increasingly turn to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity for recommendations, Profound gives brands the tools to measure visibility, track citations, correct misinformation, and improve their presence in AI-generated answers. Its platform now serves more than 1,000 enterprise brands, including Target, Walmart, and Figma, with customers reporting significant gains in AI visibility. Through products such as Profound Index and AI Marketer, Cadwallader is making an emerging discovery channel measurable and actionable for marketers. The company has raised $155 million at a $1 billion valuation, and over 15% of the Fortune 500 use the platform.

Founder & CEO, Propeller (Omnicom Health)

Charlie Flax has spent two decades anticipating healthcare marketing’s next frontier, from omnichannel strategy to AI-powered execution. As Propeller’s founder and CEO, he has made experimentation an operating principle, equipping all 133 employees with AI training and embedding new capabilities across the Omnicom Health agency, showing how adoption of a new technology can be a people-first process. Today, 80% of client brands use fully agentic workflows, cutting project time by 30%. The approach delivers in healthcare’s most demanding environments: Propeller executed a Johnson & Johnson direct-to-consumer launch within 48 hours of FDA approval. With 10 new agency of record wins and a growing client roster, Flax is proving regulated marketing can move faster.

Launching a campaign on Amazon’s advertising platform used to be a weeklong, multi-specialist process. To streamline that process, Gaëtan Godart of Programmads has stripped away the technical complexity with Talk to Launch, an AI agent that lets users build Amazon DSP campaigns through natural-language conversations with Claude. The innovation compresses the time needed from idea to execution into as little as an hour, eliminates handoffs between three specialists, and cuts advertiser onboarding from four weeks to nearly instant. The approach exemplifies Programmads’ evolution from platform partner to technology innovator, complementing its award-winning Adsecura platform as the company posted 45% revenue growth in 2025.

Publicis Media Exchange claimed the top spot in COMvergence’s 2025 new business rankings, the icing on a historic year for global CEO Joel Lunenfeld that saw more than $10 billion in new client billings including Coca-Cola, Mars, Paramount, and Kenvue. Lunenfeld built creator and sports marketing into Publicis Groupe’s fastest-growing strategic platforms, integrating acquisitions (160over90) and key hires (Suzy Deering as CMO of Publicis Sports), as well as embedding identity, audience intelligence, and ROI measurement into media planning. His innovations helped make creator campaigns accountable to the same performance standards as traditional media. Promoted to global CEO of PMX from U.S. CEO in February, he is scaling that model worldwide.

Within six weeks of becoming CEO of ReachTV in April, Rachel Jacobson secured the network’s biggest deal yet: live coverage of all 104 FIFA World Cup matches across more than 80 U.S. airports, reaching 51 million monthly travelers. The partnership attracted new advertisers (including UnitedHealth, St. Jude, Klarna, and Polymarket), sold out inventory, and helped make airport media a more compelling proposition for brands seeking engaged audiences beyond streaming and digital platforms. FIFA programming drove audience concentration 25% above non-game periods, while ReachTV revenue rose 16% year-over-year through Q2, making the case for expanding the industry’s definition of premium inventory to OOH and travel media.

VP of Global Ad Platform Partnerships & Business Development, Roku

Scale is great, but performance is better. Miles Fisher is helping close streaming TV’s accountability gap, building the partnerships that make connected TV measurable against real business outcomes. The latest tool, launched in April with Fisher leading the strategy and partner development, is Roku Create, which unites premium inventory with retailer and audience data, simplifying campaign targeting and purchase measurement. He also helped make Roku the first major streaming publisher to optimize campaigns against outcomes in real time through iSpot. A Nielsen integration strengthens cross-platform measurement, while an Amazon Ads partnership expands authenticated reach to 80 million U.S. households. These partnerships and integrations drove advertising revenue 25% higher year-over-year to $673 million in Q2 2026, outpacing both the U.S. OTT and digital advertising markets.

R/GA is calibrated for the new intelligence era under Melissa Jackson Parsey. She oversaw the development of Intelligent Brand Systems and built its proprietary core, BrDNA, a proprietary framework that makes brand values, behaviors, and judgment legible to AI, enabling more adaptive and consistently on-brand experiences. The technology has shifted the business from one-off campaigns to AI-powered brand systems that can constantly iterate, raising clients’ long-term strategic value. Her vision extends beyond creative execution to challenge agency economics, championing value-based partnerships over time-based billing. She has embedded AI training and tools across R/GA while leading strategy for launches including Fox One and Google Health, helping to fuel 35% year-over-year revenue growth in Q1 2026.

Leading a team of more than 500 marketers, State Farm’s Alyson Griffin has given the insurer a more modern and culturally relevant way to speak to the next generation of policyholders. Challenging insurance’s reliance on price wars and saturation advertising, Griffin has repositioned Jake from State Farm as a cross-platform cultural force, spanning gaming, creators, sports, and premium entertainment to reach Gen Z and millennial audiences. In a first for the insurer, Griffin partnered with Netflix to bring Jake into the basketball comedy Running Point, generating 2.3 billion impressions, while the branded series Gamerhood drove 65.6 million engagements and lifted Gen Z favorability eight points. Griffin’s broader strategy delivered an eight-point YoY increase in brand likeability.

At 53, after three decades in advertising, PJ Pereira became a beginner again, rebuilding Silverside as an AI-native creative company. His model brings filmmakers, designers, and technologists together in workflows that make ambitious ideas faster to produce and easier to scale. For Coca-Cola, a five-person team generated more than 70,000 clips in a month for “Holidays Are Coming,” earning top marks for creative effectiveness. For Svedka, Pereira helped deliver what was widely recognized as the first Super Bowl commercial produced primarily with generative AI. Under his leadership, Silverside’s revenue grew from $50,000 to $2.4 million in one year.

At Skai, Mor Klier is building the infrastructure for AI to run marketing operations, not simply assist them. Over the past year, he launched several category-first products, including Skai Studio, which coordinates AI agents to execute workflows from performance monitoring to budget adjustments, and Skai MCP, an open interface connecting organizations’ own agents to Skai’s data and execution capabilities. The platform now serves over 1,500 users across more than 200 organizations, with reported efficiency gains of up to 50%. By pairing autonomous execution with human oversight and open architecture, Klier is advancing a new operating model for marketing.

After a decade leading creative research at Google, Ben Jones left to build Sundogs, an independent intelligence company decoding what makes video work across platforms. With video now accounting for 82% of internet traffic, Sundogs’ technology analyzes thousands of clips frame by frame, turning creative cues into actionable signals. Rather than hoard its findings, Jones has elected to publish Sundogs’ research, boosting its relevance industry-wide and pushing companies to rethink platform-specific content. The company’s creator scoring model serves brands including Nestlé and Unilever, while a Circana study linked its creative signals to up to 60% higher sales lift. In two years, Sundogs surpassed $6 million in revenue, all while helping the broader advertising industry make the kinds of ads people will actually watch.

As AI democratizes art, outsiders are challenging agencies at their own game, and Rogier Vijverberg is working to give the industry an edge. At SuperHeroes, he launched Jimmy, a collective of AI and CGI artists; Lois, a global artist management platform for storytellers committed to human-crafted work; and The Robins, an 80-person Gen Z insight collective. Working together, these three branches have delivered results such as “Made with Lenovo Yoga” generating 1.3 billion views, lifting Gen Z brand awareness from 4% to 43%, and helping to drive a 23% increase in global AI PC sales. Through free AI education and artist-led experimentation, Vijverberg is expanding access to the tools of the future while championing human imagination.

Mental health care has a capacity problem, but AI can narrow the gap—if it’s done responsibly. In June, Talkspace CMO Katelyn Watson spearheaded the launch strategy for Tee by Talkspace, an AI-powered mental health guide developed with clinical oversight, setting a model for bringing sensitive AI products to market. More broadly, over the past year she’s repositioned the brand from a subscription-based therapy service to an insurance-first mental health platform spanning therapy, psychiatry, and self-guided support. And rather than celebrities, she let real Talkspace users speak to its effectiveness. Under Watson’s leadership, Talkspace grew revenue 22% annually and payer revenue 38%, while expanding into Medicare and TriCare, eventually leading to Universal Health Services acquiring the platform in August.

Mac Cummings saw that generative AI would affect much more than search, and transformed Terakeet from an enterprise search marketing company into a reputation management partner. The Reputation Operating System combines proprietary intelligence, strategic counsel, and continuous monitoring to help brands shape how they appear across AI platforms, search, and news. Its proprietary intelligence platform Presidio helps companies identify emerging threats and influence the information AI uses to generate answers. And recognizing that there’s a darker side to reputation management, Cummings recruited former FBI executive Matt Gorham as a strategic advisor on disinformation and cybersecurity.

In the 10 years since Neil Waller co-founded Whalar Group in 2016, the creator economy went from being worth less than $2 billion to $300 billion. And Whalar has grown alongside it under Waller’s guidance: The creator and social agency’s group turnover rose 32% in 2025 to $165 million, attracting investment from Marc Benioff, Shopify, and Hollywood producer Neal H. Moritz at a $400 million valuation. An already banner year culminated in the acquisition of Whalar’s agency business by Accenture Song in June, which has allowed Waller to realign with his original mission: doubling down on creators and building with them at every step. With the assets he retained in the deal—Whalar’s talent management platform Foam; Lighthouse Studios, where creators build scalable media networks and original IP; and the new media company Scalable covering the industry—Waller is helping creators turn viral fame into durable business success.

Competing for attention in an AI-driven marketplace needs a new playbook. Recognizing that traditional SEO no longer guarantees discovery, The Darl CEO Lara Schmoisman developed AI Visibility Optimization frameworks that help brands earn citations and recommendations from generative search platforms. Her Creative Growth methodology connects storytelling and visual identity to conversion data, linking creative decisions to commercial results. Beyond client work, Schmoisman educates marketers on emerging search behaviors and challenges entrenched industry conventions through her podcast, Coffee N5, with more than 1.5 million downloads, and her Unpopular Opinions newsletter.

Head of Creative at The Kitchen North America, Kraft Heinz

To develop work across 27 distinct Kraft Heinz brands that feels authentic to each of them, Simon Au has built an entrepreneurial model inside the CPG giant’s in-house agency The Kitchen. As head of creative for North America, he’s enabled teams to take culturally relevant ideas from concept to launch in as little as four hours, a model that has produced ideas that feel more like entertainment rather than advertising. Heinz KegChup generated more than 1 billion earned impressions, while “Draft Kraft, Get Kraft” helped drive 50,000 additional boxes of Kraft Mac & Cheese sold weekly. Today, The Kitchen produces over two-thirds of Kraft Heinz North America’s brand media output; in the past year, its work has generated more than 20 billion earned impressions and 40 million engagements.

VP of Integrated Marketing Experiences, The Coca-Cola Company

To optimize Coca-Cola’s marketing model, Robin Triplett is uniting data, media, technology, social, and commerce across a $1 billion-plus portfolio of over 17 brands. Her data-led system has doubled media ROI, generated more than $150 million in efficiencies, and increased first-party data by 148%, with the model scaling across more than 10 global markets. By connecting brand investment to commerce and measurement, Triplett is moving marketing beyond individual campaigns toward continuous, intelligence-led growth. Her leadership extends to industry standards through the Media Rating Council and IAB, while internal learning initiatives have helped team engagement rise 24 points.

The rules of B2B marketing are changing fast, and Chris Koehler has been working to infuse the same surprise and delight as B2C. At customer engagement platform Twilio, he has embedded AI across marketing operations, cutting research and content development from weeks to less than a day and increasing account-based marketing output fivefold without adding headcount. He’s also advancing AI-powered brand discovery, with visitors referred by large language models converting at roughly three times the rate of traditional search traffic. Koehler pairs automation with creative ambition, using cultural partnerships, influencer campaigns, and sharper storytelling to make enterprise technology resonate. His premise: As AI scales content, distinctive brands matter more.

Making conversational AI into a viable business required Koah CEO Nic Baird to rebuild its advertising infrastructure from the ground up. Recognizing that legacy adtech couldn’t account for how people research and make decisions in AI chats, he rebuilt Koah around user intent and real-time behavioral analytics. The results are striking: Koah delivers clickthrough rates roughly four times higher than legacy adtech across AI environments and has served more than 65 million native ad impressions, all backed by a human team that has grown 175% over the past 12 months. Publishers including Liner and Luzia have reported significant performance gains, while Koah’s $20.5 million Series A signals growing investor confidence in a new advertising channel.

Premium television is now as easy to buy as social ads through the work of James Borow, who built the Universal Ads platform that enables businesses of any size to create, buy, and measure TV campaigns through a single interface. In the past year, he’s led the rollout of new capabilities including a free self-service Ads Manager, full-funnel reporting, and the industry’s first shoppable premium CTV offering, which brought in 21 new publisher partners and 16 API partners, extending potential reach to 90% of U.S. households. Universal Ads’ performance-focused approach helped increase Jones Road Beauty’s new-customer revenue by 90%, while campaigns for independent pizzerias drove a 5% incremental lift in orders. Borow also hired David Shaw to lead the platform’s international ambitions, including launching in the U.K. earlier this year.

Is it possible to know the performance of an ad before it runs? Jehan Hamedi pioneered a category he’s dubbed Perceptual AI: technology that predicts how shoppers respond to product imagery, and launched Vizit Spark, a generative AI engine designed to create ecommerce visuals proven to increase sales across more than 5,000 product categories. Built on millions of purchase decisions and billions of visual data points, the platform serves eight of the world’s 10 largest consumer packaged goods companies, as well as longstanding partners Mars, L’Oreal, and Colgate-Palmolive. Across products analyzed by Vizit’s AI, 95% see measurable gains in conversion, units sold, or revenue. Hamedi’s 47 U.S. patents underscore his pioneering work in visual intelligence.

Andrea Bendzick is bringing a marketer’s experience and a CFO’s rigor to the longstanding brand vs. performance marketing debate. As CEO of Wpromote x Giant Spoon, she paired the performance agency with the Cannes Lions-winning creative shop—and partnered with AI platform Smartly—to unite creative ambition with best-in-class performance tools. Her biggest contribution is the Care Index, developed with Northwestern University’s Medill School to quantify how consumer affinity predicts revenue. Tested across more than 100 brands, the model predicted next-month revenue with 90% accuracy. She’s also launched an AI-focused rotational program, equipping junior strategists to tackle client challenges with AI from the start and putting their skills to use in real-world challenges facing agency clients.

As May Habib sees it, enterprise AI’s real opportunity isn’t simply generating content faster, but changing how the work of marketing and revenue teams gets done by connecting the systems that shape a brand. With Writer, she’s built an AI platform that helps nearly a third of the Fortune 500 operationalize brand standards, creative judgment, and customer knowledge through AI agents. Recent releases include Playbooks for repeatable workflows, Skills that encode brand expertise, and the latest Palmyra X6 model. Working together, these systems turn a company’s unique assets into shared infrastructure. At Vodafone, Writer improved search rankings 30% and doubled content engagement; at Boots, it cut SEO audits from weeks to minutes; and at Clorox, it reduced ecommerce listing management time by 85% across thousands of products and retail platforms.

Brandon Hardin is a freelance writer. He's previously worked at Check My Ads, BuzzFeed News, Facebook and Bloomberg View.

#7467. Future of Marketing Briefing: SharkNinja’s McLaren deal treats F1 fandom as the asset

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →

SharkNinja got a taste of F1 fandom when its products turned up in Brad Pitt’s racing film last year. Fans warmed to the brand and plenty finally twigged that Shark and Ninja were the same company. Then the buzz faded.

“The movie was great but it spiked and then it left,” said Laura Dyer, svp of global brand and partnerships at SharkNinja. “What’s great about this is it’s going to continue.”

“This” is a five-year sponsorship of McLaren and it got off to an early start. F1 sponsors tend to arrive over the winter, ready for their logos to be unveiled on the new car in February. SharkNinja turned up in mid-September, with most of the season already run, because it asked McLaren whether anything could go live before the year was out. McLaren said yes, which hands the brand a few months of practice ahead of 2027.

The practice matters since SharkNinja has never backed a sports property this big. Its previous sports deals were built around a single moment. At the 2025/1015 Women’s Rugby World CUp it was an official appliance partner, running standards at match venues, a fan zone at Battersea Power Station and a social series on matchday prep. A year earlier it put Thierry Henry, Peter Crouch and Bastian Schweinsteiger on a faux video call to squabble over who could host the best Euro 2024 watch party. Both were finished within weeks. McLaren, on the other hand, gave SharkNinja four racing series for five years. McLaren engineers in its labs and a direct line to drivers Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

That last part is what Dyer is most focused on. Where Norris and Piastri do appear, she wants them helping shape the idea, which is a change from the old sponsor routine of a driver turning up, reading the lines and leaving. “Getting them to do the things that they’re comfortable with is way better than handing someone a script and saying ‘there you go’,” Dyer continued. Fans follow the drivers as closely as the teams these days so keeping both onside matters. That goes double for a brand hoping to win those fans over on social media.

Most of that content will run on Mclaren’s channels and SharkNinja’s, and nothing goes live until both sides have signed it off. Even then, it won’t automatically land on Norris or Piastri’s accounts. “Their channels are theirs to own and theirs to editorialize,” said Dyer. If Norris or Piastri’s post about a blender, it’ll be because they fancied it.

That puts the onus on the content itself, though Dyer was frank that SharkNinja’s yardstick for it is still rough. Her answer on engagement, she warned, would be “really wooly.” Comments, shares and dwell time all go into the mix, weighed together, with reach a step behind. F1 and McLaren fans are fiercely loyal and Dyer said the brand is “really respectful of that”. Success as she put it, is a fan seeing a post and thinking. “‘oh yeah, like wicked. I totally get it’. Rather than this feels like advertising.”

Further out, SharNinja will track brand recognition and whether putting McLaren behind a specific product line shifts sales. As Dyer explained: “When we go hard at a product line with McLaren, we want to see whether or not that changes the trajectory of sales.”

Down the line, McLaren could even have a hand in the products as well the marketing. A set number of hours a year, the team’s engineers sit with SharkNina’s in Needham, Massachusetts, to “literally pen to paper solve problems together,” as Dyer put it. Battery life is one area they’ll dig into. Whether anything ends up with McLaren’s name on the box is an open question, and one Dyer didn’t answer. The engineering link was a big part of why SharkNinja picked McLaren, though. The brand is “really obsessive about the concept of marginal gains,” she said. “If we can get a battery to last like 50 seconds longer or get a fan to be 10% more efficient, we’ll do it.”

Sports sponsorship has been heading this way for a while. Live sport is one of the few remaining moments when a huge audience watches the same thing at once, and brands have been paying more to be part of it. What they’re buying has changed with the price. A logo on the hoardings and ad slots in the broadcast used to be the deal. These days marketers want to know what the fans themselves are worth, whether those fans follow the team or the people in its cars and kits.

“We operate more like an agency than a lot of traditional rights holders in that we insight on entering every conversation talking about the brand first,” said Ryan Fischer, president at Fenway Sports Management on an Advertising Week New York panel earlier this month. [We’re] understanding their objectives and strategies, then trying to identify the insight, whether that’s a consumer insight or a story we can help amplify, and letting that lead where we go within the portfolio rather than starting withoutselves.”

SharkNinja’s appearance in the F1 movie predated Dyer’s arrival but she was there to help execute it. Before it came out, she said “people saw us as Shark and Ninja”, said Dyer. Afterward, it was ‘Oh, they’re SharkNina,” she continued. The fan response caught the team off guard. “We were all pleasantly surprised by the sentiment and engagement with our brand in that movie by a fan base that I think really got us,” Dyer said. “That was definitely the inflection point to say okay, we should go further into the sport.”

The aim of it, like most sponsorships of this scale, is younger fans. Yes, F1’s global audience tops 900 million worldwide but the brand isn’t trying to carve that up — at least not yet. As Dyer put it: “We’re here for everyone, truthfully, and we want to stay for everyone.”

Forget the holiday season, it’s the Halloween campaigns you want to get right.

What’s scarier for a marketer: a campaign that fails to scare anyone, or a campaign that scares its audience so much they never want to buy the product again?

For Cheetos, apparently, the answer is a demon covered in orange snack dust.

The brand’s latest Halloween ad, “Man at The Bottom of The Bag” was ranked the ninth-scariest ad of all time by creative and media intelligence platform DAIVID. The spot, which is part of Cheetos’ Flavor of Fear collaboration with horror studio Blumhouse Productions, is predicted to leave 15.3% of viewers experiencing intense fear. Even HBO Max’s Halloween trailer, which promotes its season of spooky films, ranked 10th.

It turns out Halloween ads are (shockingly) losing some of their bite. This year’s campaigns were 32% less likely to provoke intense fear than those released in 2025 according to DAIVID — which means they’re less scary, sure, but not necessarily less effective.

DAIVID compiled the ranking using its AI-powered creative intelligence technology, which predicts the emotional responses audiences are likely to have towards ads, as well as its potential impact on brand and business metrics. And ads were ranked according to the percentage of viewers predicted to experience intense fear, defined as an emotional response score between eight and 10 on a 10-point scale.

Which begs the question, what came top of the all-time scary ads chart?

In first place was 2025’s I Choose Freedom campaign: “End The Horror”, which predicted 24.5% of viewers would feel intense fear after watching it.

Second place went to 2025’s Universal: “Dare To Answer The Black Phone”, which predicted 21.6% of viewers would experience intense fear.

Third place went to the Six Flags: “Tick, Tick, Tick” from 2024, where 19.5% of viewers were predicted to experience intense fear.

And let’s not forget Cheetos in ninth place, followed by HBO Max in 10th.

Still, there is some good news. The average Creative Effectiveness Score, according to DAIVID, sat at 5.84 out of 10 last year, and rose slightly to 5.85 for 2026.

Simply put, scaring the living daylights out of consumers can remain optional. But making the ad work is the real trick — or treat.

“Given that there is almost never only one perfect option for a decision, we’re confident that we can actually provide really interesting, compelling advertising models for agentic use cases… I’m really actually excited about the advertising opportunities in an agentic world.”

— Google’s svp and chief business officer Philipp Schindler, responding to an analyst question about the transition from search to agentic use during the company’s latest earnings call.

#7466. Amazon’s Ads nears $20 billion in Q3 as it bets on agentic AI to fuel further growth

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Amazon posted Q3 revenues of $201.9 billion today (Oct. 29), up 12% year-on-year, with its advertising offering generating almost $20 billion during the period, also up 12% during the period, making it one of the fastest-growing business units within the enterprise.

Those perusing the earnings report will note how revenue fell from $19.81 billion in Q2 to $19.64 billion in Q3, a decline of approximately 0.9%, although one caveat is that the sequential comparison is complicated by Prime Day occurring in Q2 this year rather than Q3.

While Amazon has not provided a specific dollar Q4/FY 2026 revenue forecast for its advertising services division — total revenue is expected to be in the range of $240 to $247 billion — it is expected to be a key pillar in its overall growth strategy.

“We expect year-over-year advertising revenue to grow in the high teens in fourth quarter 2026,” reads its official filing, which also trumpeted its recent launch of Amazon Ads Agent, a key growth engine for the division.

Intuitively, Amazon is putting AI at the center of its advertising business, previewing the consolidation of previously separate buying tools into a single platform that gives its technology greater responsibility for planning, executing, and optimizing campaigns — a concern for some.

Unveiled at the e-commerce giant’s flagship advertising conference, unBoxed, in San Francisco, California, last month, Amazon Ads Agent brings sponsored advertising, display, video, and audio into a unified buying experience.

The platform builds on Amazon’s earlier integration of its demand-side platform and advertising console, extending its conversational AI assistant across campaign creation, targeting, optimization, measurement, and customer support.

Advertisers can now use natural-language instructions to plan campaigns, generate creative, forecast audience reach, adjust budgets, and analyze performance. The system can also recommend and execute optimizations, reducing the manual work traditionally associated with programmatic advertising.

Delving deeper into Amazon’s publicity material, two offerings underpin the overhaul: Full-Funnel Campaigns and Digital Video Audio, or DVA+, as it’s more commonly termed.

One key aspect is Full-Funnel Campaigns, which combine sponsored ads, display, video, and streaming TV within a single campaign. Advertisers specify their products, creative and budget, while Amazon’s AI determines how campaigns run and continuously optimize toward objectives including new-to-brand customers and long-term sales.

The system also shares signals across upper- and lower-funnel advertising, including campaigns running on third-party open-internet inventory, with Amazon claiming beta testing shows up to 67% higher return on long-term ad spend and 29% lower cost per new-to-brand customer than manually configured full-funnel campaigns.

Meanwhile, DVA+ consolidates sponsored display, sponsored TV, and programmatic display, video, and audio buying. Advertisers can select an objective, budget and creative, leaving targeting and optimization to Amazon, or use advanced settings to retain conventional DSP controls.

For Amazon, the commercial opportunity extends beyond simplifying campaign management, as making programmatic buying accessible to smaller advertisers without specialist teams could expand adoption of its advertising infrastructure.

Meanwhile, integrating sponsored advertising with upper-funnel formats gives Amazon another opportunity to capture budgets traditionally managed through separate agency teams and buying platforms.

However, Amazon’s expansion comes amid renewed scrutiny of how large advertising platforms operate, a familiar debate in countless antitrust filings, and one underlined by recent charges against the e-commerce giant’s ad offering. In August, the Federal Trade Commission and 22 state attorneys general ⁠sued Amazon over alleged deceptive and unfair advertising auction practices.

The complaint alleges Amazon secretly introduced surcharges into auctions, resulting in Sponsored Products advertisers paying their own winning bids approximately 80% of the time by 2024, despite representations concerning second-price auctions. Amazon disputes the allegations, which remain unproven in court.

While the lawsuit concerns existing auction practices rather than the newly launched agentic platform, it highlights questions surrounding the transparency of automated advertising systems. Sources consulted by Digiday, who asked to remain anonymous to protect industry relationships, noted the maxim of “caveat emptor,” or, more simply, “buyer beware.” They cautioned:

Amazon maintains that automation does not necessarily require advertisers to surrender control. Speaking ahead of the formal unveiling of the new platform, Kelly MacLean, vp, Amazon demand-side platform, told Digiday that DVA+ advertisers retain authority over objectives, products, creative approval, budgets, pacing, flight dates, and location targeting.

Advanced settings also preserve controls over bidding, audience targeting, supply selection, and frequency. MacLean characterized that configuration as “human-led, AI-supported,” maintaining that buyers can retain the conventional DSP experience while using AI-assisted recommendations.

Amazon also says it provides reporting on where ads are delivered and is developing explanations for its agent’s recommendations. However, those explanations remain a work in progress, with MacLean acknowledging that Amazon is still determining how much information advertisers need to understand the rationale behind automated decisions.

Asked whether the new tooling would explain how individual Sponsored Ads auction prices were determined, including the role of reserve or calculated prices, Amazon did not commit to providing that information. Furthermore, company spokespeople maintained that the company “strongly disagrees with the FTC’s filing.”

Speaking separately with Digiday ahead of the recent unBoxed launch, Amit Bhattacharyya, Amazon Ads’ vp, Full-Funnel Products, AI & Modeling, acknowledged limitations in the controls available through Full-Funnel Campaigns.

For example, advertisers approve creative but cannot select individual channels or specific audiences. “We are figuring out how to give them more transparency on the audience side,” he told Digiday.

Bhattacharyya also noted that Amazon provides format-level reporting, while its long-term sales measurement uses shopping signals to predict sales over 12 months and then displays accumulated actual sales against those forecasts.

For Alex Brownstein, founder of AHB Advisors and a former McKinsey consultant, the challenge extends beyond whether Amazon provides reporting. “Transparency on an agent buy comes in five layers, and Amazon is more open on some than others,” he said.

Those layers encompass data, decisions, pricing, delivery and results. Brownstein also noted that DVA+ offers publisher-level reporting, while full-funnel campaigns provide format-level visibility without equivalent detail about channel pricing.

He also questioned how advertisers can independently validate outcomes when Amazon controls both the buying technology and much of the underlying purchase data. “Amazon is open where openness brings it more of the budget and closed where its advantage sits,” Brownstein said.

To mitigate any risk, Brownstein suggested advertisers use their own customer data and independent incrementality testing to assess whether Amazon’s reported performance translates into additional sales.

Meanwhile, Jay Mandel, co-founder of the Marketing Accountability Council, raised a related concern about the incentives governing automated buying decisions. “My concern is whose interests the AI agent serves when Amazon’s revenue goals and the advertiser’s business goals diverge,” he told Digiday.

Mandel argued that advertisers should be able to audit automated changes, inspect fees and inventory decisions, and challenge platform performance claims using independent measurement. He further opined, “If spending less with Amazon is better for the advertiser, will its agent recommend that?”

Amazon’s new platform offers advertisers a simpler route into programmatic buying while extending the company’s influence over how advertisers allocate budgets, and that’s a story that it’s selling to Wall Street.

However, its longer-term success will depend not only on whether automation improves performance, but also on whether advertisers can independently determine how those results were achieved, a story Madison Avenue will be more eager to hear.

#7464. Letter From the Founder: Adcolor’s Vision Changed Who the Industry Could See

Twenty years ago, I was tired of watching extraordinary people wonder whether they belonged in an industry their talent was helping to build.

I knew those people. Sometimes, I was them.

Their work was shaping culture, yet recognition didn’t always follow. I watched talented people question their futures because they couldn’t see a path forward. I understood how lonely that could feel even in a room full of people.

I founded Adcolor because I wanted people who had been overlooked or underestimated to find one another and build relationships that could help them go further. And I believed that getting ahead came with a responsibility to reach back.

For 20 years, this community has shown what those words can mean in someone’s life. People who came to Adcolor looking for direction now help others find theirs. Our awards and conference gave that community a place to gather. To shine and be seen.

Through our Futures and Leaders programs, we deepened our investment in their careers. Adcolor in Music extended that work into an industry where our community’s influence has always deserved greater acknowledgement. But so much of our impact happens beyond anything we can put on a program.

I think about the introductions that changed careers and the people who might have left these industries if they hadn’t found the support to stay. Their presence has changed the work. Their leadership has changed what others believe is possible.

I am deeply proud of what we have built together. I also know that 20 years of impact does not make an organization immune to the rollbacks. We have faced pressures before that have required difficult decisions about what we can sustain.

As I look back, there have been moments when our resources could not meet our ambitions. As a founder, that is painful to acknowledge. It is also something I owe this community to share and reflect on as we evaluate what our next 20 years should look like.

We are listening to a community that is hurting and whose needs have evolved, asking what meaningful support looks like at this pivotal point in our history.

That same care is guiding our 20th anniversary celebration. I want us to celebrate our history knowing we are also doing the work to sustain our future. I have had to find the nerve for this part, too. There is vulnerability in acknowledging that a route needs to change, especially when you care so deeply about where you promised to go.

But I know where our roots are. They are in the experience of being underestimated and creating a way out of no way. They are in people who made time for us before anyone knew our names. I carry those people with me, and I know many of you do, too. Those roots give us the confidence to consider different routes forward.

We will keep pouring into the talent telling new stories and driving innovation, while finding ways to make that support more useful and sustainable.

That conviction is part of why we chose our 2014 Catalyst honoree, Charles D. King, founder of Macro, as our 2027 Beacon Award honoree. The progression from Catalyst to Beacon carries meaning for us. Through Macro, Charles has put his belief in storytellers of color into practice, building a business that helps bring their perspectives to audiences. His work reflects the connection between recognizing talent and investing in what that talent can do.

For a community that has too often had to wait for someone else’s permission, there is power in seeing someone create a route of their own and open it to others. Charles’ example gives someone else a reason to believe they can build, too.

When I think about Adcolor’s future, I often picture someone who hasn’t found us yet. They may be questioning whether there is room for them in this business. Or they may be doing well by every visible measure while quietly wondering where they can go to feel understood. I want Adcolor to be there when they come looking. That is what keeps me committed to the work, especially when the work is hard.

To everyone who has given something of themselves to Adcolor, thank you. Some of you believed when there was little to point to. Others found us along the way and made this community your own. You have helped carry a vision that has always been bigger than any one person.

Thank you to the Adcolor Team, Board of Directors, Adcolor Industry Coalition, Advisory Board, Community Group Leads, Leaders Advisory Board, our community of exceptional vendors, corporate partners, and hundreds of alumni! And to ADWEEK, thank you for helping tell our community’s stories and recognizing its influence on the industry.

Twenty years ago, I found the nerve to begin. I could not have imagined where this journey would take me or how many people would help shape it. Knowing what this community is capable of gives me every reason to keep going. We are excited for what comes next, and we hope you will remain with us on the journey.

TIffany R. Warren is evp and chief diversity officer of Sony Music Group and founder and president of Adcolor.

#7462. Apple’s Safari block hands WPP a fresh case for InfoSum

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Apple’s crackdown on the tricks advertisers use to track the same person across different sites and devices keeps tearing through large parts of the ad industry. WPP (if its CEO is to be believed) has barely felt it.

Cindy Rose said as much on the company’s third-quarter earnings call today yesterday. Richard Kramer, founder of equities research firm Arete Research, asked how exposed WPP was. Minimally, according to Rose, because the holdco’s data business is no longer built around the practice Apple is now shutting down.

“What I will say is it doesn’t really impact our data solution at all because we don’t rely solely on identity matching,” Rose said on the call.

Apple sees it rather differently. In an Oct. 19 blog post titled “Blocking Identity Resolution Infrastructure,” the engineers behind Safari argued that the plumbing pitch misses the point. Each site may only be sharing its own customers’ details but the firm in the middle sees the same email arrive from all of them, which lets it connect a person’s activity across sites in a way no single site could. Apple also took issue with the idea that people agree to this, arguing that nobody signing up for a newsletter expects their address to end up with a third party or something else entirely.

Apple is hardly alone in that view. Since the General Data Protection Regulation arrived in 2018, regulators and platforms have been pulling the industry away from tracking individuals across the web, sometimes forcefully, often haltingly. Rose’s pitch is that WPP saw where that was headed.

“We bought InfoSum roughly two years ago. We’ve now fully integrated it into our WPP Open platform. It is a data collaboration platform that relies on a mix of data sources from consumer identity to our own WPP proprietary data to live signals from our ecosystem of data partners, nearly 400 of them,” said Rose. “We use all of this data to identify untapped growth audiences and predict consumer behavior and ultimately deliver growth outcomes for our clients. Therefore, I would say in the scheme of things, the impact on WPP to these iOS changes are minimal.”

Read that way, Rose was doing more than playing down a risk. She was making the case, again, for InfoSum.

It’s a case WPP has had to keep making. Plenty in the industry questioned the April 2025 deal and the doubts grew louder when Publicis agreed to pay $2.2 billion for LiveRamp this May. Publicis appeared to have bought the industry’s data switchboard. WPP appeared to have bought a niche. Five months on, LiveRamp is on Apple’s blocklist. WPP had already stopped using it by June.

The difference is where the matching happens. Apple’s block works in the browser, cutting Safari off from firms whose code collects email on a publisher’s page. InfoSum operates away from the browser. Each party’s data stays in its own sealed-off environment and in WPP’s newer setup inside the client or publisher’s own systems, with only the insights shared between them. That puts it outside the reach of what Safari is currently blocking.

“The subtext of course is that their deadly rival, Publicis, is dancing to a different tune,” said Charles Ping, managing director at M&A advisors Winterberry Group. “If Cindy can make the $2billion+ that Publicis spent on Liveramp (plus Lotame and Epsilon before that) by contrast look poor both strategically and financially on an earnings call then that’s a strategic investor message nailed.  And none of Publicis’ acquisitions have delivered significant European capability.”

None of this puts InfoSum entirely clear of Apple’s argument, of course. Consumer identity is still one of its inputs, as Rose noted, and connecting what different companies know about the same people is close to what Apple objected to. It just happens to with data the parties already hold, somewhere Apple’s browser doesn’t reach.

“In reality, this does not mean WPP is unscathed,” said Robert Webster, founder of AI marketing consultancy TAU and former WPP exec. “It also need signals to deliver on safari and those signals have been degraded from them as from everyone else. Many of the ad tech systems WPP uses are equally encumbered, if not more so by Apple’s policies — moreso because without the email match grids they are not able to bring tougher sufficiency login data to make up for Publicis’ well known advantage in match rate across email graphs.”

The comments came as WPP turnaround plan looks to be gathering momentum. Over the last quarter, its media arm’s revenue, the biggest for the holdco, returned to growth. WPP Media’s revenue excluding costs passed on to clients grew 0.3% on a like-for-like basis in the third quarter reversing a 2.8 decline in the previous quarter.

Getting there meant some tough calls along the way, none more closely watched than WPP’s decision to sit out the pitch for Coca-Cola’s North American media account while it fought to keep the roughly $2 billion Coke spends on media, data and tech everywhere else. On the call, Rose reasoned that pitching costs a lot of money and a lot of time, with no guarantee of a win at the end. That math would have carried extra weight for Rose because WPP had already lost the account to Publicis last year. Going back so soon after would have meant spending heavily to win back business Coke had chosen to move barely 18 months earlier.

“We didn’t participate in the North America pitch,” said Rose. “Mostly because we won the rest of the world, and we have a huge amount of work to do in a very short period of time. I had people, many, many, many people pitching for many, many, many weeks over the summer. I was with them myself in London and Shanghai and Mexico City.”

That said, it was not a decision that was easy.

“We made a tough call between spending yet another six weeks pitching for North America versus delivering against what we had already won,” said Rose. “It was a fine judgment call, which I made, and it is as simple as that, really. That is your question on Coca-Cola North America.”
