#7461. From Celsius to Maybelline, more brands are lining up for the NYC Marathon’s 50th anniversary

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This story was first published by Digiday sibling Modern Retail.

This year’s New York City Marathon, which marks the 50th anniversary of the modern five-borough race and is expected to break participant records, is attracting brands to the world-famous race.

It’s no surprise that footwear brands like Nike, New Balance and Hoka are hosting their own pop-ups during the New York City Marathon weekend. But the brands showing up at the annual race represent a more diverse cross-section of retail than ever before, from beauty brands like Salt & Stone to restaurants around the city capitalizing on runners looking to carb-load. As the official and first-ever beauty sponsor of the marathon, Maybelline is also hosting a series of activations around the city, starting with a pre-race shakeout run in collaboration with running sunglasses brand Rendezvous Sports, featuring product giveaways and snacks.

As major sports events, like the U.S. Open and the Olympics, increasingly dominate consumer attention, more brands are finding ways to capitalize on sports moments. The New York City Marathon, specifically, also overlaps with running culture that has grown through run clubs. By leveraging strategic pop-ups, community events and targeted sponsorships, these companies are tapping into sports marketing opportunities to drive engagement and align themselves with the active lifestyles of today’s consumers.

Ahead of the New York City Marathon, energy drink brand Celsius is opening a Club Celsius pop-up in Brooklyn, a dedicated hub for a series of activations throughout the weekend. According to the company, the pop-up is meant to bring together runners, athletes and the New York public for the marathon. Located along the marathon route in Brooklyn, Club Celsius will host experiences ranging from pre-race prep to race-day cheering to post-race celebrations, and will be live from Oct. 30 to Nov. 2.

Attendees will get to customize race-day gear and sample Celsius drinks on site. The weekend kicks off Friday with a sunset group run led by DJ duo Sidequest and “Love Island” alum Corbin Mims, along with other fitness influencers.

The pop-up also builds on Celsius’ marketing efforts during last year’s New York City Marathon. In 2025, the company popped up with a similar concept called Energy House, where it hosted a dinner and panel discussion for athletes, and offered morning stretches, yoga and a recovery zone.

Kyle Watson, chief brand officer at Celsius, said the brand’s origin as a better-for-you energy drink for fitness enthusiasts makes the famous marathon a natural fit to sponsor.

“The brand was founded in fitness, and it remains an integral part of our DNA,” Watson said.

He added that the Club Celsius space “was created for the entire running community, and our programming reflects that,” from a shakeout run led by brand partners to a post-run live dating show and Medal Monday recovery session.

Watson said running continues to evolve beyond a fitness-only activity into a social gathering. “We wanted our activation to reflect the modernity of running culture and truly serve as a social destination for the weekend,” he said.

Mattress brand Saatva is hosting its first-ever New York City Marathon pop-up this year, as part of its ongoing effort to tap into sports marketing moments.

This week, Saatva hosted a wellness event at its Flatiron store, which included a panel on training and recovery featuring five-time NYC Marathon winner Tatyana McFadden and Frank Reneau, founder of A Mile. A Minute.

Ron Rudzin, founder and CEO of Saatva, told Modern Retail that the New York City Marathon’s growing global brand “reflects how much running has evolved beyond race day into a year-round culture centered on wellness, community and performance.”

As part of its marketing efforts around running, Saatva also has sponsorships as the official mattress and restorative sleep partner of USA Track & Field and Team USA at the 2028 Summer Olympics and Paralympic Games. Rudzin pointed to the Saatva marathon-week store event as the latest piece in this strategy to help put sleep and recovery at the center of the performance conversation.

This year also marks Vuori’s first-ever New York City Marathon activation.

The company is hosting weekend-long events at its Flatiron Manhattan store, including pre- and post-marathon live DJs, snacks and limited-edition items. On race day, the brand is hosting a pop-up along the marathon route in Williamsburg with a branded newsstand and cheer signs.

Ashley Kechter, global president of Vuori, said the company decided to celebrate the event by leaning into the city’s busy atmosphere throughout the weekend. “There’s a lot that makes the NYC Marathon special, but the energy and sense of connection around it are what stand out to us as a brand,” Kechter said.

Moreover, Kechter said Vuori’s roots in athletic wear make the marathon a fit for a pop-up. The company has already been marketing in this space by hosting its own run clubs over the past few years. “Bringing people together through movement and meaningful experiences is at the heart of Vuori,” Kechter said. “So we’re excited to do that on race day and beyond.”

#7460. SDK Engineer - Python at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We're looking for a SDK Engineer - Python to join our SDK team and own how developers talk to Supabase from Python. You'll work closely with the rest of the SDK team, our Auth, Realtime, Storage, PostgREST, Functions, CLI and Docs teams, and the open-source community, helping us make the Python SDK a library Python developers genuinely enjoy using.

Python developers reach Supabase from backend services, data pipelines, notebooks, and a growing number of AI agents and agent frameworks. The Python SDK is how all of them talk to the platform: database queries, auth, storage, realtime and edge functions, in both sync and async flavors.

This is a library-authoring role, and the work happens in the open: public repos, public issue trackers, and API decisions whose consequences last for years. If you get satisfaction from a type checker that catches the bug before your users do, from an async client that cleans up after itself, and from an issue tracker that isn't a graveyard, you'll like it here.

This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

Build and evolve our Python SDK across database, auth, storage, realtime and functions, with both sync and async APIs that feel natural in Python.

Start new things. Alongside the maintenance work, find what's missing, make the case for it, and build it. Nobody will hand you the list.

Work in the open. Triage inbound issues, review and shepherd outside contributions, keep CI and release automation healthy, and hold a clear, kind line on scope.

Own the typing experience. Make the SDK fully typed and checker-friendly, so autocomplete and static analysis stay correct in real codebases.

Keep us honest across environments. Multiple Python versions, sync and async frameworks, workers, serverless and notebooks — with dependency ranges that don't fight our users' projects. Test it, don't assume it.

Work on realtime. Long-lived websocket connections, reconnection, and subscription and presence semantics.

Track the platform. When auth, realtime, storage, postgrest or edge functions ship a change, make sure the SDK reflects it, and that we say so in the changelog.

Design in public. Write the RFCs, migration guides, release notes and docs. Treat a breaking change as a deprecation path plus a migration story, not a version bump.

Make our SDK legible to AI coding agents, which are now a major consumer of it.

Know modern Python typing deeply. You use generics, protocols, overloads and TypedDict as design tools, run strict type checking, and fix type errors without reaching for Any.

Have authored or maintained a published library with a public API and users outside your own company. You know what it costs to change something people depend on.

Know the maintainer side of open source. Issue triage at volume, reviewing outside PRs, release automation, changelogs and semver, security reports, and saying no to a feature request without losing the person who asked.

Are fluent in asyncio and have opinions on how a library should serve both sync and async callers.

Know Python packaging for libraries: pyproject.toml, wheels, modern tooling, version support policy, and why libraries shouldn't pin their dependencies tightly.

Test as a habit: unit, type-level and end-to-end against a real stack. Every fix comes with a regression test.

Write well. Design docs, changelogs and issue replies are a large part of the output here, much of it public, and we're async by default.

Have real autonomy: you find the important work, scope it, ship it, and say what you didn't do.

Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences

Have experience in async or globally distributed teams

Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly

Bonus points if you: have run a major-version migration for a public package, know your way around JWT/OAuth, have built integrations for AI agent frameworks, or have generated idiomatic clients from a schema.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

#7459. Amid growing tension over workplace AI, agencies have a window to reimagine staffing

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This article is part of Digiday’s coverage of its Digiday Media Buying Summit. More from the series →

Marketing agencies across the ad industry have been enthusiastic adopters of AI agents. But their team structures, job descriptions and the career paths of their staff have been largely left untouched — even as the actual day-to-day work of media buyers and marketing execs has changed, and even as fluency with AI tools becomes a required skill.

“There is a baseline that everyone is expected to understand and be fluent in,” said Gila Wilensky, evp and head of data and media, North America, Monks, during a session at Digiday’s Media Buying Summit this week in Newport Beach, Calif.

At many agencies, fluency means using and developing AI agents to automate planning or media activation work. A Digiday survey published in May found that just 9% of media agencies were not pursuing agentic AI solutions of some kind.

That automation has saved time for individual workers, but few companies have successfully distributed AI gains across teams or departments. According to a recent estimate by Apollo Partners, while tech companies have improved average profit margins, and revenue-per-worker have risen among U.S. businesses since the introduction of generative AI in 2022, neither measure has improved among companies outside that sector.

That might change as the over-use of AI in corporate settings begins to make working life more tedious and more stressful — and brings tensions over individual usage of AI to the fore.

Agency attendees, speaking under Chatham House Rules at the Summit’s townhall session, said that colleagues both junior and senior are using tech as an all-purpose corner cutter — speeding up some processes but, in the same act, skipping over opportunities for critical thinking.

“I’ve been surprised by how much AI content I’m seeing come from vice presidents and C-suites,” said one attendee. “I don’t think they want to take the time.”

With that problem in mind — and the desire to capture and institutionalize AI productivity gains beyond experimental programs — some agencies are making space for staff education. At Monks, Wilensky said training of junior staff (and re-training of senior colleagues) held part of the answer.

“If we don’t provide that, things can go off the rails,” said Wilensky.

Nadja Bellan-White, group CEO of M&C Saatchi North America, said her agency had carved out an hour each week on employee timesheets that’s dedicated to training. “A learning agenda has to be operationalized throughout your organization,” she said. “You have to have a culture of always learning, always pushing forward.”

Monks was also beginning to review hiring for its early-career roles, Wilensky added. “We’re not hiring less for junior talent. But it’s [being] more strategic about who you hire and what tasks you want junior talent to do,” she said. “I don’t think that junior team members are going to be sitting [and] piecing spreadsheets and recording spreadsheets all day… that work is taken off of their plates.”

Meanwhile, access to tools is limited for some job roles, with developers or engineers getting access to more powerful (and more expensive) AI models — a measure principally designed to control compute costs, but which can serve to limit exposure to AI tools where they’re unhelpful.

Such measures represent early efforts to reconcile traditional ad agency staffing models with AI.

There are signs that AI is provoking some marketers to rethink their jobs. Freelance programmatic and strategy consultants have become avid users of the technology, while the Wall Street Journal recently reported a rise in companies employing marketing ‘engineers’, whose expertise was augmented by AI tooling.

Agencies, however, are only just now beginning to seriously consider how teams might be organised differently. That isn’t itself unusual — it took roughly forty years for factory owners to take advantage of the productivity gains offered by electric light.

Agencies won’t take as long as that to begin dialing in AI gains into team structures. Wilensky suggested that senior talent would be required to inject originality and a willingness to push the envelope into agency outputs.

“AI cannot take risks. That’s always going to be our job. AI is not creative. That’s always going to be our job. So no matter what level you are in your career, there’s opportunity to be strategic, to be creative, to take risks, to test,” she said.

Early career options, she added, may instead become focused on quality assurance or maintaining the fences agencies build to prevent AI agents from going rogue.

“We don’t have this role today, but there will be a fulltime job of AI checkers. That’s my premonition,” said Wilensky. “That’s going to be a career that our kids will do when they are older – there’ll be AI checkers in the same way that people in journalism used to be like fact checkers.”

#7458. Ben Cohen Goes Guerrilla In His Next Push to Free Ben & Jerry’s

In April, Ben Cohen flew to Amsterdam in hopes of handing Magnum Ice Cream Company CEO Peter ter Kulve a 100,000-signature petition asking him to sell off Ben & Jerry’s, the brand he cofounded with Jerry Greenfield in 1978.

Security wouldn’t let him past the lobby.

Undeterred, Cohen is now back in Vermont, preparing the next salvo in his fight to wrest Ben & Jerry’s from the hands of a publicly traded company. While he won’t be going to Amsterdam this time, a battalion of 200 anthropomorphic, miniature pints of ice cream will go instead.

#7455. Media Buying Briefing: Overheard at Media Buying Summit: How AI is helping and hurting client relations and office work

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This article is part of Digiday’s coverage of its Digiday Media Buying Summit. More from the series →

Despite the headlong rush by virtually everyone in marketing and media to adopt AI tools and technology — from sophisticated agentic planning and measurement aids to things as ordinary as using an LLM to help write emails — the agency side at least finds itself leaning over its proverbial skis just a bit.

That’s one of the biggest takeaways from the two townhall sessions at last week’s fall Media Buying Summit in Newport Beach, Calif. As you know, the townhalls are held under Chatham House rules, which offer anonymity in exchange for candor when the agency-only group met to discuss their biggest challenges (and some solutions) in their jobs.

The following are direct quotes from the attendees, but have been lightly edited for space and clarity.

“We see a lot of our clients with thinner budgets, but expecting the world. And we go over hours quite a bit because they just ask for more things than are in the plan. We have to pull back sometimes and level set, but it still gets hard when the clients just expect so much.”

“It comes down to the brief. I’ve seen some of the worst briefs I’ve ever seen in my career recently, and it’s because they’re so disjointed and there’s no through line on what the not only the marketing goal is as well as the business goal … I think AI is making it worse. It’s like pontificating on a sentence structure that makes it 10 pages long instead of a sentence. And less is more when it comes to a brief. In that case, especially when you’re trying to drive down to your goals.”

“Yeah, briefs have definitely gotten worse, and they’re also like jam packed with a lot of things that feel like they start to blur together the swim lanes between what media’s job is versus a creative job or a PR driven job.”

“We’ve had living briefs of sorts. You fill out the questions first, and we have the follow up meeting, and we go through it to make sure we really understand what you think you’re putting in there. A lot of folks have those meetings after the fact, but if they are being bad clients and they’re doing things that they shouldn’t, then maybe it’s a way to circumvent that, get ahead of it before you get this word vomit brief that doesn’t mean anything.”

“We’ve just written the briefs for the clients … they give us their things and we say we’re just going to write this for you, and we write it. They’re like, ‘This is great,’ And our team also thinks this is great because our team just wrote it.”

“I’ve actually been surprised by how much AI content [there is at] a higher strategy level … places like the VPs and the C-suite. I know they know how to do these things. I don’t think they want to take the time to do it. Because this is much easier.”

“I’ve been getting more and more that even with our higher ups at the agency themselves because of that same mentality.” But we’re seeing the same thing from clients too that give us a generated prompt of what they think that they need.”

“I’ve been in meetings where I can tell every person who contributed to that meeting, it’s all AI generated slides where I’m like, ‘You’ve provided the bare minimum information and it just spit these out — you didn’t even look at them. You just threw them up there.’ It kind of has that uncanny valley feeling — they think this makes sense, but it doesn’t make sense. It’s very prevalent, probably more than we actually realize.”

“If they use it to write a quick email or to organize their thoughts, I don’t see any shame in that. But I think there’s probably a deeper level of generation happening that is leading to this output where this is a mess. This is not clear. This doesn’t feel human.”

“We actually had a client who had somebody else write a brief for them, and it was clearly written with AI. And you could tell the client didn’t have any idea what was in it because we went back to the client [and said] ‘Half of this stuff is not doable.’ It was 18 pages long. It was it was a lot.”

“If you’ve got a super long email with 50 m dashes in it, maybe call the person back and ask what they want to do, versus responding to it and having your team run around for a week trying to write the right response with 60 m dashes back. I think we should do a better job as agency leaders to train our staff to interact with the clients in a way that is personal versus just responding to back and forth emails.”

“There’s two forks in the road for the world of agencies. One fork is, ‘I’m going to fully automate everything and eliminate as many humans and costs as possible.’ The other fork in the road is, ‘I’m going to create efficiency and enable the humans I already have, and lean into expertise and make those experts more efficient at what they do, so they can deliver more value for clients.’ So, if I was working at an organization that’s going for full automation and limiting humans, I would be scared. I would argue that’s not the right strategy.”

“I tell our staff, ‘Do your resume every six months, and if you’re not learning stuff here, advancing your skill sets, you should quit and go work someplace else.’ Because you have these people that have been at agencies for 10 or 15 or 20 years. That is not the way to evolve your business and or help your clients grow. So if we’re not pushing the staff to learn new things and keep the sort of ship afloat, you’re going to have these issues where an AI bot spends $10 million versus $10,000 in a DSP, and it’s going to be like, I don’t know what to do.”

Few topics are as deeply divisive as principal media. Which is why Digiday used it to launch a new franchise at the Media Buying Summit last week: The Case For and Against.

Stagwell’s purchase of Freestar marks an expansion of the agency’s owned media practice — and provides a decent jumping off point to rehearse some of the pro and anti arguments around agencies deploying client ad spend agains owned, principal or proprietary media.

Onstage at the summit, Forrester vp and senior agency analyst Jay Pattisall argued for the practice’s use, against Crossmedia co-founder and CEO Kamran Asghar, who took the opposing view.

Pattisall said that principal media was an established way of doing business for large agencies, one that could be handled fairly in the client’s interests, provided agencies disclosed its use and provided opt-outs for skeptical clients.

“It’s here, it’s not going anywhere… so if you’re going to do it, do it well,” he said. Moreover, Pattisall said principal media could provide a release valve for agencies suffering margin compression, publishers struggling to evenly monetize inventory, and clients looking for flexibility in their media investments. “You’re getting a win-win-win,” he said.

Asghar, in contrast, said principal based media trading eroded marketing services groups’ roles as agents — and it barred agencies from meeting demand from marketers for a pricing model or relationship that rewards meeting business outcomes.

“We’ll never get to outcome-based pricing in our industry as long as principal media exists, because a revenue model of taking a kickback or a volume bonus far outweighs anything you’re going to ever earn on an outcome-based basis,” he said.

Asghar argued that if agencies are to engage in principal-based media, they should take a leaf from the financial sector’s book: separate trading and advisory  businesses properly, so that clients opting out of principal media can ensure they’re dealing with an honest broker. “There needs to be clear separation between church and state, in my mind,” he said.

“Where there’s murkiness, there’s money to be made,” he added. — Sam Bradley

Whether it’s avid fandom or long-held nostalgia, viewers with an emotional connection to a movie or a streaming series make for a fertile advertising audience, according to a report from Disney’s U.K. arm. The House of Mouse surveyed 1,100 streaming users and measured their engagement levels in an eye-tracking study, as well as a brand lift study. The bottom line? Fandom means a hyper-engaged audience:

“I think what’s driving changes in marketing expenditure is not a bad economy. It’s a good economy. I think change is being driven by technological revolution, not not by economic devolution … in our segment growth, we’re up 23% in digital transformation. We’re up 100% in the marketing cloud. If you project out growth in those two segments for the next two years, we become a fundamentally revalued company, more of a tech and tech services company.”

#7454. Amazon says more than 400M customers have used Alexa for Shopping in the last 12 months

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This story was first published by Digiday sibling Modern Retail.

During its fiscal third-quarter earnings call on Thursday, Amazon shed more light on how its conversational AI shopping assistant, Alexa for Shopping, is powering more transactions.

More than 400 million customers have now used Alexa for Shopping in the last 12 months, up from 350 million at the end of July. Meanwhile, customers who use Alexa for Shopping are spending 50% more than those who don’t, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said during the company’s earnings call on last Thursday.

The figures represent how AI shopping has become a powerful growth lever for Amazon and a way to nudge shoppers toward more sales, especially in a time when the business has matured and growth in other areas is harder to come by.

On Thursday, Amazon reported that net sales for the third quarter came in at $201.9 billion, up 12% from last year. The bulk of that came from Amazon Web Services, or AWS, which reported segment sales up 39% year over year.

Growth in many of Amazon’s e-commerce-related segments slowed during the quarter. However, much of that was because Prime Day was held at the end of June this year, rather than in mid-July. As a result, Amazon recorded the sales growth from Prime Day in the second quarter; last year, it was recorded in the third quarter.

Online Stores revenue was up 2% year over year. Last year, during the third quarter, Amazon reported that online Stores revenue grew 10% between the third quarter of 2024 and 2025.

Similarly, third-party seller services and advertising services grew 12% and 24%, respectively, between the third quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2025. By contrast, between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, they grew 9% and 11%, respectively.

The public-facing history of Alexa for Shopping goes back three years. In February 2024, Amazon released an AI shopping assistant that was then known as Rufus. In May of this year, Amazon rebranded Rufus to Alexa for Shopping, choosing to adopt the name of its conversational voice assistant many shoppers were already used to.

Since then, Amazon has made Alexa for Shopping more visible on its website and app, and added new capabilities.

Amazon has made headlines for its walled-garden approach to AI, as it has blocked platforms like ChatGPT and Meta’s Muse shopping agent from scraping its site.

Jassy hinted during Thursday’s earnings call that that may eventually change — which he has said before — but ultimately, he said, the company wants to push as many customers to Alexa for Shopping as possible.

“Though we anticipate working with horizontal agents, we believe Alexa for Shopping is going to be the primary shopping agent customers use to shop Amazon,” Jassy said.

#7451. Google search loses its free pass with buyers

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

For the better part of two decades, Google search was the line item media buyers rarely had to defend. AI Overviews complicated that. Google now answers more queries on the results page itself, which changes how often people click through to an advertiser and what each click is worth.

That, in turn, means fewer prime ad slots around the search results people see, and Google’s automated buying tools, now the default for most campaigns, are quick to pay up for the ones that remain. Q4 makes it worse as seasonal advertisers bid up CPCs in the quarter that matters most.

Nearly a month into that quarter, advertisers want to know what all that extra spend is buying. Across conversations with 18 media buyers, Digiday found clients putting Google through the kind of scrutiny usually saved for newer channels.

“We’re having to look much more closely at what happens after the click and whether those clicks are actually producing qualified leads and revenue,” said Lindsay Marty, founder of Above the Bar Marketing.

That’s left her clients increasingly open to shifting a portion of their Google search budgets into channels including Meta and Local Services Ads if performance weakens. Marty added: “The amount being questioned is generally around 10% to 20% of the Google budget when that conversation comes up.”

Google’s own numbers point the same way. Search ad revenue grew 12% in the third quarter, Alphabet’s slowest pace this year, and executives blamed part of the slowdown on AI Mode — Google’s chatbot-style search tab.

The numbers are part of a bigger shift in how people use the internet. More of them are handing the search, and sometimes the purchase itself, to AI agents, and the money underneath the web is starting to follow. Where it lands is anyone’s guess. Advertisers and their agencies are having to place their bets now.

Take Bryce Hamlin, vp of data intelligence at Power Digital. He said media mix modelling and geo-testing were showing a greater impact from upper-funnel media and less from search. Dollars tend to follow whatever the models credit.

“Google search ads are still very powerful, but in the next two-to-three years, we will see a lot of searches happen off of Google because of LLMs,” he said. “We’re already seeing the beginning of this trend.”

Hamlin said the growing use of marketing science, AI and incremental measurement is also prompting advertisers to question whether some of their Google search budget would work harder elsewhere.

“An increasing number of marketers are asking, ‘is a portion of my budget better spent elsewhere’ — to the tune of 10% to 30% of the Google search budget getting reallocated,” he added.

Accuracast’s group CEO Farhad Divecha said the percentage within the Google budgets being questioned by his team’s clients is about 10% for now, but given the dynamic and competitive nature of Black Friday and  Cyber Monday, this could change to as much as 20% to 30% quite rapidly.

The size of those budgets vary, though search remains one of the biggest lines in most media plans. It took $114.2 billion of U.S. digital ad spending last year, or 38.8% of the total, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau and PricewaterhouseCoopers. For mid-sized and larger advertisers that employ agencies, a Google search budget can run from tens of thousands of dollars a month into the millions.

Branded keyword CPCs rose 5% in the third quarter, roughly in line with non-branded terms, according to Michelle Merklin, vp of search at Tinuiti.

“CPCs keep rising,” she continued, though she’s keeping a closer eye on how much search there is to buy. Impressions and clicks climbed over the same period, which leaves advertisers paying a bit more for a bigger pool of demand.

Some buyers have done the math on that trade and don’t like the answer.

“It’s not just traffic, but also the ROI from Google that’s been squeezed in recent years, making it less attractive as a channel,” said Divecha. “We definitely see advertisers looking at other options to invest budgets in, especially ChatGPT.”

He said Accuracast’s clients are looking at alternatives and could move money away from Google if click volumes began to dip. Some execs are finding that channels outside search play a greater role in driving conversions than traditional attribution models suggest. The agency’s AI-led campaign management platform, Unyte.AI, for example, automatically reallocates budget away from Google when returns weaken, shifting spend to other platforms delivering incremental conversions at a better return on investment, Divecha explained.

More of that money is landing on Meta and TikTok, where advertisers are trying to build awareness and consideration earlier in the funnel. According to Merklin, some advertisers were reallocating budgets from less efficient parts of search, including campaigns targeting competitors’ keywords or “conquesting.” But she said most advertisers managed by Tinuiti were seeking incremental budget or reallocating spend from elsewhere, rather than cutting search to fund upper-funnel activity; the trend contributed to a 16% rise in Facebook ad spend among Tinuiti’s U.S. clients in the third quarter.

“You have to create the demand before it can be captured,” she explained. “There’s been a shift recently into the mid and upper funnel in order to produce more brand search volume.”

That shift doesn’t necessarily mean advertisers are abandoning search altogether. Some see paid search as increasingly important as organic traffic comes under pressure.

“It’s only [becoming] more important to be in that paid space because organic search traffic is being impacted,” said Casey Sheehan, vp, group director at RPA.

That said, fewer buyers treat it as the bedrock of a media plan.

“What’s coming up more in client conversations is the need to be present earlier in the discovery journey,” said Mark Byrne, director of paid media at Brave Bison. “Google search remains strong at capturing existing demand, while paid social and YouTube help build awareness and consideration before someone actively searches.”

It’s a rethink that reaches all the way down to the search results page, where paid and organic listings now get judged together. Byrne said advertisers were looking more closely at where they needed to bid to capture valuable traffic, and where they could pull back, weighing the combined impact on revenue, return on ad spend and cost per acquisition.

“From our perspective the most effective strategy is to have a really strong presence in your organic AI citations, and then also a strong paid search presence,” said Wpromote’s head of paid search Valerie Dorer.

On that basis, what’s happening to search ad spending is arguably to be expected as Google’s ads business adjusts around however people are going to access and share information moving forward. Indeed, ads in AI Mode are already expanding to new markets in Brazil, Mexico, and the United Kingdom while it is also scaling the ads already present in markets like Australia, Canada, India and Kenya.

Victor Batista, global search lead at Jellyfish, put a finer point on it. He said clients were not reducing their overall Google spend “in a targeted manner”. Instead, the “Google ecosystem is expanding its footprint in discussions as the AI experience is enhanced and more widely understood,” he added.

Clients are, in other words, identifying opportunities to shift spending from traditional keyword-based search campaigns to AI-powered alternatives such as AI Max and Performance Max, while also increasing investment in YouTube and Demand Gen. Overall, Batista said, budget diversification remained “generally contained within the Google ecosystem.”

Google remains a major channel for capturing existing demand, particularly when consumers are actively searching for products or services. But as search behavior changes and advertisers take a closer look at which channels are driving incremental returns, Google is facing greater scrutiny over its place in clients’ media plans.

“The incremental 10% to 20% is becoming less automatic,” said Marty. “Advertisers increasingly want Google to prove that spend is still the best use of those dollars.”

In response to this article, a Google spokesperson said: “Every day, millions of businesses choose Search Ads to drive growth. AI Overviews create new opportunities for brands to be discovered and help shoppers make more confident decisions. As Search becomes more conversational, our AI-powered campaigns help advertisers capture these new opportunities, while keeping them firmly in control.”

#7450. Hollywood’s King of Culture Is Building a Billion-Dollar Entertainment Empire

Charles D. King may not be a household name like Steven Spielberg, Alfred Hitchcock, and Walt Disney. But in Hollywood, he operates in the same echelon.

King joined these luminaries at the top of his industry as the recipient of the Producers Guild of America Milestone Award in 2024, recognizing his “immeasurable contribution to the film industry” as the founder of multi-platform media company Macro, dedicated to bringing BIPOC stories to life.

But it wasn’t until 2025 that King’s Hollywood clout came to bear on a deal unprecedented in Tinseltown history.

The Warner Bros. horror thriller Sinners, written and directed by Ryan Coogler, took in $279.7 million domestically, according to Box Office Mojo, making it the seventh highest-grossing movie of the year—and the only one in the top 10 not based on a popular IP.

Arguably, however, the most groundbreaking part of the film happened behind the scenes. King was part of the team—along with Coogler’s agent at William Morris Endeavor, Craig Kestel; his attorney Jonathan Gardner; and WME COO Dan Limerick—that negotiated the deal giving Coogler final cut, first-dollar gross participation, and ownership of the film’s rights after 25 years.

“We knew Sinners was going to be special,” King told ADWEEK. “The ownership deal was well earned given Ryan’s extraordinary track record and is in alignment with deal precedent for a select number of very accomplished filmmakers.”

He added: “I hope this deal serves as a reminder to Hollywood and beyond of the enormous potential upside of partnering with extraordinary storytellers and original voices.”

Trailblazing seems to be in King’s DNA. Years earlier, he became the first Black partner at Hollywood powerhouse agency WME in its over 100-year history—and the first at any major Hollywood talent firm.

Now, King is focused on scaling his own entertainment empire with Macro. Founded in 2015, the film, TV, and digital content studio has grown to include a talent representation arm, M88, and a creative agency, Brand Macro. This past September, Macro acquired the streaming platform Allblk from AMC Global Media to further its distribution and storytelling ambitions.

His goal is to build Macro into a billion-dollar company through culture-shaping work that uplifts underrepresented voices. That mission has produced lauded films such as Judas and the Black Messiah, Fences, and Sorry to Bother You, but “impact can be measured in a lot of ways,” he noted.

“There’s the careers that we’ve launched by financing films by first-time filmmakers,” King said. “We’ve had productions where we’re making sure there’s diversity and a range of folks hired as part of our crews. There’s the make-up of the creatives of our company and everyone that we partner with, which is extraordinarily diverse.”

King has been living by that ethos long before it took shape as Macro. Coogler, who became the first Black winner of the Best Original Screenplay Oscar for Sinners (not to mention directing Marvel’s Black Panther franchise), met King in 2012 and remembers his strong influence at Hollywood’s ground level as an agent.

“He made sure our voices were heard in those agency hallways, advocating for the value of Black filmmakers and the value of Black stories,” Coogler told ADWEEK.

As CEO of Macro, King’s ability to bring financing “makes all the difference in the world” when it comes to getting projects greenlit, Coogler added, as does his business savvy acquired from years of experience. “Just him having so much earned knowledge from his position as an agent and his position as a producer and financier and being able to share his business strategy with like-minded folks has been such a great tool to have,” Coogler said.

“And it’s been a joy to watch them build community through the work that Stacey [Walker King, chief brand officer of Macro and King’s wife] does,” he added.

Walker King also runs Brand Macro, the company’s marketing agency. In addition to working with brands, Brand Macro also focuses on building community through events that bring together Black and POC talent, such as Macro Lodge at the Sundance Film Festival and the Macro HBCU Summit, which connected students interested in entertainment with industry insiders.

For his work in elevating, financing, and championing diverse creative talent, Charles D. King is the recipient of the Adcolor | ADWEEK 2027 Beacon Award.

“I feel incredibly blessed that a vision I had more than three decades ago has grown into something that resonates so deeply with people—not just Black filmmakers, but Latino, Asian, LGBTQ+, and white storytellers who feel that the traditional system hasn’t made room for the stories they want to tell,” King said. “I think one of the most powerful things we’ve built is belief. Belief in what’s possible.”

After King graduated from Howard University’s School of Law in 1996, he moved to Hollywood to set out on the path that would lead to Macro. But King remembers the vision for the company starting much earlier.

Growing up in Decatur, Ga., King got his first taste of entrepreneurship watching his father, a physician, start and build a medical practice.

He also experienced firsthand the power of representation in entertainment. On the television drama L.A. Law, he idolized Blair Underwood’s portrayal of the “charismatic” and “intelligent” Black law firm associate Jonathan Rollins.

“There was the power of content and [seeing] an aspirational person,” King said. “I saw myself in this person and thought, ‘I could be like that guy one day.’” King has since worked with Underwood on two Macro projects, the 2020 film Really Love and the upcoming Netflix romantic drama Don’t Ever Wonder. “It’s such a beautiful, full-circle moment,” he said.

But his path shifted between his sophomore and junior years at Howard. While working a summer job at MTV in New York, a lawyer told King he’d make “a good lawyer—but a great agent.”

When King graduated, he inked his vision in the Howard Law commemoration book. Asked what he’ll be doing in 10 years, King wrote: “Be at the helm of a diversified entertainment and media company.”

Despite his mother being a writer and a poet, King never wanted to be a creative force himself. Instead, he realized early on that he had a talent for seeing potential in others, and leveraged this to immense success as an agent. He signed multi-hyphenates like Coogler and Tyler Perry, the filmmaker and actor behind the Madea franchise, before they became household names.

When King keys into what he looks for in people, he names qualities like vision, ambition, and brilliance. “I would also say authenticity,” he added. “People who authentically know who they are as artists and as people, and you see that throughline in everything that they touch.”

Investing in people with a strong point of view has brought industry accolades as well. The 93rd Academy Awards nominated Macro’s historical drama Judas and the Black Messiah for six Oscars, making King, Coogler, and Shaka King (no relation) the first all-Black producing team to be up for Best Picture. (The film ultimately won two Oscars: Best Supporting Actor for Daniel Kaluuya and Best Original Song.)

“That experience—I’ll take it with me forever,” King said. “That movie meant so much to all of us. Everyone on that movie is bonded for life. To really be in it as a producer, and to then get the blessing of being the first film from an all-Black producer unit to get an Oscar nomination, was just truly icing on the cake.”

King says his ability to connect with people from different backgrounds is “just part of who I am.” He remembers being “really small and skinny” before having a growth spurt in high school, enabling him to relate to people who were “not necessarily as accepted socially.”

“I’m more inclined in that direction, as opposed to being someone who only wants to talk to who’s in the ‘in crowd,’” he said. “I’m going to interface with people who I think are intelligent and talented, and who I enjoy spending time with.”

When he started in the mailroom at what was then William Morris Agency, he was the only Black trainee and worked hard to “build the bottom of my pyramid” through relationships.

“I was dropped into a pot of gold to understand this industry from the ground floor up,” King said. “I recognized the uniqueness of the opportunity, and I cultivated and built relationships with everyone,” from his fellow mailroom trainees to assistants at other agencies and young executives just getting their start.

Now, at Macro, he’s reached the top of his proverbial pyramid, able to build community the way he wants. He estimates between 350 and 400 interns have come through Macro since its founding, several of whom have gone on to become “executives at every one of the major talent agencies.” Macro alumni have also won Emmys, and sit in the C-suites of companies around Hollywood. Among them is Mark Wright, vice president of film and TV at Higher Ground, the production studio of Barack and Michelle Obama.

For King, a major part of turning out future executives is fostering a culture of collaboration at the beginning of their careers: “Everyone at our company has a voice, and great ideas can come from anywhere.”

King launched Macro during the production boom of the Peak TV era in the mid-2010s. According to the New York Times, the number of TV shows in the U.S. jumped 52% in about six years, from 349 in 2013 to 532 in 2019. During that time, studios also implemented DEI policies in response to campaigns such as 2015’s #OscarsSoWhite, creating a robust pipeline for diverse talent and projects.

Seven years later, Hollywood is undergoing massive shifts, from how shows are produced to consolidation among the major studios. The number of TV shows and feature films being made has dropped significantly. In October, Paramount Skydance closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Studios. And new forms of content, like made-for-social microdramas, are cutting into audience share.

But King continues to rely on what’s gotten him this far: faith, relationships, and his deep knowledge of people and the industry.

And in some ways, these shifts have provided unprecedented leverage for the people who can break through the noise. In March, Macro announced a multi-year first-look, co-financing, and distribution deal with Sony Pictures.

The acquisition of streaming platform Allblk, founded by BET’s Bob Johnson in 2014, gives Macro a direct distribution channel and a closer relationship with its audience.

“I have been looking at Allblk for 12 years,” King said. “We think that having ownership of this platform will serve our business well as potentially a provider of content. But, more broadly, it’s a larger market opportunity that we saw needed to be unlocked.”

And there could be more deals to come, with King considering acquiring assets being “spun out” from consolidating media giants and pushing further into producing live events.

He also recognizes AI as a tool for efficiency and the “democratization of opportunity,” with creators being able to build their own audiences. But he made clear that AI should “never replace real storytelling, writing, and acting,” and that protecting intellectual property is a priority.

“Our vision forward will continue to be to assess the marketplace and adapt,” King said. “That’s one of the benefits of being a smaller, more nimble institution, as opposed to a much larger institution where it’s harder to pivot and maneuver. We’ve had to make adjustments like every thoughtful company, making sure we’re right-sizing our organization for future growth, and for where the market is headed.”

According to Coogler, “change seems to be the law” of Hollywood, but King is well positioned to succeed.

“From what I’ve seen, people who can be both patient but can also act fearlessly, and people who have good taste and great relationships with talent, seem to always be able to make the moments of transition work best for themselves,” Coogler said. “And Charles is both of those things.”

Whatever the future holds, King lives by a piece of advice from his grandmother: “Go out there and be yourself.” He credits staying true to his principles and vision with guiding him from the agency mailroom to starting Macro and becoming an Oscar-nominated producer.

“I’m just Charles King,” he said. “I’m not changing who I am. And I’ve tried my best to operate with that same compass and treating people the way I would want to be treated.”

“He has a great heart,” Coogler added. “It’s very rare to find somebody who is this talented at business but who’s a good person at the core.”

Richard Lowe is a freelance writer based in Los Angeles.

#7449. Giggly Squad’s SiriusXM deal signals a shift from podcast networks to creator ecosystems

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Last month, SiriusXM signed a multi-year deal with creators Paige DeSorbo and Hannah Berner for their Giggly Squad podcast reportedly valued at $160 million. Weeks later, the duo sold out four different nights for a live podcast tour at Madison Square Garden. That unprecedented deal signals a broader shift in podcasting: platforms are competing for creator-led businesses, not just shows.

“It’s even caught us on our heels, honestly, the demand for Giggly,” said Kelli Hurley, vp and head of content and podcast partnership at SiriusXM. “We were prepared, we were all hands on deck, but it has been just unprecedented in terms of what we’re seeing from the marketplace.”

Tom Webster, partner at trade association Sounds Profitable, said that despite podcast reach remaining flat since 2024, 8% of people who have consumed a podcast say they started in just the last 30 days. That’s a steady influx of new customers, and platforms like Spotify, Apple, and SiriusXM are trying to court them.

SiriusXM svp of podcast content Adam Sachs started working in podcasting 15 years ago, and he’s had a bird’s-eye view of the shifting landscape.

“The power of the network was what mattered [back then]. We would have these horizontal networks with a bunch of different shows in the network that all shared a sensibility,” he explained. “Now the approach is way more verticalized. We’re working with specific talent as opposed to a specific network, and helping them build a vertical ecosystem where their fans can engage. It’s sort of flipped.”

Building those vertical ecosystems can involve simple, expected things like helping a creator with their AV setup to far-reaching, off-platform support that includes IRL events.

“When we’re making these deals, we are increasingly thinking about a podcast as audio, video, social, and live. It’s those four legs of the stool, and we want to be a part of all of it,” said Sachs.

SiriusXM isn’t the only platform looking to work with creators beyond just hosting their show. Bryan Barletta, partner at Sounds Profitable and president of Podcast Movement, said Amazon’s investment in the NFL brother duo podcast, New Heights, signals a major shift in the partnership dynamic.

“We’re entering a new phase of podcasting where a distinct upper tier of creators is emerging, with significant separation from those coming up behind them,” he said.

The top tier of podcasting is drawing live audiences at arena scale. Giggly Squad is the first female-hosted podcast to headline Madison Square Garden, and tickets that averaged in the mid-$100s sold out fast. The sheer scope of the Giggly deal led Sirius to take a step back, according to Hurley. “In the past couple of weeks we took a total pause…we’ve got to do a full reset in how we want to go to market with this asset,” she said.

And brands are increasingly looking to get involved at multiple points in a creator podcast’s presence, from branded equipment to distribution support to showing up at IRL events. Now, more brands are heading into partnership talks wanting to “buy a creator,” according to Hurley. They’re asking for exclusivity, but Sirius wants to give them more.

“[We want] to be a one-stop shop,” she said.

Other platforms are offering a variety of ways for creators to connect with brands. Substack recently launched early access signups for dynamic ad insertion and plans for creators to leverage programmatic sponsorships in early 2027. Beehiiv just launched similar tools, dropping dynamic ad insertion, campaign management, and programmatic access just this past week.

“It gives creators more flexibility: run their own sponsor campaigns, put current ads into older episodes, and open unsold spots to programmatic demand when there’s a match,” said Ainsley Rossitto, head of podcast at beehiiv.

Since the mid-2020s, podcasts have aggressively pivoted to video. Sounds Profitable reports that now, only 17% of Americans expect a podcast to be audio-only. Substack’s head of video, Zach Taylor, told Digiday that half of their 350 highest revenue creators were using both audio in video in April 2024. “By February 2025, that number had grown to 82%,” he said.

The inclusion of a video component for podcasts makes it easier for discovery, as show clips can circulate on other social media platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram.

“Your podcast doesn’t have to be on video, but you have to have video,” said Barletta. Sounds Profitable’s research showed 84% of podcast clip consumers say clips led them to become regular podcast listeners at least sometimes.

Sachs said SiriusXM is seeing algorithmic growth through YouTube because of its built-in discoverability.

There are new pivots on the horizon: short-form content and a return to traditional radio. Sachs said Sirius is looking to do more with creators who are short-form-only content (monetizing their content, empowering them to do live events, and maybe even getting them on the radio), and are also supporting podcasters like Giggly Squad in creating their own radio shows — all in service of grabbing bigger slices of that audience pie.

“The radio audience is very distinct from the podcast audience; it’s a really disparate audience in terms of demographics, so we don’t see that as cannibalization at all. We see it as incremental reach,” Sachs said. “Giggly Squad is going to have a significant radio component, as well.”

#7448. People Inc. is building custom APIs to make its journalism easier for AI agents to use

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

People Inc. is moving toward custom APIs to help AI agents access its content more efficiently.

Rather than making AI systems shift through full webpages, People Inc., is giving them the article text and key details in a simpler format, according to Jon Roberts, People Inc.’s chief innovation officer.

“If you are an agent and you’re reading an HTML page, 90% of the content is junk meant for a browser to read, not an agent,” Roberts told delegates at Digiday’s Media Strategies London event. “It will really distract the agent, and it will be incredibly expensive to process all these tokens that it doesn’t need.”

The custom APIs strip out that extra material, sending the article text in Markdown along with details such as who wrote it and when it was published or updated and other “trust signals that matter.” The move comes as People Inc. shifts its broader investment priorities: the company laid off about 6% of its workforce last week. The cuts underscore the pressure on publishers to find durable businesses as AI reshapes how audiences discover and access journalism.

People Inc. first gave partners access to its content through web crawling, then through Amazon S3 buckets, which let the company send updates and retract content. It is now moving toward custom APIs, Roberts said, because crawling is an inefficient way for AI systems to get information.

Strategically, that could make access more efficient and give People Inc. greater control over how its journalism is delivered to AI partners.

“Every token that needs to be processed is expensive,” said Roberts. “If you throw it the entire HTML header, that’s abuse. Right, that’s not reasonable.”

AI companies are beginning to recognize the importance of knowing when publishers created or updated content, Roberts said. People Inc. is building those details into its content for its own AI tools, then using what it learns to offer AI partners a more useful way to access that material. The publisher is not focused on advertising directly to AI agents, he added.

The urgency comes as traffic from AI agents and agentic browsers grew 7,851% year over year, according to HUMAN’s 2026 State of AI Traffic report.

The challenge is already pressing for publishers trying to distinguish useful, customer-led agents from bots scraping content. “We need to act quickly on it because it’s not going to be something in the future — it’s happening now,” Daily Mail director of SEO and editorial commerce Carly Steven said at Digiday’s Media Strategies London event. “So that is a fairly urgent need that we all need to address and get our heads around,” she added.

Publishers are testing different ways to adapt their content and services for AI systems. People Inc. is moving toward structured access for AI partners. The Economist is experimenting with making marketing and B2B sales material outside of its paywall more easily readable for agents. Time has also converted its pages from HTML to Markdown and has even started to sell ads to those agents visiting its site.

Alongside figuring out which automated requests to allow, publishers are experimenting with how to package their journalism for AI systems. Forbes is also testing how to make some content more usable by AI agents. For its Vetted product reviews, the publisher has created Markdown versions of its content and an “MCP layer” while exploring separate presentations for booths and human readers.

Nina Gould, Forbes’ chief innovation officer, said the approach could help the publisher reach people using AI tools, but emphasized that the strategy is still developing a planned ChatGPT product-recommendation plugin that has not yet gone live. “On something like ads for agents, we’re still working on that,” she added.

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

As Fingerprint scales with large enterprise customers in financial services and fraud prevention, we're investing in application security as a dedicated, first-class discipline. We're looking for a Senior Manager, Application Security to lead that investment, reporting directly to the VP of Engineering. You will personally own and build the AppSec program, and you will also manage a small team of experienced practitioners who run IT operations and compliance.

This is a VP-direct role with high autonomy and high visibility. Enterprise customers regularly ask about Fingerprint's security posture. You'll be the person who owns that answer.

Cross-functional Leadership & Communication

This role is AppSec-first with a management scope that spans IT and compliance. That shape is deliberate. Application security is where we're investing next, and we want someone who can personally build it — not just oversee it. At the same time, IT and compliance are already run by experienced practitioners who don't need a domain expert over them; they need a leader who gives them direction, context, and prioritization.

What this means in practice: you will be hands-on in AppSec and hands-off-but-accountable in IT and compliance. We don't expect you to arrive as an expert in IT operations or GRC. We do expect you to learn those domains quickly — well enough within your first few months to evaluate your team's work, make prioritization calls across all three disciplines, and represent each of them credibly to leadership and customers. The judgment to know when to rely on your team vs. when to drive the decision yourself is what distinguishes the right candidate.

This is a role for someone who is still a strong practitioner in AppSec and has grown into leading people — not for someone who has moved entirely out of technical work, and not for a pure individual contributor who hasn't managed before.

At Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team.  Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.

#7445. How political creators are juggling platforms to find the three Rs: reach, revenue and rules

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Political creators need platforms that can deliver reach, revenue and clear rules. But no single platform reliably provides all three: YouTube offers ad revenue, Instagram can deliver huge audiences without paying creators and TikTok’s moderation and engagement can be unpredictable.

“A good platform for a political creator does four things,” said Ryan Schram, executive director of the Center for the Creator Economy at Syracuse University. “It helps new audiences find your work, it pays you fairly for that work, it tells you clearly what the rules are, and it lets you keep your relationship with your audience if you leave. Most platforms do one or two of those well. Very few do all four.”

Schram said that political creators gravitate to where political conversations are already happening, noting a 2024 PEW Research study that found that 85 percent of the most-followed news influencers are on X, half are on Instagram, and 44 percent are on YouTube.

“Journalists, campaigns, and elected officials are on X, and its users come for news. The catch is that creators and audiences aren’t in the same places,” Scharm said. “Audiences are larger on YouTube and Facebook, so the most successful political creators publish on several platforms rather than relying on one.”

Ahead of particularly contentious U.S. midterm elections, influencers are shaping narratives and highlighting key issues. Digiday spoke with six political creators and Schram about which platforms they are finding most fruitful, and which they’re struggling with.

YouTube remains a mainstay for many news and politics creators. “YouTube has the largest news audience and pays the most,” said Scharm. “It’s paid out more than $100 billion over four years and shares 55% of ad revenue.”

As far as the algorithm that drives that revenue, a YouTube spokesperson told Digiday it does “not favor or penalize content based on political orientation.” There are instances where YouTube’s systems “elevate high-quality voices,” like when major breaking news happens and the platform gets a special “breaking news shelf” on the homepage.

YouTube has leaned into news creators over the last few years, with its news, civics and podcast partnerships program, led by Brendan Feldman, offering advice on how to grow and monetize their channels. “For these last few years, a lot of focus has been on the real renaissance of journalists coming to YouTube, many in an independent capacity…and how we can best support them in building really vibrant businesses on our platform, connecting with audiences,” said Feldman.

Creator Aaron Parnas said he focuses on YouTube and Facebook in terms of monetization, though it’s only about 1 percent of his revenue pie.

“YouTube is the platform most worth investing in and also the hardest to grow on,” said V Spehar of Under the Desk News. “But if someone was just starting, I’d say focus on YouTube. It’s the most stable and fairly monetizes – but it’s hard to grow. So you may have to create for YouTube first, and then use clips to build discoverability by posting the clips on all socials until you figure out which social platform you perform best on.”

Several of the creators Digiday spoke with said Instagram has good engagement, but at least one mentioned the platform isn’t a revenue source. “I don’t make a penny because Instagram doesn’t pay out for anything, in terms of Reels. So I make zero money on Instagram, but I had 450 million views last month,” said Parnas, who added he gets much higher viewership on the platform than elsewhere, but frustratingly isn’t earning anything for that elevated engagement.

Newly independent news creator Mark Istook, said he found Instagram to be easier to predict, and the comments are far less “poisonous and toxic” than on sibling Meta-owned platform, Facebook.

The jury is split on Instagram’s utility. While creator Grant Hermes found Instagram might as well be a “black box” in terms of understanding its underlying structure, creator Adam Mockler, however, has figured it out, boasting 90 million views a month on the platform.

Mockler pulls in even more views on Facebook, boasting 120 million on the platform which he called an “underdog” that has been “really swinging lately.”

“I genuinely think Zuckerberg changed something when Trump got into office,” he said. “They opened politics back up on Facebook, and it allowed advertisers to buy up spots on political stuff again.” It’s performing so well, Mockler has doubled down, putting more resources and more team members, he did not offer specifics, on the platform, even hiring an intern that helps post on the platform.

Parnas said he also focuses on Facebook because it, along with YouTue, is where the most revenue comes from.

Mockler also told Digiday he’s leaning into Reddit, a platform notoriously difficult to break through.

“We had a 17-year-old high schooler posting on Reddit for a while…I view Reddit as more valuable than TIkTok right now,” Mockler said, adding about 70 percent of the intern’s role was him posting his appearances on CNN or other traditional news platforms in several subreddits, while the rest was on the official Mockler Media Reddit account, all to get people to engage with his content and find him on other platforms. “I view it as internal PR,” Mockler said.

Spehar and others said TikTok has been a tough platform lately, with inconsistent flagging and engagement hampering their revenue and reach.

“[TikTok] blocks political content or mislabels it as ads and live streams focusing on politics can be falsely reported. Overall it’s hard to get your perspective out if you don’t already have a big channel at this point,” Spehar said, adding the platform is still a good place for creators to build, but is more saturated than it once was.

Parnas placed TikTok on the third rung of his monetization scheme, underneath YouTube and Facebook and alongside Instagram and Istook said the platform should be more reliable when it comes to engagement, but is “all over the map” after it closed a deal with the U.S. earlier this year.

“My views on TikTok have remained very, very consistent over the past year,” said Parnas. Yet just a few days ago, one of his political videos got stuck in an “under review” stage for nearly three hours. “I just took it down,” he said.

Istook said he has the biggest audience on TIkTok but found the platform the least predictable in terms of engagement. “Something will do millions of views, and something else will do 1,500, which just is hard to make sense of with a follower count like I have,” he said.

#7444. Staff Application Security Engineer at Fingerprint

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

Fingerprint's device intelligence platform processes billions of identification events for some of the world's most security-conscious companies — financial institutions, fraud prevention operators, and enterprises that rely on us to stop attackers. That makes our own application security a product feature, not a back-office function: our customers' adversaries are, by definition, motivated to probe what we build.

As we scale with large enterprise customers, we're investing in application security as a dedicated, first-class engineering discipline. Security is already part of how our teams build — scanning in the pipeline, a Cloud Platform team that treats security as a partner, and a mature compliance posture — and we're now standing up a focused AppSec function, led by a Senior Manager, Application Security who owns the program and strategy, to take it to the next level. You will be the founding senior engineer of that function — the person who turns strategy into a working secure SDLC, finds and fixes what matters, and raises the security bar across engineering through technical depth, tooling, and influence.

This is a hands-on Staff role. You will design, build, and operate — not just advise.

Threat Modeling, Security Reviews & Vulnerability Management

Incident Response & Detection (application layer)

This is the senior individual-contributor counterpart to the Senior Manager, Application Security. The manager owns the program, the strategy, and the team; you own the technical depth and the execution. The two roles are designed to work as a pair: you'll bring the findings, the engineering judgment, and the ground truth from inside the codebase, and together you'll decide what to prioritize.

As a Staff engineer, you are expected to operate with a high degree of independence — scoping ambiguous problems, setting technical direction for AppSec, and driving multi-quarter initiatives without needing day-to-day direction. As the founding engineer of a dedicated AppSec function, the patterns, tooling, and standards you establish will be the foundation the practice grows on.

This is not a role for someone who wants to primarily write policy or manage a program from a distance. It's for an engineer who finds real bugs, builds real tooling, and earns the trust of other engineers by making their code better.

At Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team.  Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.
